lessons.title: Using Earth's Resources and Sustainability
lessons.content_html:
Using Earth’s Natural Resources

Humans rely on the Earth’s natural resources to survive and develop. Some of these resources are finite — they will eventually run out because they are being used faster than they can be replaced. Fossil fuels and metal ores are finite resources. Others are renewable, meaning they can be replaced at the same rate they are used, such as timber from managed forests.

Chemistry plays a key role in improving the way we use natural resources. For example, agriculture uses synthetic fertilisers to improve crop yields, and industry develops new materials like polymers and alloys from Earth’s raw materials. The challenge is to do this sustainably — meeting our needs today without preventing future generations from meeting theirs.

Key Fact

Natural resources can be classified as finite (non-renewable — will run out) or renewable (can be replaced). Sustainable development means using resources at a rate that does not compromise future availability.

Potable Water

Potable water is water that is safe to drink. It is not the same as pure water — potable water still contains dissolved substances, but at levels that are not harmful. In the UK, most potable water comes from surface water sources such as rivers and reservoirs.

Making water potable in the UK involves three main stages:

1. Filtration — Water passes through filter beds made of sand and gravel. This removes large particles such as leaves, soil, and debris.

2. Sedimentation — Chemicals are added that cause fine particles to clump together and sink to the bottom, forming a sediment that can be removed.

3. Sterilisation — The water is treated with chlorine, ozone, or ultraviolet light to kill harmful bacteria and other microbes. This makes the water safe to drink.

In some countries where fresh water is scarce, desalination is used to produce potable water from seawater. This can be done by distillation (boiling and condensing) or by reverse osmosis (forcing water through membranes that filter out salt ions). Both methods require large amounts of energy, making desalination expensive.

Waste Water Treatment

Water that has been used in homes, agriculture, and industry becomes waste water. Domestic waste water includes sewage from toilets, sinks, and showers. Industrial and agricultural waste water may contain harmful chemicals, heavy metals, or organic waste.

Waste water must be treated before being released back into the environment to prevent pollution and the spread of disease. Treatment involves several stages:

Screening — Large objects such as rags and plastic are removed using metal grilles.

Sedimentation — The sewage is held in large tanks where solid material settles as sludge. The liquid effluent is separated off.

Anaerobic digestion of sludge — The sludge is broken down by bacteria in the absence of oxygen. This produces biogas (mainly methane), which can be used as a fuel, and a solid residue that can be used as fertiliser.

Aerobic treatment of effluent — The liquid effluent is treated with aerobic bacteria (in the presence of oxygen) to break down remaining organic matter. The treated water is then safe to release into rivers or the sea.

Life Cycle Assessments

A life cycle assessment (LCA) examines the environmental impact of a product at every stage of its life — from “cradle to grave.” This helps companies and consumers make informed choices about which products are more environmentally friendly.

The four stages of an LCA are:

Stage 1

Extracting Raw Materials

Mining ores, drilling for oil, or harvesting crops. Considers energy used, land damage, and water consumption.

Stage 2

Manufacturing & Processing

Turning raw materials into the product. Considers energy input, waste produced, and pollutants released.

Stage 3

Use & Distribution

Transporting the product to consumers and energy used during its lifetime (e.g. fuel for a car, electricity for a phone).

Stage 4

Disposal

What happens at end of life — landfill, incineration, or recycling. Each has a different environmental cost.

Key Fact

LCAs can be subjective — some environmental impacts (like the effect on local wildlife) are difficult to measure and involve value judgements. This means different LCAs of the same product can reach different conclusions depending on what is prioritised.

Reducing Our Impact — The Three Rs

The simplest way to reduce the environmental impact of products is to follow the three Rs: reduce, reuse, recycle. Reducing means using fewer resources in the first place. Reusing means finding new purposes for products instead of discarding them. Recycling means processing waste materials into new products.

Recycling metals is particularly important. Extracting metals from ores requires large amounts of energy (usually from fossil fuels) and produces waste rock and toxic gases. Recycling aluminium, for example, uses only about 5% of the energy needed to extract it from bauxite ore.

Extracting Metals from Low-Grade Ores

As high-grade metal ores become scarce, scientists have developed new methods to extract metals from low-grade ores and even from waste. Two key biological methods are phytomining and bioleaching.

Phytomining: Certain plants are grown on land that contains low concentrations of metal compounds. The plants absorb the metal ions through their roots and accumulate them in their tissues. The plants are then harvested and burned. The ash contains a higher concentration of metal, which can be extracted by smelting or electrolysis.

Bioleaching: Bacteria are used to break down low-grade ores. The bacteria produce an acidic solution called a leachate, which contains dissolved metal compounds. The metal can then be extracted from this solution, often by displacement using a more reactive metal or by electrolysis.

Both methods are slower than traditional mining but are more environmentally friendly because they do not require huge amounts of energy or produce large volumes of waste rock.

Key Fact

Phytomining uses plants to absorb metals from soil; bioleaching uses bacteria to dissolve metals from low-grade ores. Both are sustainable alternatives to traditional mining for extracting copper and other metals.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on this topic often ask you to compare methods (e.g. desalination vs. filtration, phytomining vs. bioleaching) or evaluate the use of LCAs. Remember that LCAs involve subjective judgements — always explain why some data is hard to quantify. For 6-mark extended responses, use a clear structure: state a point, explain the science, then link it to the environmental or economic impact.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Natural resources are either finite (e.g. fossil fuels, ores) or renewable (e.g. timber). Sustainable development means using resources without compromising future supply.
  • Potable water is made safe by filtration, sedimentation, and sterilisation. In water-scarce areas, desalination of seawater is used but requires significant energy.
  • Life cycle assessments analyse a product’s environmental impact from cradle to grave, but some impacts are difficult to measure objectively. Reduce, reuse, and recycle are the simplest ways to lower environmental impact.

• Bioleaching uses bacteria to produce a leachate containing dissolved metal compounds (1)
• Metal is then extracted from the leachate by displacement or electrolysis (1)
• Advantage: both use less energy than traditional mining / produce less waste rock (1)
• Both are more environmentally friendly / sustainable (1)
Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: A company is choosing between using plastic bags or paper bags for its products. Explain how a life cycle assessment could be used to determine which bag is more environmentally friendly. In your answer, refer to all four stages of a life cycle assessment.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed explanation covering all four LCA stages with specific examples for both bags. Clear comparison and a reasoned conclusion.
Mid band (3-4): Explains at least two or three stages with some comparison between the two bags.
Lower band (1-2): Simple statements about one or two stages, limited comparison.
Indicative content:
• Raw materials: plastic from crude oil (finite), paper from trees (renewable but requires land)
• Manufacturing: energy needed to produce each; pollution from plastic production vs. chemical treatment of paper pulp
• Use: plastic bags can be reused more times; paper bags are less durable
• Disposal: plastic is not biodegradable and persists in landfill/oceans; paper is biodegradable but releases methane in landfill
• LCA is subjective — different conclusions depending on what is prioritised (e.g. carbon footprint vs. ocean pollution)
• Neither option is clearly 'better' — the best choice depends on which environmental impacts are considered most important

lessons.title: Alkenes, Alcohols and Carboxylic Acids
lessons.content_html:
Functional Groups

Organic chemistry is the study of carbon compounds. Carbon atoms can form four covalent bonds, which allows them to build chains and rings of almost unlimited size. The properties of an organic molecule depend on its functional group — the specific atom or group of atoms within the molecule that controls how it reacts. Alkenes, alcohols, and carboxylic acids are three important homologous series, each defined by a different functional group.

Alkenes

Alkenes are hydrocarbons that contain at least one carbon–carbon double bond (C=C). This double bond is their functional group. The general formula for alkenes is CₙH₂ₙ, where n is the number of carbon atoms. The simplest alkene is ethene (C₂H₄), followed by propene (C₃H₆) and butene (C₄H₈).

Key Fact

Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons because they contain a C=C double bond. Alkanes are saturated because they contain only single C–C bonds. This single difference in bonding gives the two families very different reactivity.

Because alkenes have a double bond, they are more reactive than alkanes. The double bond can “open up” and allow other atoms to add across it. This type of reaction is called an addition reaction.

Addition of hydrogen (hydrogenation): Alkenes react with hydrogen gas in the presence of a nickel catalyst at about 150 °C. The hydrogen atoms add across the double bond, converting the alkene into an alkane. For example: ethene + hydrogen → ethane (C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆). This reaction is used industrially to harden vegetable oils into margarine.

Addition of water (hydration): Alkenes react with steam in the presence of a phosphoric acid catalyst at high temperature and pressure. This produces an alcohol. For example: ethene + steam → ethanol (C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH). This is the industrial method for making ethanol.

Addition of halogens: Alkenes react rapidly with halogens such as bromine. Ethene decolourises bromine water from orange to colourless, forming a colourless dibromo compound. This is the standard test to distinguish alkenes from alkanes — alkanes do not decolourise bromine water because they have no double bond to react with.

Key Fact

Test for alkenes: Shake the substance with bromine water. If the bromine water changes from orange to colourless, the substance is an alkene (unsaturated). If it stays orange, the substance is saturated (an alkane).

Alcohols

Alcohols are a homologous series of organic compounds whose functional group is the hydroxyl group (–OH). The general formula for alcohols is CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH. The first four members are methanol (CH₃OH), ethanol (C₂H₅OH), propanol (C₃H₇OH), and butanol (C₄H₉OH).

Alcohols dissolve in water to form neutral solutions — they do not produce H⁺ ions, so they are not acidic. They react with sodium metal to produce hydrogen gas and a sodium alkoxide. Alcohols also burn in air, releasing energy, which makes them useful as fuels. Ethanol is the alcohol in alcoholic drinks and is widely used as a solvent and as a fuel (often blended with petrol).

There are two ways to make ethanol on an industrial scale:

Hydration of ethene: Ethene (from cracking crude oil) reacts with steam using a phosphoric acid catalyst at 300 °C and 60–70 atm. This is a continuous process that produces pure ethanol quickly, but it uses a non-renewable feedstock (crude oil).

Fermentation: Yeast converts sugars (e.g. glucose from crops) into ethanol and carbon dioxide at about 25–35 °C in the absence of oxygen: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide (C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂). Fermentation uses a renewable feedstock (sugar from plants) and requires low temperatures, so energy costs are low. However, the process is slow (batch process), and the ethanol produced is impure — it must be separated from the mixture by fractional distillation.

Key Fact

Hydration of ethene is faster and gives purer ethanol but uses a non-renewable feedstock. Fermentation is slower and gives impure ethanol but uses a renewable feedstock and lower temperatures. Exam questions often ask you to compare these two methods.

Carboxylic Acids

Carboxylic acids contain the functional group –COOH (also written as –CO₂H). This group contains both a C=O double bond and an O–H bond. The first members of the series are methanoic acid (HCOOH), ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH — found in vinegar), propanoic acid, and butanoic acid.

Carboxylic acids dissolve in water to produce weak acidic solutions. They ionise only partially — only a small proportion of the acid molecules release H⁺ ions at any one time. This means a solution of ethanoic acid has a higher pH (is less acidic) than a solution of hydrochloric acid of the same concentration.

Carboxylic acids show the typical reactions of acids, but they react more slowly because they are weak acids:

With metal carbonates: Carboxylic acids react with carbonates to produce a salt, water, and carbon dioxide. For example: ethanoic acid + sodium carbonate → sodium ethanoate + water + carbon dioxide (2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COONa + H₂O + CO₂).

With water: Carboxylic acids dissolve in water and partially dissociate, producing H⁺ ions. The solution is acidic but weakly so.

With alcohols: Carboxylic acids react with alcohols in the presence of an acid catalyst to form esters. For example: ethanoic acid + ethanol → ethyl ethanoate + water. Esters often have pleasant, fruity smells and are used in flavourings, perfumes, and solvents.

Strong acids (e.g. hydrochloric acid, sulfuric acid) completely ionise in water — every acid molecule releases H⁺ ions. Weak acids (e.g. ethanoic acid, citric acid) only partially ionise — most of the acid molecules remain intact in solution. At the same concentration, a strong acid has a lower pH, reacts faster, and conducts electricity better than a weak acid because it has a higher concentration of H⁺ ions.

Do not confuse acid strength with concentration. Strength refers to the degree of ionisation. Concentration refers to how much acid is dissolved per unit volume of solution. A concentrated weak acid (e.g. concentrated ethanoic acid) can still have a higher pH than a dilute strong acid.

Key Fact

Carboxylic acids are weak acids because they only partially ionise in water. At the same concentration, ethanoic acid has a higher pH, reacts more slowly, and produces less gas with carbonates than hydrochloric acid (a strong acid).
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about organic chemistry, always identify the functional group first — it determines the reactions. For “compare” questions on making ethanol, structure your answer around the feedstock (renewable vs non-renewable), the conditions (temperature, catalyst), the rate (fast continuous vs slow batch), and the purity of the product. For the bromine water test, state the colour change and what it tells you about the bonding.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Alkenes contain a C=C double bond, making them unsaturated. They undergo addition reactions and decolourise bromine water from orange to colourless.
  • Alcohols contain the –OH functional group. Ethanol can be made by hydration of ethene (fast, non-renewable) or fermentation of sugars (slow, renewable).
  • Carboxylic acids contain the –COOH group and are weak acids — they partially ionise in water and react with carbonates and alcohols (forming esters).

Alkenes have a C=C double bond which allows addition reactions — bromine adds across the double bond, decolourising bromine water. Alcohols have an –OH group, which means they can combust as fuels, dissolve in water forming neutral solutions, and react with sodium to produce hydrogen. Carboxylic acids have a –COOH group which makes them weak acids — they partially ionise in water producing H⁺ ions. They react with carbonates to produce CO₂, and with alcohols to form esters.

lessons.title: Polymers: Addition, Condensation and Natural
lessons.content_html:
What Are Polymers?

A polymer is a very large molecule formed when many small molecules called monomers bond together in a repeating pattern. The word “polymer” comes from the Greek for “many parts.” Polymers can be synthetic (made by humans) or naturally occurring. Everyday synthetic polymers include poly(ethene), PVC, and PTFE, while natural polymers include proteins, starch, and DNA.

The process of joining monomers together is called polymerisation. There are two main types of polymerisation you need to know for GCSE Chemistry: addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation. Each works in a different way and produces a different type of polymer.

Addition Polymerisation

addition polymerisation occurs when many unsaturated monomer molecules (alkenes) join together. The carbon–carbon double bond (C=C) in each monomer “opens up,” allowing the monomers to link into a long chain. No other substance is produced — the only product is the polymer itself.

The simplest example is poly(ethene). Ethene (C₂H₄) is the monomer. Under high pressure and with a catalyst, thousands of ethene molecules open their double bonds and bond together to form a long-chain polymer. The repeating unit of poly(ethene) looks the same as the monomer but with single bonds on each side instead of a double bond.

Key Fact

In addition polymerisation, the only product is the polymer. No atoms are lost or gained — the polymer has the same empirical formula as the monomer. The letter n in the equation represents a very large number of monomer molecules joining together.

To show addition polymerisation in an equation, write n monomer molecules on the left with the C=C double bond shown. On the right, draw the repeating unit inside brackets with a single bond extending from each side of the bracket. Place n as a subscript outside the brackets. The key change: the double bond in the monomer becomes a single bond in the polymer.

Common examples include poly(propene) from propene, and poly(chloroethene) — better known as PVC — from chloroethene. In each case, identify the alkene monomer, open the double bond, and extend the chain. Exam questions often ask you to draw the repeating unit given the monomer, or to identify the monomer from the polymer.

Condensation Polymerisation

condensation polymerisation is different from addition polymerisation in two important ways. First, the monomers have two functional groups — one on each end of the molecule. Second, a small molecule (usually water) is released every time two monomers join together. This by-product is the reason it is called “condensation” polymerisation.

Condensation polymers include polyesters and polyamides. To form a polyester, a dicarboxylic acid reacts with a diol. The –COOH group on the acid reacts with the –OH group on the alcohol, forming an ester link (–COO–) and releasing a molecule of water (H₂O) each time.

Key Fact

The crucial difference: addition polymerisation produces only the polymer, while condensation polymerisation produces the polymer and a small molecule by-product (usually water). This is the most common comparison question in the exam.

A polyamide forms when a dicarboxylic acid reacts with a diamine. The –COOH group reacts with the –NH₂ group, forming an amide link (–CONH–) and releasing water. Nylon is a well-known synthetic polyamide.

amino acids are special monomers because each molecule contains both an amine group (–NH₂) and a carboxylic acid group (–COOH). This means amino acids can undergo condensation polymerisation with each other. When two amino acids join, a peptide bond forms (a type of amide link) and water is released. Chains of amino acids form polypeptides, and one or more polypeptides fold into a protein.

Naturally Occurring Polymers

Many of the most important molecules in living organisms are polymers. You need to know three key examples for the exam: proteins, starch, and DNA. Each is built from smaller monomer units through condensation polymerisation.

Proteins are natural polyamides. They are condensation polymers of amino acids linked by peptide bonds. There are 20 different amino acids found in nature, and the order in which they join determines the protein’s shape and function. Proteins act as enzymes, hormones, antibodies, and structural materials such as collagen and keratin.

starch is a natural polymer made from glucose monomers joined together by condensation reactions. Plants produce starch to store energy. Cellulose is another glucose-based polymer, but the glucose units are arranged differently, giving cellulose rigid, structural properties. Both starch and cellulose release water molecules when their monomers join.

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a polymer made from nucleotide monomers. Each nucleotide contains a sugar, a phosphate group, and a base. Nucleotides join by condensation reactions to form the two strands of the DNA double helix. The sequence of bases along the strand carries the genetic instructions for building proteins.

Key Fact

All three naturally occurring polymers — proteins, starch, and DNA — are formed by condensation polymerisation. In every case, monomers join together and water molecules are released as by-products.

Comparing the Two Types of Polymerisation

Exam questions frequently ask you to compare addition and condensation polymerisation. The table below summarises the key differences.

Addition polymerisation: monomers are alkenes with C=C double bonds; only one product (the polymer); no by-product; examples include poly(ethene), poly(propene), PVC. Condensation polymerisation: monomers have two functional groups (e.g. –OH and –COOH); two products (the polymer and a small molecule, usually water); examples include polyesters, nylon, proteins, starch, DNA.

Question: A polymer is formed from monomers with two different functional groups. Water is also produced. What type of polymerisation is this?

Answer: This is condensation polymerisation. The clues are: (1) the monomers have two functional groups, not a C=C double bond, and (2) a small molecule (water) is produced as a by-product. In addition polymerisation, there is no by-product — only the polymer is formed.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The most common exam question on this topic asks you to compare addition and condensation polymerisation. Always state three differences: (1) the type of monomer used, (2) whether a by-product is formed, and (3) give a named example of each. For 6-mark extended response questions, link your answer to naturally occurring polymers such as proteins and DNA to show breadth of knowledge. Remember — if water is produced, it is condensation polymerisation.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Addition polymerisation joins alkene monomers by opening C=C double bonds, producing only the polymer with no by-product.
  • Condensation polymerisation joins monomers with two functional groups, producing the polymer and a small molecule (usually water).
  • Proteins (from amino acids), starch (from glucose), and DNA (from nucleotides) are all naturally occurring condensation polymers.

practice_questions.text: Compare addition polymerisation and condensation polymerisation. In your answer, refer to the types of monomer involved and the products formed.
practice_questions.marks: Addition polymerisation uses unsaturated monomers / alkenes with C=C double bonds (1) and produces only the polymer / no by-product (1). Condensation polymerisation uses monomers with two functional groups, e.g. –OH and –COOH (1) and produces the polymer and a small molecule, usually water (1).

practice_questions.text: Proteins, starch, and DNA are all naturally occurring polymers. For each one, identify the monomer it is made from and explain how the monomers join together. Include the type of polymerisation involved.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): All three polymers correctly identified with their monomers and clear explanation of condensation polymerisation for each, including reference to water as a by-product.
Mid band (3-4): Two or three polymers with monomers identified; some explanation of how monomers join but may lack detail or miss the by-product.
Lower band (1-2): One polymer and monomer correctly identified; limited explanation of polymerisation.
Indicative content:
• Proteins are made from amino acid monomers joined by peptide bonds (a type of amide link)
• Starch is made from glucose monomers joined by condensation reactions
• DNA is made from nucleotide monomers joined by condensation reactions
• All three form by condensation polymerisation
• In each case, water is released as a by-product when monomers join
• The sequence / arrangement of monomers determines the polymer’s function

glossary_terms.definition: A very large molecule made by joining many small monomer molecules together in a repeating pattern.
A small, reactive molecule that joins with others to form a polymer chain.
A chemical reaction in which many monomer molecules join together to form a polymer.
A type of polymerisation in which unsaturated monomers (alkenes) open their double bonds and join together, producing only the polymer with no other product.
A type of polymerisation in which monomers with two functional groups join together, forming a polymer and releasing a small molecule (usually water) as a by-product.
A specific group of atoms within a molecule that determines how that molecule reacts.
A condensation polymer formed when dicarboxylic acid monomers react with diol monomers, releasing water.
A condensation polymer containing amide links (–CONH–), formed when dicarboxylic acid monomers react with diamine monomers.
Small organic molecules that contain both an amine group (–NH₂) and a carboxylic acid group (–COOH); they are the monomers of proteins.
A biological polymer made of long chains of amino acids folded into a specific 3D shape; proteins carry out most functions in living cells.
A natural carbohydrate polymer made of many glucose monomer units joined by condensation reactions; plants use it to store energy.
Deoxyribonucleic acid — a large polymer made of nucleotide monomers arranged in a double helix; it carries the genetic code in living organisms.
The monomer of DNA, consisting of a sugar, a phosphate group, and one of four bases (A, T, C, or G).

lessons.title: Chemical Tests for Ions
lessons.content_html:
Identifying Ions

In chemistry, you often need to identify which ions are present in an unknown substance. Ions are charged particles formed when atoms gain or lose electrons. Metal atoms lose electrons to form cations (positive ions), while non-metal atoms gain electrons to form anions (negative ions). There are reliable chemical tests for identifying both types, and you need to know them all for your exam.

Flame Tests

A flame test is used to identify certain metal ions. When compounds containing these metals are heated in a flame, the metal ions emit light of a characteristic colour. To carry out a flame test, you dip a clean nichrome wire loop into hydrochloric acid, then into the sample, and hold it in the blue flame of a Bunsen burner.

Key Fact

You must memorise these flame test colours: lithium — crimson, sodium — yellow, potassium — lilac, calcium — orange-red, copper — green. The wire must be cleaned with hydrochloric acid between tests to avoid contamination.

Lithium (Li⁺): Produces a crimson (deep red) flame. Lithium compounds are used in batteries and fireworks — the red colour in fireworks often comes from lithium salts.

Sodium (Na⁺): Produces a strong yellow flame. Sodium is so common as a contaminant that its yellow colour can mask other flame colours, which is why the wire must be thoroughly cleaned.

Potassium (K⁺): Produces a lilac (pale purple) flame. This can be hard to see if sodium is also present, as the yellow colour dominates.

\(Calcium (Ca^{2}⁺):\) Produces an orange-red flame. This is distinct from lithium’s crimson — calcium’s colour has more orange in it.

\(Copper (Cu^{2}⁺):\) Produces a green flame. Copper compounds are also responsible for the green colour in some fireworks.

Testing with Sodium Hydroxide Solution

Some metal ions cannot be identified by flame tests. Instead, you add a few drops of sodium hydroxide solution (NaOH) to a solution of the unknown compound. If certain metal ions are present, an insoluble metal hydroxide forms as a coloured precipitate.

Key Fact

Sodium hydroxide precipitate colours: aluminium — white (dissolves in excess NaOH), calcium — white (does not dissolve in excess), magnesium — white (does not dissolve in excess), copper(II) — blue, iron(II) — green, iron(III) — brown.

\(Aluminium ions (Al^{3}⁺):\) Form a white precipitate of aluminium hydroxide, Al(OH)3. Crucially, this precipitate dissolves when excess NaOH is added. This distinguishes aluminium from calcium and magnesium, which also give white precipitates but do not dissolve in excess.

\(Calcium ions (Ca^{2}⁺):\) Form a white precipitate of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2. This does not dissolve in excess NaOH.

\(Magnesium ions (Mg^{2}⁺):\) Form a white precipitate of magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)2. This does not dissolve in excess NaOH. It is distinguished from calcium by flame test (calcium gives orange-red; magnesium gives no flame colour).

\(Copper(II) ions (Cu^{2}⁺):\) Form a blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide, Cu(OH)2.

\(Iron(II) ions (Fe^{2}⁺):\) Form a green precipitate of iron(II) hydroxide, Fe(OH)2. Sometimes called a “sludgy green” or “dirty green” colour.

\(Iron(III) ions (Fe^{3}⁺):\) Form a brown precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide, Fe(OH)3. This is a distinctive rusty brown colour.

Testing for Carbonate Ions

Carbonate ions (CO3²¯) are tested by adding dilute hydrochloric acid to the substance. If carbonates are present, the mixture fizzes and produces carbon dioxide gas. You confirm that the gas is carbon dioxide by passing it through limewater (calcium hydroxide solution) — if the limewater turns milky (cloudy white), carbon dioxide is confirmed.

Key Fact

The test for carbonates: add dilute acid → fizzing observed → gas turns limewater milky. The word equation is: carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide. For example: CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2

Testing for Halide Ions

Halide ions — chloride (Cl¯), bromide (Br¯), and iodide (I¯) — are identified by adding dilute nitric acid followed by silver nitrate solution (AgNO3). The nitric acid is added first to remove any interfering carbonate or sulfite ions that could give false positives.

Chloride ions (Cl¯): Form a white precipitate of silver chloride (AgCl). Ag⁺ + Cl¯ → AgCl

Bromide ions (Br¯): Form a cream precipitate of silver bromide (AgBr). Ag⁺ + Br¯ → AgBr

Iodide ions (I¯): Form a yellow precipitate of silver iodide (AgI). Ag⁺ + I¯ → AgI

Testing for Sulfate Ions

Sulfate ions (SO4²¯) are identified by first adding dilute hydrochloric acid to remove any carbonate ions, then adding barium chloride solution (BaCl2). If sulfate ions are present, a white precipitate of barium sulfate (BaSO4) forms. The ionic equation is: Ba²⁺ + SO4²¯ → BaSO4

Key Fact

To test for sulfates: add dilute HCl, then barium chloride solution. A white precipitate of barium sulfate confirms sulfate ions are present. The HCl is added first to prevent false positives from carbonates.

Flame Emission Spectroscopy

Flame emission spectroscopy is an instrumental method of analysis that works on the same principle as flame tests but is far more accurate and sensitive. A sample is introduced into a flame, and the light emitted is passed through a spectroscope, which separates it into individual wavelengths. Each element produces a unique line spectrum — like a chemical fingerprint.

Sensitivity: Instrumental methods can detect very small quantities of an element — even trace amounts that chemical tests would miss. This makes them essential in forensic science, environmental monitoring, and quality control.

Speed and accuracy: Machines analyse samples much faster than manual chemical tests and produce quantitative results (exact concentrations), not just qualitative ones (present or absent). They are also more reliable because they remove the subjectivity of judging colours by eye.

Multiple elements: Flame emission spectroscopy can identify several different metal ions in a single sample. It can also measure their concentrations by comparing the intensity of emitted light against reference samples of known concentration.

Small sample size: Only a very small amount of sample is needed for analysis, which is useful when the sample is rare, expensive, or limited in quantity.

Cost: The equipment is expensive to buy and maintain. Specialist staff are needed to operate and calibrate the instruments.

Interpretation: Results must be interpreted using a database of reference spectra. Without this, raw data is meaningless. The instruments also need regular calibration against known standards to ensure accuracy.

Practical Tips for Ion Tests

When carrying out chemical tests for ions in a practical or answering exam questions about them, remember these key points. Always clean equipment between tests to avoid contamination. The order of reagent addition matters — adding nitric acid before silver nitrate for halides, and hydrochloric acid before barium chloride for sulfates. When describing observations, use precise colour terms: “white precipitate” rather than “it went white,” and “the limewater turned milky” rather than “it changed.”
lessons.exam_tip_html: Ion test questions are very common on Paper 2. Learn the tests as a table — ion, reagent, observation — and practise recalling them without notes. When asked to describe a test, state the reagent added and the expected observation. For “explain” questions, include the ionic equation and name the precipitate formed. A common mistake is confusing the halide precipitate colours — remember W-C-Y (white, cream, yellow) for chloride, bromide, iodide. If asked to compare flame tests with flame emission spectroscopy, always mention that instrumental methods are more sensitive, accurate, and can measure concentrations.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Flame tests identify metal ions by colour: lithium (crimson), sodium (yellow), potassium (lilac), calcium (orange-red), copper (green). Sodium hydroxide solution produces coloured precipitates for aluminium (white, dissolves in excess), calcium and magnesium (white), copper(II) (blue), iron(II) (green), and iron(III) (brown).
  • Carbonates fizz with dilute acid and produce CO2 (confirmed by turning limewater milky). Halides are tested with acidified silver nitrate: chloride (white), bromide (cream), iodide (yellow). Sulfates give a white precipitate with acidified barium chloride.
  • Flame emission spectroscopy is an instrumental method that is more sensitive, accurate, and can measure concentrations — but the equipment is expensive and needs specialist operation.

practice_questions.text: A student has 50 cm³ of a solution containing 0.10 mol/dm³ of copper(II) sulfate. Calculate the number of moles of copper(II) sulfate in the solution.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Correct substitution: moles = concentration × volume = 0.10 × (50/1000) (1)
• Correct answer: 0.005 mol / 5 × 10⁻³ mol (1)

Allow error carried forward if substitution is correct but arithmetic is wrong.

practice_questions.text: A student adds sodium hydroxide solution to an unknown solution and observes a white precipitate. When excess sodium hydroxide is added, the precipitate dissolves. Explain what metal ion is present and why this test is needed.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• The metal ion is aluminium / Al³⁺ (1)
• Aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric, so it dissolves in excess NaOH (1)
• This distinguishes aluminium from calcium and magnesium, which also form white precipitates but do not dissolve in excess NaOH (1)

Accept: 'the white precipitate dissolving in excess shows it is aluminium, not calcium or magnesium' for the third mark.

practice_questions.text: Compare the use of flame tests with flame emission spectroscopy for identifying metal ions. Explain why flame emission spectroscopy is preferred in forensic laboratories.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Flame tests give qualitative results only (identify the ion present) while flame emission spectroscopy gives quantitative results (measures concentration) (1)
• Flame emission spectroscopy is more sensitive — it can detect trace amounts that flame tests would miss (1)
• Flame emission spectroscopy is more accurate / reliable because it removes the subjectivity of judging colour by eye (1)
• It can identify multiple elements in a single sample (1)
• Only a very small sample is needed, which is important when evidence is limited in forensic work (1)

Max 4 marks. Must include at least one comparison point for full marks.

practice_questions.text: A forensic scientist analyses an unknown white powder. She dissolves it in water and carries out a series of tests. With dilute nitric acid and silver nitrate, a cream precipitate forms. With dilute hydrochloric acid, there is no fizzing. With sodium hydroxide solution, a white precipitate forms that does not dissolve in excess. Identify the ions present in the powder and explain the evidence for each conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): All ions correctly identified with full explanation of the evidence for each. Clear, logical structure.
• Cream precipitate with acidified silver nitrate indicates bromide ions (Br⁻) are present, because silver bromide (AgBr) is cream-coloured.
• No fizzing with acid means carbonate ions are absent.
• White precipitate with NaOH that does not dissolve in excess indicates either calcium (Ca²⁺) or magnesium (Mg²⁺) ions. If it dissolved in excess, it would indicate aluminium.
• To distinguish calcium from magnesium, a flame test could be performed — calcium gives orange-red; magnesium gives no colour.
• The powder is likely calcium bromide or magnesium bromide.
Mid band (3-4): Most ions identified with some explanation, but may miss the carbonate conclusion or the calcium/magnesium distinction.
Lower band (1-2): One or two ions identified with limited explanation.

lessons.title: Materials, Corrosion, Haber Process and Fertilisers
lessons.content_html:
Corrosion

Corrosion is the destruction of a metal caused by reactions with substances in the environment. Most metals corrode when exposed to air and water over time. The most familiar example is the rusting of iron and steel.

Rusting is the corrosion of iron. It only happens when iron is in contact with both oxygen and water. The chemical name for rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide. Unlike the oxide layers on aluminium, rust is soft and flaky, so it falls away from the surface and exposes fresh metal underneath. This means rusting continues until all the iron has corroded.

Key Fact

Iron requires both oxygen and water to rust. Remove either one and rusting does not occur. This is the basis for all rust prevention methods.

Preventing Corrosion

Since rusting needs oxygen and water, prevention methods work by creating a barrier between the iron and these reactants, or by using a more reactive metal to protect the iron.

Painting: A layer of paint stops oxygen and water reaching the iron surface. Used on bridges, cars, and railings. If the paint is scratched or chips off, the iron underneath will rust.

Oiling or greasing: A thin coat of oil or grease creates a waterproof barrier. Used on moving parts such as bicycle chains and machine components, where paint would crack or wear off.

Electroplating: Coating the iron with a thin layer of another metal (such as tin, chromium, or nickel) using electrolysis. Tin cans are steel coated with tin. If the coating is breached, the iron underneath can still rust.

Galvanising: Coating iron or steel with a layer of zinc. Zinc acts as a barrier, but it also provides sacrificial protection — even if the coating is scratched, the zinc corrodes instead of the iron because zinc is more reactive.

Sacrificial protection uses a block of a more reactive metal (usually zinc or magnesium) attached to or near the iron structure. The more reactive metal oxidises preferentially, donating electrons to the iron and preventing it from reacting. This method is used on ships’ hulls, underground pipes, and offshore oil rigs. The sacrificial block must be replaced periodically as it is gradually consumed.

Alloys

An alloy is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements (usually other metals, but sometimes non-metals like carbon). Alloys are made because pure metals are often too soft for practical use. In a pure metal, the atoms are arranged in regular layers that can slide over each other easily. In an alloy, atoms of different sizes disrupt the regular layers, making it harder for them to slide. This makes alloys harder and stronger than pure metals.

Key Fact

Most metals in everyday use are alloys, not pure metals. The different-sized atoms in an alloy disrupt the regular arrangement of layers, preventing them from sliding and making the alloy harder.

Steel is an alloy of iron and carbon (0.1–2% carbon). Low-carbon steel is easy to shape and used in car bodies. High-carbon steel is harder and used in cutting tools. Stainless steel contains chromium (and often nickel) and resists corrosion — used in cutlery, surgical instruments, and kitchen sinks.

Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin — hard and resistant to corrosion, used for statues and ship propellers. Brass is copper and zinc — harder than pure copper, used in musical instruments and plumbing fittings. Gold alloys are gold mixed with silver, copper, or zinc to make them harder — pure gold (24 carat) is too soft for jewellery.

Ceramics, Polymers, and Composites

Ceramics are non-metallic solids made by heating. Examples include clay pottery, bricks, and glass. Ceramics are very hard, resistant to heat and corrosion, but they are brittle — they shatter rather than bend when force is applied.

Composites are materials made by combining two or more different materials. Each component keeps its own properties, but together the composite has improved characteristics that neither material has alone. The two parts are a matrix (the background material that binds everything together) and a reinforcement (the material that adds strength or stiffness).

Concrete: Gravel or crushed stone (reinforcement) held together by cement (matrix). Strong in compression but weak in tension. Reinforced concrete: Steel bars or mesh (reinforcement) embedded in concrete (matrix) — strong in both compression and tension, used in buildings and bridges.

Fibreglass (GRP): Glass fibres (reinforcement) set in a polymer resin (matrix). Lightweight and strong, used in boat hulls, car body panels, and insulation. Carbon fibre reinforced polymer: Carbon fibres in a polymer resin. Extremely strong and lightweight, used in aircraft, racing cars, and tennis rackets.

The Haber Process

The Haber process is the industrial method for making ammonia (NH₃). Ammonia is a vital chemical because it is used to make fertilisers, nitric acid, and cleaning products. Without the Haber process, there would not be enough food to feed the world’s population.

The raw materials are nitrogen (obtained from the air by fractional distillation of liquid air) and hydrogen (obtained from natural gas or the cracking of hydrocarbons). The balanced equation is:

Key Fact

N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)

This reaction is reversible — it can go in both directions. The yield of ammonia is only about 15%, so unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled back through the reactor.

The conditions used in the Haber process represent a compromise between rate and yield:

Temperature: About 450 °C. The forward reaction is exothermic, so a lower temperature would give a higher yield. However, too low a temperature makes the reaction too slow. 450 °C is a compromise — fast enough to be economical, but the yield is only about 15%.

Pressure: About 200 atmospheres. There are 4 molecules of gas on the left (1 N₂ + 3 H₂) and only 2 on the right (2 NH₃). High pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with fewer gas molecules — the products. Higher pressures would give even higher yields, but they are expensive and dangerous.

Catalyst: An iron catalyst is used. It speeds up the reaction so equilibrium is reached faster. The catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium or the yield — it just helps the system get there more quickly.

The forward reaction is exothermic, so Le Chatelier’s principle says a lower temperature would shift equilibrium to the right and increase yield. But at low temperatures, the particles have less kinetic energy, fewer successful collisions occur, and the rate of reaction is too slow to be practical. The chosen temperature (450 °C) gives a reasonable rate with an acceptable yield. The unreacted gases are recycled to maximise overall conversion.

Similarly, very high pressures would increase yield further, but the cost of building and maintaining equipment that can withstand extreme pressures, along with increased safety risks, means 200 atmospheres is the economically practical compromise.

NPK Fertilisers

NPK fertilisers contain three essential elements that plants need for healthy growth:

Nitrogen (N) — promotes leaf and stem growth. Phosphorus (P) — promotes root development and helps with energy transfer. Potassium (K) — helps with disease resistance, flower and fruit development, and overall plant health.

Without these minerals, crops grow poorly. Intensive farming removes these elements from the soil faster than natural processes can replace them, so farmers add fertilisers to maintain crop yields and feed growing populations.

Key Fact

The nitrogen in NPK fertilisers comes from ammonia (via the Haber process). Ammonia can be reacted with nitric acid to produce ammonium nitrate (NH₄NO₃), a widely used nitrogen fertiliser. Phosphorus comes from phosphate rock, and potassium comes from potassium chloride or potassium sulfate mined from the ground.

In the laboratory, NPK fertilisers can be made by mixing the correct proportions of compounds containing nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. For example, mixing ammonium sulfate (provides N), potassium phosphate (provides P and K), and potassium chloride (provides K) in the right ratio produces a balanced NPK fertiliser. Industrially, ammonium nitrate is produced by neutralising ammonia solution with nitric acid: NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on the Haber process often ask you to explain why specific conditions are used. Always link your answer to Le Chatelier’s principle and the idea of compromise — state the effect on both rate and yield, then explain why the chosen condition is a balance between the two. For “compare and explain” questions on corrosion prevention, name the method, state whether it uses a barrier or sacrificial protection, and explain how it works at the particle or reactivity level.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Iron rusts when exposed to both oxygen and water — prevention methods use barriers (paint, oil, electroplating) or sacrificial protection (zinc/magnesium corroding instead of the iron).
  • Alloys are harder than pure metals because different-sized atoms disrupt the regular layers and prevent them from sliding. Composites combine a matrix and reinforcement for improved properties.
  • The Haber process makes ammonia (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃) at 450 °C, 200 atm, with an iron catalyst — conditions are a compromise between rate and yield. Ammonia is used to make NPK fertilisers.

practice_questions.text: Describe how galvanising protects iron from rusting.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Iron/steel is coated with a layer of zinc (1)
• Zinc acts as a barrier, preventing oxygen and water from reaching the iron surface (1)
• If the coating is scratched, zinc provides sacrificial protection because it is more reactive than iron and corrodes preferentially (1)

Max 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: The Haber process produces 12 tonnes of ammonia from one batch. The theoretical maximum yield is 80 tonnes. Calculate the percentage yield.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Percentage yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100 (1)

Allow ecf if formula is correct but arithmetic is wrong.

practice_questions.text: Explain why alloys are harder than pure metals.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• In a pure metal, atoms are arranged in regular/ordered layers (1)
• These layers can slide over each other easily, making the metal soft (1)
• In an alloy, atoms of different sizes disrupt the regular arrangement/layers (1)
• This prevents the layers from sliding, making the alloy harder and stronger (1)

Max 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: Compare the use of painting and sacrificial protection as methods of preventing the corrosion of iron. Explain which method would be more suitable for protecting an underwater steel pipe.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Painting creates a barrier between the iron and oxygen/water (1)
• If the paint is scratched or damaged, the iron underneath will be exposed and can rust (1)
• Sacrificial protection uses a more reactive metal (e.g. zinc or magnesium) attached to the iron (1)
• The more reactive metal corrodes instead of the iron, even if the surface is damaged (1)
• Sacrificial protection is more suitable for underwater pipes because paint would be difficult to maintain/inspect/repair underwater, and sacrificial blocks continue to protect even when the surface is damaged (1)

Max 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: The Haber process uses a temperature of 450°C and a pressure of 200 atmospheres. The forward reaction is exothermic. Explain why these conditions are used and why they represent a compromise.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed explanation covering both temperature and pressure, with clear links to Le Chatelier’s principle and the concept of compromise between rate and yield. E.g. The forward reaction is exothermic, so by Le Chatelier’s principle a lower temperature would shift the equilibrium to the right and increase the yield of ammonia. However, at low temperatures the rate of reaction is very slow because particles have less kinetic energy and there are fewer successful collisions. 450°C is a compromise — it gives a reasonable rate while still producing an acceptable yield (~15%). Unreacted gases are recycled. High pressure favours the forward reaction because there are 4 molecules of gas on the left and only 2 on the right. 200 atm gives a good yield, but higher pressures would be more expensive and dangerous to maintain. An iron catalyst is used to speed up the reaction without changing the equilibrium position.
Mid band (3-4): Explains either temperature or pressure well, or gives a basic account of both. May mention compromise but lacks full development.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements about conditions with limited or no reference to equilibrium, rate, or compromise.

lessons.title: Energy Stores, Transfers and Power
lessons.content_html:
Energy Stores

In physics, energy is described as being held in different energy stores. Energy is never created or destroyed — it is simply transferred from one store to another. This principle is known as the conservation of energy.

You need to know eight energy stores. Each one describes a different way that energy can be held within a system.

Key Fact

The eight energy stores are: kinetic, thermal, chemical, gravitational potential, elastic potential, electrostatic, magnetic, and nuclear. You must be able to identify which stores are involved in any energy transfer scenario.

Kinetic energy is the energy store of any moving object. A car on a motorway, a sprinter in a race, and air molecules in a warm room all have energy in their kinetic store.

Thermal energy is associated with the temperature of an object. The hotter something is, the more energy it has in its thermal store. When you heat water in a kettle, energy is transferred to the thermal store of the water.

Chemical energy is the energy stored in chemical bonds. Food, fuels such as petrol and natural gas, and batteries all store energy chemically. This energy is released during chemical reactions.

Gravitational potential energy (GPE) is the energy stored by an object that has been raised above the ground. The higher the object, the greater its mass, and the stronger the gravitational field, the more GPE it has.

Elastic potential energy is stored in objects that have been stretched or compressed, such as springs, rubber bands, and trampolines. When the object returns to its original shape, this energy is released.

Electrostatic energy is stored when electric charges are separated. Magnetic energy is stored when magnets are pushed together or pulled apart. Nuclear energy is stored in the nuclei of atoms and released during nuclear reactions such as fission and fusion.

Energy Transfers

Energy can be transferred between stores in four main ways, known as energy transfer pathways. These are: mechanically (when a force acts on an object), electrically (when charge flows through a circuit), by heating (when there is a temperature difference), and by radiation (such as light waves or sound waves).

For example, when a ball is dropped from a height: energy is transferred from the gravitational potential store to the kinetic store as the ball falls (mechanically, by the force of gravity). When the ball hits the ground, some energy is transferred to the thermal store of the ball and the ground (by heating), and some to the surroundings as sound (by radiation).

Key Fact

Energy is always conserved. In a closed system, the total energy before a transfer equals the total energy after. Energy that seems to “disappear” has actually been transferred to less useful stores — usually the thermal store of the surroundings.

In any transfer, some energy is dissipated (spread out) into less useful stores, usually as thermal energy in the surroundings. This is why no energy transfer is 100% efficient in practice. A light bulb, for example, is supplied with energy electrically from the mains. It transfers that energy to light (useful) and to the thermal store of the surroundings (wasted).

Calculating Kinetic Energy

The amount of kinetic energy an object has depends on its mass and speed. The equation is:

\(Kinetic energy = \frac{1}{2} \times mass \times speed^{2}\)
Ek = ½ mv²

Where Ek is kinetic energy in joules (J), m is mass in kilograms (kg), and v is speed in metres per second (m/s). Notice that speed is squared — this means doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy.

Question: A car has a mass of 1200 kg and travels at 15 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

Answer: Ek = ½ × 1200 × 15² = ½ × 1200 × 225 = 135,000 J (or 135 kJ).

Calculating Gravitational Potential Energy

Gravitational potential energy depends on the mass of the object, the gravitational field strength, and the height above the ground:

\(GPE = mass \times \text{gravitational field strength} \times height\)
Ep = mgh

Where Ep is gravitational potential energy in joules (J), m is mass in kilograms (kg), g is gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram (N/kg) — on Earth, g = 9.8 N/kg — and h is height in metres (m).

Question: A 0.5 kg ball is held 4 m above the ground. Calculate its gravitational potential energy. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

Answer: Ep = 0.5 × 9.8 × 4 = 19.6 J.

Elastic Potential Energy

When a spring is stretched or compressed within its limit of proportionality, it stores elastic potential energy. The equation is:

\(Elastic \text{potential energy} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{spring constant} \times extension^{2}\)
Ee = ½ ke²

Where Ee is elastic potential energy in joules (J), k is the spring constant in newtons per metre (N/m), and e is the extension in metres (m). Like kinetic energy, extension is squared — doubling the extension quadruples the energy stored.

Work Done and Energy Transfer

Work done is the scientific term for energy transfer. When a force causes an object to move through a distance, work is done on that object. The equation is:

\(Work done = force \times distance\)
W = Fs

Where W is work done in joules (J), F is force in newtons (N), and s is distance along the line of action of the force in metres (m). One joule of work is done when a force of one newton moves an object one metre.

Key Fact

Work done = energy transferred. These two quantities are always equal. If 500 J of work is done on an object, then 500 J of energy has been transferred. The unit for both is the joule (J).

Power

Power is the rate at which energy is transferred, or equivalently the rate at which work is done. A more powerful device transfers the same amount of energy in less time. The equations are:

\(Power = \text{energy transferred} \div time\)
P = E/t

\(Power = \text{work done} \div time\)
P = W/t

Power is measured in watts (W). One watt means one joule of energy is transferred per second. A 60 W light bulb transfers 60 joules of energy every second. For larger values, kilowatts (kW) are used: 1 kW = 1000 W.

Question: A motor transfers 15,000 J of energy in 5 minutes. Calculate its power.

Answer: First convert time: 5 minutes = 300 seconds. Then P = E/t = 15,000 ÷ 300 = 50 W.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In Combined Science, calculation questions on energy are very common. Always show your working clearly: write the equation, substitute values with units, and give your final answer with the correct unit (J for energy, W for power). Watch out for unit conversions — time must be in seconds for power calculations, and speed must be in m/s for kinetic energy. In “explain” questions about energy transfers, name the specific energy stores (not just “energy”) and state how the energy is transferred between them.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • There are eight energy stores (kinetic, thermal, chemical, gravitational potential, elastic potential, electrostatic, magnetic, nuclear) and four transfer pathways (mechanically, electrically, by heating, by radiation).
  • Key equations: Ek = ½mv², Ep = mgh, Ee = ½ke², W = Fs, and P = E/t. You must be able to select and apply the correct equation for each scenario.
  • Energy is always conserved — it cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores. Dissipated energy (usually thermal) is wasted, not lost.

practice_questions.text: Describe the energy transfers that occur when a car brakes and comes to a stop. Explain why the brakes get hot and discuss the implications of the conservation of energy in this situation.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed, well-organised response that correctly identifies energy stores and transfer pathways, explains heating of brakes, and links to conservation of energy with appropriate terminology.
Indicative content:
• The car has energy in its kinetic store while moving (1)
• When the brakes are applied, friction acts between the brake pads and disc (1)
• Work is done by friction, transferring energy from the kinetic store to the thermal store of the brakes (1)
• The brakes get hot because the thermal energy store of the brake pads and discs increases (1)
• The car slows down as its kinetic energy decreases (1)
• Energy is conserved — the kinetic energy lost equals the thermal energy gained by the brakes and surroundings (1)
• The thermal energy is dissipated to the surroundings and cannot easily be recovered for useful purposes (1)
Mid band (3-4): Identifies key energy stores and explains why brakes get hot, but may lack detail on conservation of energy or dissipation.
Lower band (1-2): Basic reference to energy transfer with limited explanation or incorrect store names.

glossary_terms.definition: Descriptions of the ways in which energy can be stored — there are eight energy stores you need to know.
The principle that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred from one store to another or converted from one form to another.
The energy store associated with a moving object — the faster it moves and the greater its mass, the more kinetic energy it has.
The energy store associated with the temperature of an object — the hotter it is, the more energy is in its thermal store.
The energy stored in the bonds between atoms in fuels, food, and batteries — released during chemical reactions.
The energy stored by an object raised above ground level — depends on mass, gravitational field strength, and height.
The energy stored in a stretched or compressed elastic object such as a spring or rubber band.
The four ways energy moves between stores: mechanically (by a force), electrically (by a current), by heating, or by radiation (light or sound waves).
Energy that is transferred to stores that are not useful — typically the thermal store of the surroundings, often described as wasted energy.
The energy transferred when a force moves an object through a distance — measured in joules (J). Work done equals force times distance.
The SI unit of energy — one joule is the energy transferred when a force of one newton moves an object one metre.
The rate at which energy is transferred or work is done — measured in watts (W), where 1 watt equals 1 joule per second.
The SI unit of power — one watt equals one joule of energy transferred per second.
A measure of how stiff a spring is — the force needed to extend or compress it by one metre, measured in newtons per metre (N/m).

lessons.title: Conservation of Energy, Efficiency and Energy Resources
lessons.content_html:
The Principle of Conservation of Energy

One of the most important ideas in physics is the conservation of energy. This principle states that energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be transferred from one store to another, or dissipated to the surroundings. The total amount of energy in a closed system always stays the same.

A closed system is one where energy cannot enter or leave. An insulated flask of hot water is a good example — the thermal energy stays inside the flask because the insulation prevents transfer to the surroundings. In a closed system, any energy transferred away from one store must appear in another store.

Key Fact

Energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transferred between stores. In a closed system, the total energy before a transfer is always equal to the total energy afterwards.

Energy Transfers and Dissipation

When energy is transferred, some of it usually ends up in stores that are not useful. This energy is said to be dissipated (or “wasted”). Dissipated energy is transferred to the thermal energy store of the surroundings, where it spreads out and becomes increasingly difficult to use.

Consider a light bulb. Electrical energy is transferred to the light’s thermal and light energy stores. The light is useful, but the heat given off is wasted energy. The wasted thermal energy heats the surroundings and cannot easily be recovered. This is why no device is ever 100% efficient in practice.

A bungee jumper standing on a platform has energy in the gravitational potential energy store. As they fall, this transfers to the kinetic energy store. When the bungee cord stretches, kinetic energy transfers to the elastic potential energy store of the cord. At each stage, some energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings through air resistance and stretching of the cord. The total energy remains the same throughout.

Engineers design systems to minimise dissipation. Lubrication reduces friction between moving parts, so less energy is wasted as heat. Thermal insulation (such as loft insulation, cavity wall insulation, double glazing, and draught excluders) reduces unwanted thermal energy transfer from buildings. In a house, the biggest heat losses occur through the roof and walls, so insulating these areas has the greatest impact.

Calculating Efficiency

Efficiency tells us how good a device is at transferring energy usefully. It compares the useful output energy (or power) to the total input energy (or power).

The equation is:

\(Efficiency = \text{useful output energy transfer} \div \text{total input energy transfer}\)

This gives a decimal between 0 and 1. Multiply by 100 to get a percentage. You can also use power instead of energy:

\(Efficiency = \text{useful output power} \div \text{total input power}\)

Key Fact

Efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy. It can never be greater than 1 (100%) because energy is always dissipated. A higher efficiency means less energy is wasted.

A motor has a total input energy of 500 J and transfers 350 J usefully to the kinetic energy store of a load. Calculate its efficiency.

Step 1: Write the equation: Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input.
Step 2: Substitute: Efficiency = 350 ÷ 500 = 0.70.
Step 3: Convert to percentage: 0.70 × 100 = 70%.
This means 70% of the energy is usefully transferred and 30% is dissipated (wasted).

Energy Resources — Renewable and Non-Renewable

The world relies on a mix of renewable and non-renewable energy resources to generate electricity, heat buildings, and power transport. You need to know the advantages and disadvantages of each type.

Non-Renewable Resources

Fossil fuels (coal, oil, and natural gas) are the most widely used non-renewable resources. They were formed over millions of years from the remains of dead organisms. Burning them releases carbon dioxide (a greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change) and sulphur dioxide (which causes acid rain).

Nuclear energy uses uranium or plutonium as fuel. Nuclear power stations produce no greenhouse gases during operation, and a small amount of fuel produces a large amount of energy. However, they are expensive to build and decommission, and used fuel rods produce radioactive waste that must be stored safely for thousands of years. The 1986 Chernobyl disaster highlighted the dangers of nuclear accidents.

Key Fact

Non-renewable resources will run out. The three fossil fuels are coal, oil, and natural gas. Nuclear fuel (uranium/plutonium) is also non-renewable. Fossil fuels release CO2 (global warming) and SO2 (acid rain).

Renewable Resources

Renewable resources will not run out because they are replenished naturally. Most produce no greenhouse gases during operation, but they each have limitations.

Wind power: Wind turns turbine blades, transferring kinetic energy to electrical energy via a generator. Wind power produces no CO2, but turbines only generate electricity when the wind blows — making them unreliable. Some people also consider them unsightly or noisy.

Solar power: Solar cells convert sunlight directly into electricity. Solar panels are renewable and cost nothing to run once installed, but they depend on sunlight and produce no electricity at night or on very cloudy days.

Hydroelectric power: Rainwater is collected in a reservoir and released downhill through turbines to generate electricity. It produces no CO2 during operation and can respond quickly to changes in demand. However, building the dam requires flooding a valley, which destroys habitats.

Tidal power: Water trapped at high tide is released through turbines to generate electricity. Tidal power is highly reliable because tides are predictable, but barrages can harm marine wildlife and are expensive to build. Tidal power is driven by the gravitational pull of the Moon, not by energy from the Sun.

Geothermal power: Water is pumped down into hot rocks deep underground and returns as steam to turn turbines. It is only available in volcanic areas or places with hot rocks near the surface, which limits where it can be used.

Biomass: Fuel made from living or recently living organisms (such as wood, animal waste, or crops). Biomass is considered carbon neutral because the CO2 released when burned equals the CO2 the organisms absorbed during growth. However, growing and transporting biomass does have a carbon footprint.

Trends in Energy Use

The UK is shifting from fossil fuels towards renewable sources. Demand for electricity varies throughout the day and across seasons — it peaks in the evening and in winter. Fossil fuel and nuclear power stations provide reliable base load supply. Hydroelectric and gas-fired power stations can start up quickly to meet sudden increases in demand. Renewable sources like wind and solar contribute a growing share but cannot always guarantee supply because they depend on weather conditions.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In energy questions, always state which energy store energy is being transferred from and to (e.g. “from the kinetic store to the thermal store of the surroundings”). For efficiency calculations, show every step: write the equation, substitute values, then give your answer as a decimal and a percentage. When comparing energy resources, structure your answer with clear advantages and disadvantages of each — and always link your points to reliability, environmental impact, or cost.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Energy is always conserved — it cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores. Dissipated energy spreads to the thermal store of the surroundings and is no longer useful.
  • Efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy. No device can be 100% efficient because some energy is always dissipated. Lubrication and insulation reduce unwanted transfers.
  • Non-renewable resources (fossil fuels, nuclear) will run out and fossil fuels release greenhouse gases. Renewable resources (wind, solar, tidal, hydroelectric, geothermal, biomass) won’t run out but many are weather-dependent and unreliable.

lessons.title: Circuits: Current, Resistance and Potential Difference
lessons.content_html:
What Are Current, Resistance and Potential Difference?

Every electrical circuit relies on three linked quantities. Current is the flow of electrical charge around a circuit. It is measured in amperes (A) using an ammeter, which is always connected in series — in line with the component being tested.

Potential difference (p.d.) is the energy transferred per unit of charge that passes between two points. It is measured in volts (V) using a voltmeter, which is always connected in parallel — across the component.

Resistance is a measure of how much a component opposes the flow of current. It is measured in ohms (Ω). The higher the resistance, the harder it is for current to flow.

Key Fact

In most circuits the charge carriers are electrons. Conventional current flows from positive to negative, but electrons actually move from negative to positive.

Ohm’s Law

The relationship between potential difference, current and resistance is given by the equation:

\(\text{potential difference} = current \times resistance\)

\(V = I \times R\)

where V is potential difference in volts, I is current in amperes, and R is resistance in ohms. You need to be able to rearrange this equation: \(I = V \div R\) and \(R = V \div I\).

This equation applies to all components, but Ohm’s law specifically states that for some conductors, the current is directly proportional to the potential difference — provided the temperature remains constant. A component that behaves this way is called an ohmic conductor because its resistance stays the same regardless of the current flowing through it. A fixed resistor at constant temperature is a good example.

Key Fact

V = IR is the equation linking potential difference, current and resistance. Ohm’s law is the statement that current is directly proportional to p.d. at constant temperature — this only applies to ohmic conductors.

Question: A resistor has a resistance of 15 Ω. The current flowing through it is 0.4 A. Calculate the potential difference across the resistor.

Answer: V = I × R = 0.4 × 15 = 6.0 V

Question: A lamp has a potential difference of 12 V across it and a current of 2.5 A flowing through it. Calculate the resistance.

Answer: R = V ÷ I = 12 ÷ 2.5 = \(4.8 \, \Omega\)

Investigating I–V Characteristics

One of your required practicals asks you to investigate the I–V characteristics of different circuit components. The basic circuit uses a variable power supply (or a battery with a variable resistor), an ammeter in series, a voltmeter in parallel across the component, and the component itself.

You change the potential difference using the variable supply, record the ammeter and voltmeter readings at each setting, then reverse the connections and repeat for negative values. Plotting current (y-axis) against potential difference (x-axis) gives an I–V characteristic graph. The shape of this graph tells you about the component’s behaviour.

I–V Graphs for Key Components

Ohmic conductor (fixed resistor at constant temperature): The graph is a straight line through the origin. This means current is directly proportional to potential difference — doubling the p.d. doubles the current. The resistance is constant and can be calculated from the gradient.

Filament lamp: The graph is a curve that starts steep and flattens out. As current increases, the filament heats up and its resistance increases. At higher p.d. values, the same increase in voltage produces a smaller increase in current. The graph is symmetrical — reversing the p.d. gives the same shape in the opposite direction.

Diode: A diode allows current to flow in only one direction. In the forward direction, current flows once the p.d. reaches about 0.7 V (the threshold voltage), and then rises steeply. In the reverse direction, the resistance is very high and essentially no current flows. The I–V graph shows current only on one side of the origin.

Straight line through origin = ohmic conductor (e.g. fixed resistor). Constant resistance.

Curve that flattens (symmetrical) = filament lamp. Resistance increases with temperature.

Current in one direction only = diode. Very high resistance in reverse.

In the exam you may be given a graph and asked to identify the component, or asked to sketch the I–V graph for a named component. Make sure you practise both.

Special Resistors: LDRs and Thermistors

Some components have a resistance that changes in response to the environment. These are useful in sensing circuits.

A light-dependent resistor (LDR) has a resistance that depends on light intensity. In bright light, the resistance of an LDR is low. In darkness, the resistance is high. LDRs are used in circuits that detect light levels — for example, automatic street lights that switch on when it gets dark.

A thermistor (in GCSE, this means an NTC thermistor) has a resistance that depends on temperature. As the temperature increases, the resistance of a thermistor decreases. As the temperature decreases, the resistance increases. Thermistors are used in temperature-sensing circuits — for example, thermostats that control central heating.

Key Fact

LDR: more light → lower resistance. Thermistor: higher temperature → lower resistance. Both are used in sensing circuits. Remember: for both components, the resistance goes down when the stimulus (light or heat) goes up.

In a filament lamp, the metal filament heats up as current flows. Hotter metal atoms vibrate more, creating more obstacles for the electrons — so resistance increases with temperature.

In a thermistor, the semiconductor material releases more charge carriers as it heats up, making it easier for current to flow — so resistance decreases with temperature.

In an LDR, photons of light release charge carriers in the semiconductor — more light means more carriers and lower resistance.

Charge Flow and Current

Current is linked to charge flow by the equation:

\(\text{charge flow} = current \times time\)

\(Q = I \times t\)

where Q is charge in coulombs (C), I is current in amperes (A), and t is time in seconds (s). One ampere means one coulomb of charge passes a point in the circuit every second.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In calculation questions, always write the equation first, substitute the values with units, and show your working clearly. If asked to “explain” how the resistance of a filament lamp changes, link your answer to temperature: as current increases, the filament heats up, metal ions vibrate more, so resistance increases. For the required practical, be ready to describe the circuit, name the measuring instruments (ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel), and explain how you would obtain negative readings by reversing the connections.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • V = IR links potential difference (V), current (I) and resistance (R). Ohm’s law states current is directly proportional to p.d. at constant temperature — true for ohmic conductors only.
  • I–V graphs show how components behave: straight line (resistor), curve (filament lamp), one-way flow (diode). Know how to sketch and identify each.
  • LDR resistance falls in bright light; thermistor resistance falls as temperature rises. Both are used in sensing circuits.

A resistor whose resistance decreases as the temperature increases.
