lessons.title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
lessons.content_html:
What Are Electromagnetic Waves?

Electromagnetic waves (EM waves) are transverse waves that transfer energy from one place to another. Unlike sound waves, they do not need a medium to travel through — they can pass through a vacuum (empty space). All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed through a vacuum: 3 × 108 m/s, the speed of light.

EM waves are produced when charged particles oscillate (vibrate). They consist of oscillating electric and magnetic fields that are perpendicular to each other and to the direction the wave travels. The key equation linking wave speed, frequency, and wavelength is:

Key Fact

\(\text{wave speed} = frequency \times wavelength\)   (v = f × λ). For all EM waves in a vacuum, v = 3 × 108 m/s. This means waves with a higher frequency have a shorter wavelength, and waves with a lower frequency have a longer wavelength.

The Electromagnetic Spectrum

The electromagnetic spectrum is the entire range of EM waves, arranged in order of wavelength and frequency. There are seven main types, and you must learn them in order from longest wavelength to shortest:

\(Radio waves \rightarrow Microwaves \rightarrow Infrared \rightarrow Visible light \rightarrow Ultraviolet \rightarrow X-rays \rightarrow Gamma rays\)

As you move from radio waves to gamma rays, the frequency increases and the wavelength decreases. The boundaries between different types are not sharp — the spectrum is continuous, and one type blends gradually into the next.

A common mnemonic is: Running Men In Vests Usually X-ray Giraffes (Radio, Microwaves, Infrared, Visible, Ultraviolet, X-rays, Gamma). Alternatively, remember that the spectrum goes from the longest waves you encounter daily (radio) to the most energetic and penetrating (gamma). In the exam, being able to place any given wave type in the correct position on the spectrum is a frequently tested skill.

Radio Waves and Microwaves

Radio waves have the longest wavelength and lowest frequency of all EM waves. Wavelengths range from about 1 mm to several kilometres. They are used for television and radio broadcasts, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, and communication with satellites. Radio waves can diffract (bend) around hills and buildings, which is why you can receive radio signals even when you are not in direct line of sight of the transmitter.

Microwaves have shorter wavelengths than radio waves (roughly 1 mm to 30 cm). They are used in satellite communications, mobile phone signals, and microwave ovens. In a microwave oven, the waves are absorbed by water molecules in food, causing them to vibrate and heat up. Microwaves can penetrate through the atmosphere and clouds, making them ideal for satellite transmissions.

Infrared Radiation

Infrared radiation (IR) is emitted by all objects that have a temperature above absolute zero. The hotter an object is, the more infrared it emits. This is the basis of thermal imaging cameras, which detect temperature differences and display them as colour maps — used by firefighters to find people in smoke-filled buildings, and by police helicopters to track suspects at night.

Other uses include electric heaters and toasters (which emit infrared to warm food and rooms), TV remote controls, optical fibre communication, and cooking. When infrared is absorbed by the skin, it is felt as warmth. Excessive exposure can cause skin burns.

Visible Light

Visible light is the only part of the EM spectrum that the human eye can detect. It occupies a very narrow band between infrared and ultraviolet. White light is made up of a continuous spectrum of colours — red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet — which can be separated using a prism. Red light has the longest wavelength within this band, and violet has the shortest.

Visible light is used for vision (obviously), photography, fibre optic communication, and illumination. Different surfaces absorb, reflect, or transmit different wavelengths, which is why objects appear as different colours. A red shirt, for example, reflects red wavelengths and absorbs most other colours.

Ultraviolet Radiation

Ultraviolet radiation (UV) has a shorter wavelength and higher frequency than visible light. The Sun is the main natural source of UV. It is also produced by sun lamps and tanning beds. UV radiation causes the skin to produce vitamin D, which is essential for healthy bones.

However, overexposure to UV can cause sunburn, premature skin ageing, and increases the risk of skin cancer. UV can also damage the eyes, potentially leading to cataracts. Protective measures include wearing sunscreen, sunglasses, and limiting time in direct sunlight. UV is used to detect forged banknotes (special inks fluoresce under UV), in sterilisation of water and medical equipment, and in energy-efficient fluorescent lamps.

Key Fact

UV, X-rays, and gamma rays have enough energy to cause ionisation — they can knock electrons out of atoms, creating ions. This is why they are called ionising radiation. Ionising radiation can damage cells and DNA, increasing the risk of cancer.

X-rays

X-rays have very short wavelengths and very high frequencies. They can pass through soft body tissue but are absorbed by dense materials such as bone and metal. This property makes them invaluable in medicine for producing images of bones to check for fractures, and in airport security scanners to inspect luggage.

Medical X-rays work because bone absorbs X-rays more than soft tissue. A photographic plate or digital detector is placed behind the patient, and an X-ray beam is passed through the body. Bones appear white on the image (they block the X-rays), while soft tissue appears darker (X-rays pass through). CT scans use X-rays taken from multiple angles to build a detailed 3D image of internal organs and structures.

Because X-rays are ionising, radiographers take precautions: they stand behind lead-lined screens, patients wear lead aprons to protect areas not being imaged, and exposure times are kept as short as possible. The benefits of diagnosis must outweigh the small risk of cell damage from the radiation.

Gamma Rays

Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength and highest frequency of all EM waves. They originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom — typically from radioactive decay. Gamma rays are the most penetrating type of EM radiation, passing through most materials including body tissue and thin metal sheets. Only thick lead or several metres of concrete can significantly reduce their intensity.

Uses of gamma rays include: sterilising medical instruments and food (killing bacteria without heat), treating cancer through radiotherapy (focused beams destroy tumour cells), and as a medical tracer when a patient is injected with a gamma-emitting substance so doctors can track its path through the body. Because gamma rays are strongly ionising, overexposure can cause cell damage, mutations, radiation sickness, and cancer.

Key Fact

All EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum (3 × 108 m/s), but they differ in wavelength and frequency. The higher the frequency, the more energy the wave carries — this is why gamma rays are more dangerous than radio waves.

Radio waves: TV, radio broadcasts, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi. Danger: No significant danger at normal exposure levels.

Microwaves: Satellite communication, mobile phones, cooking food. Danger: Internal heating of body tissue if absorbed (though levels from phones are very low).

Infrared: Heaters, thermal cameras, remote controls, cooking. Danger: Skin burns from excessive exposure.

Visible light: Vision, photography, fibre optics. Danger: Eye damage from very intense sources (e.g. lasers, looking directly at the Sun).

Ultraviolet: Fluorescent lamps, detecting forgeries, sterilisation, vitamin D production. Danger: Sunburn, premature ageing, skin cancer, cataracts.

X-rays: Medical imaging, security scanners, CT scans. Danger: Cell damage and increased cancer risk (ionising).

Gamma rays: Sterilisation, cancer treatment (radiotherapy), medical tracers. Danger: Cell damage, mutations, cancer, radiation sickness (most ionising).
lessons.exam_tip_html: In Physics Paper 2, you will often be asked to compare different EM waves or link a specific wave type to its uses and dangers. Always state whether the wave is ionising or non-ionising, name a specific use with a brief explanation of how it works, and identify the hazard. For “explain” questions, make sure you connect the property (e.g. short wavelength, high penetration) to the use or danger — do not just list facts. For calculation questions using v = f × λ, remember that all EM waves in a vacuum travel at 3 × 108 m/s.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • All EM waves are transverse, travel at 3 × 108 m/s in a vacuum, and differ only in wavelength and frequency. The spectrum runs: radio → microwave → infrared → visible → ultraviolet → X-ray → gamma.
  • Each type has specific uses linked to its properties — e.g. X-rays penetrate soft tissue (medical imaging), infrared is emitted by warm objects (thermal cameras), radio waves diffract around obstacles (broadcasting).
  • UV, X-rays, and gamma rays are ionising — they can damage cells and DNA, increasing cancer risk. Know the precautions for each.

practice_questions.text: Compare the uses and dangers of X-rays and gamma rays. Explain one similarity and one difference.

Award up to 4 marks:
Similarity (up to 2 marks):
• Both are ionising radiation (1)
• Both can damage cells/DNA and increase cancer risk (1)

Difference in use (up to 2 marks):
• X-rays are mainly used for medical imaging (e.g. checking for broken bones) because they pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone (1)
• Gamma rays are used for sterilising medical equipment or treating cancer (radiotherapy) because they are more penetrating and can destroy cells inside the body (1)

Accept other valid comparisons, e.g. gamma rays originate from the nucleus, X-rays from electron transitions; gamma rays have shorter wavelength/higher frequency.

practice_questions.text: Electromagnetic waves have many uses in everyday life and medicine. Evaluate the benefits and risks of using electromagnetic radiation, referring to at least three different types of EM wave in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Thorough, balanced evaluation covering three or more EM wave types with specific benefits and risks. Reaches a justified conclusion about whether benefits outweigh risks or how risks can be managed.
Indicative content:
• Radio waves: enable communication (TV, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth) with no significant health risks at normal levels (benefit outweighs risk)
• Infrared: used in heaters and thermal imaging cameras (benefit: locating people in fires) but excessive exposure causes skin burns
• UV: enables vitamin D production and sterilisation but is ionising — causes sunburn, skin cancer, and cataracts. Risk managed by sunscreen and limiting exposure
• X-rays: vital for diagnosing fractures and diseases (CT scans) but ionising — radiographers use lead shielding and short exposure times to minimise risk
• Gamma rays: used in radiotherapy (destroying cancer cells) and sterilisation but most ionising and dangerous. Benefits in cancer treatment are considered to outweigh the risks
• Conclusion: EM radiation is essential in modern life and medicine; risks are managed through safety precautions and limiting exposure
Mid band (3-4): Sound coverage of at least two EM types with some benefits and risks but limited evaluation or missing conclusion.
Lower band (1-2): Basic points about one or two EM types with little development. May only describe benefits or risks, not both.

lessons.title: Magnets, Electromagnetism and the Motor Effect
lessons.content_html:
Magnetism as a Non-Contact Force

magnetism is a non-contact force — it acts at a distance without objects touching. Unlike gravity, which acts between all masses, magnetism only acts between three types of object: permanent magnets, induced magnets, and electromagnets. Only certain materials are magnetic: iron, steel, nickel, and cobalt.

Every magnet has two poles — a north pole and a south pole. The poles are where the magnetic field is strongest. When two magnets are brought together, like poles repel and unlike poles attract. If you hang a bar magnet on a string so it can spin freely, its north pole will point towards geographic north — this is how a compass works.

Key Fact

Like poles repel. Unlike poles attract. The poles are where the magnetic forces are strongest.

Permanent and Induced Magnets

A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field all the time. It does not need electricity or another magnet to work. Bar magnets, horseshoe magnets, and fridge magnets are all permanent magnets. Steel is used to make permanent magnets because it does not lose its magnetism easily.

An induced magnet is a magnetic material that becomes magnetised only when it is placed inside a magnetic field. For example, bringing a permanent magnet close to an iron nail turns the nail into a temporary magnet. The induced magnet’s poles always line up so that the nearest pole is opposite to the permanent magnet’s pole — this means induced magnets are always attracted to the permanent magnet, never repelled.

Steel retains its magnetism when removed from a magnetic field, making it ideal for permanent magnets. Iron magnetises more strongly than steel but loses its magnetism quickly once removed from the field — this makes iron better for temporary or induced magnets. Electromagnets use an iron core precisely because the magnetism must switch on and off with the current.

Magnetic Field Lines

A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where a magnetic force acts. We represent it using field lines. These lines always run from the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet. Where the lines are close together the field is strong; where they spread apart the field is weak.

You can reveal field lines by sprinkling iron filings around a bar magnet or by tracing the direction a plotting compass needle points as you move it around the magnet. Two unlike poles placed near each other produce field lines that curve between them (attraction). Two like poles produce lines that push away from each other (repulsion).

Key Fact

Magnetic field lines always point from north to south. Closer lines mean a stronger field. The field is strongest at the poles.

Electromagnets

When an electric current flows through a wire, it produces a magnetic field around the wire. The field lines form concentric circles centred on the wire. If you increase the current, the field gets stronger. Reversing the current reverses the direction of the field.

Winding the wire into a coil called a solenoid concentrates the magnetic field. Inside a solenoid, the field lines are parallel and evenly spaced — this is a uniform magnetic field. The field pattern around a solenoid looks very similar to the field around a bar magnet, with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other.

Adding an iron core inside a solenoid creates an electromagnet. The iron core becomes an induced magnet and greatly increases the field strength. Three ways to make an electromagnet stronger are: increase the current, add more turns of wire, or use a softer iron core. When the current is switched off, the iron core loses its magnetism almost immediately — this is what makes electromagnets so useful.

Electromagnets are used in scrapyard cranes (pick up and drop steel cars by switching the current on and off), circuit breakers (an excessive current magnetises a coil which trips a switch to break the circuit), electric bells (the electromagnet attracts an iron armature to strike the bell, then the circuit breaks and the process repeats), and relays (a small current in one circuit activates an electromagnet that closes a switch in a separate, higher-power circuit).

The Motor Effect

When a conductor carrying a current is placed inside a magnetic field, it experiences a force. This is called the motor effect. The force acts at right angles to both the direction of the current and the direction of the magnetic field. If either the current or the magnetic field is reversed, the direction of the force reverses too.

The size of the force depends on three factors: the magnetic flux density (how strong the field is, measured in tesla, T), the current through the conductor (in amps, A), and the length of the conductor inside the field (in metres, m). The equation is:

Key Fact

\(Force = \text{magnetic flux density} \times current \times length\)
F = B × I × l
where F is in newtons (N), B is in tesla (T), I is in amps (A), and l is in metres (m).

Fleming’s Left-Hand Rule

Fleming’s left-hand rule tells you the direction of the force (and therefore the direction of motion). Hold your left hand with the thumb, first finger, and second finger all at right angles to each other:

First finger — direction of the magnetic Field (north to south). Second finger — direction of the Current (positive to negative). Thumb — direction of Motion (the force on the conductor).

Step 1: Identify the direction of the magnetic field (from north to south pole of the magnets). Step 2: Identify the direction of the current (conventional current flows from positive to negative). Step 3: Point your left hand’s first finger in the field direction and your second finger in the current direction. Step 4: Your thumb now points in the direction the wire will move. If the question gives two of the three directions, use the rule to find the third.

Electric Motors

An electric motor uses the motor effect to produce continuous rotation. A rectangular coil of wire sits between the poles of two permanent magnets. When current flows through the coil, the two sides of the coil experience forces in opposite directions (one side is pushed up, the other is pushed down), creating a turning effect.

The coil would stop after half a turn because the forces would then act to push it back the other way. To prevent this, a split-ring commutator reverses the direction of the current every half turn. This means the forces always push the same side of the coil in the same direction, keeping it spinning continuously. Carbon brushes maintain electrical contact with the spinning commutator.

Key Fact

Three ways to make an electric motor spin faster: increase the current, use a stronger magnet (greater magnetic flux density), or add more turns of wire to the coil.

The key components are: a rectangular coil of insulated wire mounted on an axle so it can rotate, two permanent magnets with opposite poles facing each other to create a uniform field, a split-ring commutator attached to the coil that reverses the current direction every half turn, and carbon brushes that press against the commutator to connect the coil to the power supply. The coil rotates because the two sides experience forces in opposite directions due to the motor effect.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For calculation questions using F = B × I × l, always show your working: write out the formula, substitute values with units, and calculate. If you need to rearrange, use the formula triangle. For “Explain” questions about the motor effect or electric motors, state the physics rule first (e.g. “a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force”), then explain each step of the process in order. When asked about Fleming’s left-hand rule, always state which finger represents which quantity — field, current, and motion.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Permanent magnets produce their own field; induced magnets only become magnetic inside an external field and are always attracted to the permanent magnet.
  • An electromagnet is a solenoid with an iron core — its strength depends on current, number of turns, and the core material. It can be switched on and off.
  • The motor effect (F = B × I × l) describes the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, and Fleming’s left-hand rule gives the direction of that force. A split-ring commutator keeps a DC motor spinning continuously.

practice_questions.text: Describe the magnetic field pattern around a bar magnet.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Field lines go from the north pole to the south pole (1).
• The lines are closest together at the poles / the field is strongest at the poles (1).
• Accept: the lines curve around the magnet and do not cross.

practice_questions.text: A wire of length 0.25 m carries a current of 3.0 A in a magnetic field of flux density 0.40 T. Calculate the force on the wire.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• F = B × I × l = 0.40 × 3.0 × 0.25 (1)
• F = 0.30 N (1)
• Allow ecf if working is shown but arithmetic is incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Explain why an induced magnet is always attracted to the permanent magnet that causes it.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• When a magnetic material is placed in a magnetic field, it becomes temporarily magnetised / becomes an induced magnet (1).
• The induced magnet’s poles line up so that the nearest pole is opposite to the permanent magnet’s pole (1).
• Opposite / unlike poles attract, so the induced magnet is always attracted (1).

practice_questions.text: Compare the magnetic properties of a permanent magnet and an electromagnet. Explain one advantage of using an electromagnet instead of a permanent magnet in a scrapyard crane.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• A permanent magnet produces its own field at all times, whereas an electromagnet only produces a field when a current flows (1).
• A permanent magnet cannot be turned off, but an electromagnet can be switched on and off (1).
• Advantage: the crane can pick up magnetic materials when the current is on and release them by switching the current off (1).
• This means items can be moved and dropped precisely, which would not be possible with a permanent magnet (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a simple DC electric motor works. In your answer, include the role of the split-ring commutator and describe how the speed of the motor can be increased.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed and coherent explanation covering the motor effect, the role of the commutator, and at least one method to increase speed. Uses correct scientific terminology.
Mid band (3-4): Explains the basic motor effect and mentions the commutator, but may lack detail on one aspect.
Lower band (1-2): Shows limited understanding, e.g. states current and magnets are needed but does not explain the process.
Indicative content:
• A current-carrying coil is placed between the poles of two permanent magnets.
• The motor effect means each side of the coil experiences a force (in opposite directions) because the current flows in opposite directions on each side.
• These opposite forces create a turning effect / couple, causing the coil to rotate.
• The split-ring commutator reverses the direction of current every half turn so the forces continue to act in the same rotational direction.
• Carbon brushes maintain contact with the spinning commutator.
• Speed can be increased by: increasing the current, using a stronger magnet (greater flux density), or adding more turns to the coil.
• F = B × I × l may be referenced to explain how force depends on these factors.

glossary_terms.definition: A force that acts at a distance without physical contact between objects.
The region around a magnet where a magnetic material experiences a force.
A magnet that produces its own magnetic field without needing an external source of magnetism.
A material that becomes a temporary magnet when placed in a magnetic field, losing its magnetism when removed.
A coil of wire that produces a magnetic field when an electric current flows through it.
A magnetic field in which the field lines are parallel and equally spaced, meaning the field strength is the same at every point.
A solenoid with a soft iron core that behaves as a magnet only when an electric current flows through the coil.
The force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field.
A method for finding the direction of force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field using the thumb, first finger, and second finger of the left hand.
A device that converts electrical energy into rotational kinetic energy using the motor effect.
A device in a DC motor that reverses the direction of current through the coil every half turn so the coil continues to spin in the same direction.

lessons.title: Moments, Levers, Gears and Momentum Changes
lessons.content_html:
Moments and the Turning Effect of Forces

When you push a door open, you apply a force at a distance from the hinge. The door swings because your push creates a moment. A moment is the turning effect of a force around a fixed point called a pivot.

Key Fact

The moment of a force is calculated using: \(moment (Nm) = force (N) \times \text{distance from pivot} (m)\), or \(M = F \times d\). The distance must be measured perpendicular to the direction of the force.

The unit of a moment is the newton metre (Nm). A larger force or a greater distance from the pivot both produce a larger moment. This is why it is easier to open a door by pushing near the handle (far from the hinge) than by pushing close to the hinge.

A child with a weight of 420 N sits 1.6 m from the pivot of a see-saw. Calculate the moment of the force.

\(M = F \times d\) = 420 × 1.6 = 672 Nm

Always check that the distance is in metres. If you are given 20 cm, convert to 0.2 m before substituting into the equation.

Balancing Moments — The Principle of Moments

When an object is balanced (in equilibrium), the total clockwise moments about the pivot equal the total anticlockwise moments. This is the principle of moments.

On a balanced see-saw, if a heavier child sits closer to the pivot and a lighter child sits further away, the moments can be equal. You can use this principle to find an unknown force or distance:

\(F_{1} \times d_{1} = F_{2} \times d_{2}\)

Levers

A lever is a simple machine that multiplies the effect of a force. It consists of a rigid bar that turns around a pivot. By applying a small effort force at a large distance from the pivot, you can move a heavy load that is close to the pivot.

Everyday examples include crowbars, wheelbarrows, scissors, and spanners. A builder using a crowbar applies a force at the long end to lift a heavy floorboard at the short end — the long lever arm means a smaller force is needed to create the same moment.

Gears

A gear is a toothed wheel that meshes with another toothed wheel. Gears transmit the turning effect of a force from one part of a machine to another.

Key Fact

When a small gear drives a large gear, the large gear turns more slowly but with a greater moment (turning force). When a large gear drives a small gear, the small gear turns faster but with a smaller moment. Gears that mesh always turn in opposite directions.

Gears are used in bicycles, cars and clocks. A low gear on a bicycle uses a large rear gear driven by the pedals, giving a greater turning force at the wheel — useful for climbing hills. A high gear uses a smaller rear gear, giving less force but more speed on flat roads.

Momentum

Momentum is a measure of how difficult it is to stop a moving object. It depends on both mass and velocity:

\(momentum (kg m/s) = mass (kg) \times velocity (m/s)\), or \(p = m \times v\)

A heavy lorry travelling at 3 m/s has a momentum of 10,000 × 3 = 30,000 kg m/s. A bullet has much less mass, but its very high velocity gives it a large momentum too. Momentum is a vector quantity — it has both size and direction.

Force and the Rate of Change of Momentum

When a force acts on an object, the object’s momentum changes. The faster the momentum changes, the greater the force involved. This relationship is expressed as:

\(force (N) = \text{change in momentum} (kg m/s) \div time (s)\), or \(F = \Delta p / t\)

Key Fact

A fast change in momentum produces a large force, which can cause serious injury. A slow change in momentum produces a smaller force. This is why safety features are designed to increase the time over which momentum changes during a collision.

A person of mass 71 kg is in a car travelling at 25 m/s. The car crashes and stops.

Step 1 — Calculate momentum: p = m × v = 71 × 25 = 1,775 kg m/s

Step 2 — With crumple zones (crash time 0.54 s): F = 1,775 ÷ 0.54 = 3,287 N

Step 3 — Without crumple zones (crash time 0.35 s): F = 1,775 ÷ 0.35 = 5,071 N

The crumple zones reduce the force on the person by about 35% because the collision time is longer.

Safety Features in Vehicles

Modern vehicles include several features that protect occupants by increasing the time over which momentum changes, thereby reducing the force experienced:

  • Crumple zones — the front and rear of the car are designed to crumple and deform during a collision. This absorbs kinetic energy and extends the time of impact.
  • Seatbelts — stretch slightly during a crash, increasing the time it takes for the person to decelerate and spreading the force across the chest.
  • Air bags — inflate rapidly and then deflate as the person pushes into them, increasing the time of deceleration and cushioning the impact on the head and chest.

The change in momentum in a crash is fixed — the person goes from moving to stationary. Since F = Δp / t, if the time (t) increases, the force (F) must decrease for the same change in momentum (Δp). Every safety feature works on this principle: absorb the impact over a longer period to reduce the peak force on the body.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In calculation questions on moments, always check units — convert centimetres to metres before substituting. For questions on vehicle safety, explain how the feature increases the time of impact and state that this reduces the force (F = Δp / t). Examiners want both parts for full marks. If asked to “compare” two situations, calculate both values and write a concluding sentence stating which is greater and why.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A moment is the turning effect of a force: M = F × d. Levers and gears use moments to multiply forces.
  • Momentum (p = mv) describes how hard it is to stop a moving object. Force equals the rate of change of momentum: F = Δp / t.
  • Vehicle safety features (crumple zones, seatbelts, air bags) increase the collision time to reduce the force on occupants.

lessons.title: Reflection, Sound Waves and Waves for Detection
lessons.content_html:
The Law of Reflection

When a wave hits a boundary between two different materials, it can be reflected, transmitted, or absorbed. Reflection is when the wave bounces back from the surface. This applies to all types of waves — light, sound, and water waves all follow the same rules.

To describe reflection precisely, scientists use a set of standard terms. The normal is an imaginary line drawn at 90° (perpendicular) to the reflecting surface at the point where the wave hits. The incoming wave is called the incident ray, and the wave that bounces back is the reflected ray.

The angle of incidence is measured between the incident ray and the normal. The angle of reflection is measured between the reflected ray and the normal. Both angles are always measured from the normal — not from the surface of the mirror.

Key Fact

The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence always equals the angle of reflection. This is true for every type of wave at every surface.

In the exam, you may need to construct ray diagrams. Draw the mirror as a straight line, then draw the normal at 90° to the mirror at the point where the ray hits. Mark the incident ray coming in and the reflected ray going out. Use a protractor to check that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

Smooth surfaces (like a flat mirror) produce specular reflection. The reflected rays are all parallel, so a clear image is formed. This is why you can see your reflection in a mirror or in still water.

Rough surfaces scatter reflected waves in all directions. This is called diffuse reflection. Each tiny part of the surface still obeys the law of reflection, but because the surface is uneven, the reflected rays go in many different directions. No clear image is formed.

An image formed in a plane mirror is virtual (cannot be projected onto a screen), upright (not upside down), and laterally inverted (left and right are swapped). This is why the word “AMBULANCE” is written backwards on the front of ambulances — so it reads correctly in a driver’s rear-view mirror.

Sound Waves

Sound is produced when an object vibrates. These vibrations travel through a medium (solid, liquid, or gas) as a longitudinal wave. In a longitudinal wave, the particles vibrate back and forth parallel to the direction the wave travels, creating areas of compression (high pressure) and rarefaction (low pressure).

Sound waves are mechanical waves — they need a medium to travel through. Sound cannot travel through a vacuum. This can be demonstrated using a bell jar experiment: as air is pumped out, the sound of a ringing bell fades until it becomes inaudible, even though the bell is still vibrating.

Sound travels at different speeds through different materials. It travels fastest through solids (particles are closest together), slower through liquids, and slowest through gases. In air at room temperature, the speed of sound is approximately 330 m/s.

Key Fact

The range of normal human hearing is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz). Sounds below 20 Hz are called infrasound. Sounds above 20,000 Hz are called ultrasound.

When sound waves enter the ear, they cause the eardrum to vibrate. These vibrations are passed through the tiny ear bones to the inner ear, where they are converted into electrical signals sent to the brain. The eardrum and ear bones can only vibrate at certain rates, which is why our hearing is limited to the 20 Hz–20,000 Hz range.

The pitch of a sound depends on its frequency — a higher frequency means a higher pitch. The loudness of a sound depends on its amplitude — a larger amplitude means a louder sound. On an oscilloscope trace, higher pitch appears as waves closer together, and louder sound appears as taller waves.

An echo is a reflection of sound. When sound waves hit a hard, smooth surface (such as a cliff face or the wall of a cave), they bounce back and can be heard again after a short delay. Soft, rough surfaces absorb sound rather than reflecting it — this is why cinemas have padded walls and curtains to prevent echoes that would spoil the film audio.

Echo calculations are common in exams. Remember that the sound wave travels there and back, so the distance to the reflecting surface is half the total distance the sound travels. Use the equation: distance = speed × time, then divide by 2.

Ultrasound and Its Uses

Ultrasound refers to sound waves with frequencies above 20,000 Hz — beyond the upper limit of human hearing. Despite being inaudible to humans, ultrasound has many practical applications because of the way it reflects at boundaries between materials of different densities.

Key Fact

When ultrasound waves reach a boundary between two media with different densities, they are partly reflected back. A detector measures the time between the ultrasound pulse leaving the source and the reflection arriving back. This time is used to calculate the depth of the boundary.

Medical imaging: Ultrasound is widely used in pre-natal scanning to check that a foetus is developing normally. The ultrasound waves are partly reflected at the boundaries between different tissues (skin, muscle, bone, fluid). A computer combines many readings to build a detailed image. Ultrasound is preferred over X-rays for this purpose because it is non-invasive, considered safe (it does not cause cell damage like ionising radiation), and provides real-time images.

Echo sounding and SONAR (Sound Navigation and Ranging): Ships and submarines send pulses of ultrasound towards the sea floor. The pulses reflect off the bottom and return to a detector on the vessel. By measuring the time taken for the pulse to return and knowing the speed of sound in water, the depth can be calculated. SONAR is also used to detect submarines, shoals of fish, and underwater obstacles. Bats and dolphins use a natural version of this — they emit ultrasound and listen for the echoes to navigate and locate prey.

A submarine sends an ultrasound pulse to the sea floor. The pulse returns 0.35 s later. The speed of sound in water is 1,600 m/s.

Step 1: Total distance = speed × time = 1,600 × 0.35 = 560 m.
Step 2: The pulse travels to the sea floor and back, so divide by 2: 560 ÷ 2 = 280 m.
The sea floor is 280 m below the submarine.

Seismic Waves and the Structure of the Earth

Earthquakes produce seismic waves that travel through the Earth. By studying how these waves travel, scientists have been able to work out the internal structure of the Earth — something that cannot be observed directly. There are two main types of seismic wave.

P-waves (primary waves) are longitudinal waves. They cause the ground to vibrate in the same direction the wave is travelling. P-waves can travel through both solids and liquids, so they can pass through all layers of the Earth — the crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core. They are the fastest seismic waves and arrive at detection stations first.

S-waves (secondary waves) are transverse waves. They cause the ground to vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel. S-waves can only travel through solids — they cannot pass through liquids. This means S-waves are blocked by the Earth’s liquid outer core.

Key Fact

The fact that S-waves cannot travel through the outer core proves it is liquid. P-waves can travel through the outer core but change direction at the boundaries between layers. Together, the behaviour of P-waves and S-waves provides evidence that the Earth has a solid inner core, a liquid outer core, and a solid mantle (which behaves like a solid despite being able to flow very slowly).

Both types of seismic wave change speed as they travel deeper into the Earth because the density of the rock increases. This causes the waves to follow curved paths through the mantle. When they reach a boundary between layers of different density or state, they change direction suddenly — this is refraction. By mapping where P-waves and S-waves are detected on the Earth’s surface, scientists can work out the size and state of each internal layer.

After an earthquake, seismometers around the world detect the arriving waves. There is a large “shadow zone” on the far side of the Earth where no S-waves are detected at all. This shadow zone shows that the outer core is liquid, because S-waves cannot pass through liquid. P-waves are also refracted at the core–mantle boundary, creating their own shadow zone, but they do eventually reach the far side after being bent through the core.

These observations allowed scientists to discover that the Earth has a thin crust (10–100 km thick), a thick mantle that behaves as a solid, a liquid outer core made mainly of iron and nickel, and a solid inner core. Without seismic wave studies, this internal structure would remain unknown.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In questions on waves for detection and exploration, always state the type of wave (longitudinal or transverse), the medium it can or cannot travel through, and the evidence this provides. For echo and SONAR calculations, remember the sound travels there and back — divide the total distance by 2. When drawing ray diagrams, label the normal, incident ray, reflected ray, and both angles carefully using a protractor.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection — both measured from the normal. Smooth surfaces give specular reflection; rough surfaces scatter waves.
  • Sound is a longitudinal, mechanical wave. Human hearing ranges from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Ultrasound (above 20 kHz) is used in medical imaging and SONAR by detecting reflected pulses.
  • Seismic P-waves (longitudinal, travel through solids and liquids) and S-waves (transverse, solids only) provide evidence for the Earth’s layered structure — including proof that the outer core is liquid.

• When ultrasound reaches a boundary between tissues of different densities, it is partly reflected back
• A detector measures the time taken for reflections to return
• A computer uses these time measurements to build up a detailed image of the foetus

• Ultrasound provides real-time / live images so movement can be observed

glossary_terms.definition: The bouncing back of a wave when it hits a boundary between two different materials.
An imaginary line drawn at 90 degrees (perpendicular) to a reflecting surface at the point where the incoming ray hits.
The ray of light or wave approaching a reflecting or refracting surface.
The ray of light or wave that bounces back from a reflecting surface.
The angle between the incident ray and the normal line at the point of reflection.
The angle between the reflected ray and the normal line at the point of reflection.
Reflection from a smooth surface where all reflected rays are parallel, producing a clear image.
A wave in which the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer, with areas of compression and rarefaction.
A wave that requires a medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to travel through and cannot travel through a vacuum.
A reflection of sound that occurs when sound waves bounce off a hard surface and return to the listener.
Sound waves with frequencies above 20,000 Hz (above the range of human hearing), used in medical imaging, sonar, and industrial applications.
Sound Navigation and Ranging — a technique that uses pulses of sound (usually ultrasound) to measure distances underwater by timing the echo.
Waves of energy that travel through the Earth, produced by earthquakes or explosions. The two main types are P-waves and S-waves.
Primary waves — longitudinal seismic waves that travel through both solids and liquids. They are the fastest seismic waves and arrive first at a detector.
Secondary waves — transverse seismic waves that can only travel through solids. They are slower than P-waves and cannot pass through the liquid outer core.

lessons.title: Lenses, Visible Light and Black Body Radiation
lessons.content_html:
Lenses and Refraction

A lens forms an image by refracting light. When light passes from air into glass it slows down, and when it leaves the glass it speeds up again. The curved surfaces of a lens bend the light in a controlled way, either bringing rays together or spreading them apart.

There are two key terms you must know for ray diagrams. The principal focus (also called the focal point, F) is the point where parallel rays of light either converge or appear to diverge from after passing through the lens. The focal length is the distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.

Convex (Converging) Lenses

A convex lens is thickest at the centre. It refracts parallel rays of light inwards so that they converge and meet at the principal focus on the other side of the lens. This is why convex lenses are also called converging lenses.

The type of image a convex lens produces depends on where the object is placed relative to the focal point. If the object is beyond the focal point (further from the lens than F), the lens produces a real image. A real image is formed where the refracted rays actually meet, and it can be captured on a screen. Real images are always inverted (upside down). Cameras and projectors use convex lenses in this way.

If the object is placed between the focal point and the lens (closer than F), the refracted rays diverge. They appear to come from a point on the same side as the object, producing a virtual image. A virtual image is upright, magnified, and cannot be projected onto a screen. This is how a magnifying glass works.

Key Fact

Convex lens images: Object beyond F → real, inverted image (can be on a screen). Object between F and the lens → virtual, upright, magnified image (magnifying glass).

Concave (Diverging) Lenses

A concave lens is thinnest at the centre. It refracts parallel rays of light outwards so they spread apart. If you trace the diverging rays back, they appear to come from a single point on the same side as the incoming light — this is the principal focus of a concave lens.

A concave lens always produces a virtual image, no matter where the object is placed. The image is always upright, smaller than the object, and on the same side as the object. Concave lenses are used in spectacles to correct short-sightedness (myopia).

For a convex lens, draw two rays from the top of the object: (1) a ray parallel to the principal axis that refracts through the focal point on the other side, and (2) a ray through the centre of the lens that continues straight. Where the two refracted rays meet is the top of the image.

For a concave lens, draw: (1) a ray parallel to the principal axis that refracts and appears to come from the focal point on the same side as the incoming light, and (2) a ray through the centre of the lens that continues straight. Trace the diverging rays back with dashed lines to find the virtual image.

Magnification

Magnification tells you how much bigger or smaller the image is compared to the object. It is calculated using the equation:

\(magnification = \text{image height} \div \text{object height}\)

Magnification is a ratio, so it has no units. Both heights must be measured in the same unit (mm or cm). A magnification greater than 1 means the image is larger than the object; less than 1 means it is smaller.

Key Fact

Magnification equation: magnification = image height ÷ object height. This is a ratio with no units. A magnification of 5 means the image is 5 times larger than the real object.

Visible Light and Colour

Visible light is a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum. It is the only part that human eyes can detect. The visible spectrum ranges from red (longest wavelength, about 700 nm) to violet (shortest wavelength, about 400 nm), with the colours blending smoothly into each other — they do not have sharp boundaries.

The colour of an opaque object depends on which wavelengths of light it reflects and which it absorbs. A red jumper reflects red light and absorbs all other colours. A white object reflects all wavelengths equally, while a black object absorbs all wavelengths.

A colour filter works by absorbing certain wavelengths of light and transmitting others. A red filter absorbs all colours except red, so only red light passes through. A blue filter transmits only blue light.

When you view a coloured object under coloured light, the object can only reflect the colours present in the light. A red shirt under red light still looks red (it reflects the red light). But a red shirt under blue light looks black — there is no red light to reflect, and it absorbs the blue light.

Transparent objects transmit all light through them (e.g. clear glass). Translucent objects transmit some light but scatter it, so you cannot see clearly through them (e.g. frosted glass). Opaque objects do not transmit any light.

Specular reflection occurs when light reflects off a smooth surface (such as a mirror or still water). All the reflected rays travel in the same direction, producing a clear reflected image.

Diffuse reflection occurs when light hits a rough surface (such as paper or fabric). The reflected rays scatter in many different directions, so no clear image is formed. Most objects around us cause diffuse reflection.

Black Body Radiation

All objects, no matter what their temperature, continuously emit and absorb infrared radiation. The hotter an object is, the more infrared radiation it emits in a given time. This is why you can feel the warmth radiating from a hot radiator or a bonfire even without touching it.

A perfect black body is defined as an object that absorbs all of the radiation incident upon it. It does not reflect or transmit any radiation. Because a good absorber is also a good emitter, a perfect black body is also the best possible emitter of radiation at any given temperature.

Key Fact

A perfect black body absorbs all radiation falling on it and emits radiation at the maximum possible rate for its temperature. Dark, matt surfaces are better absorbers and emitters than light, shiny surfaces.

As the temperature of an object increases, the intensity of radiation emitted at every wavelength increases. However, the intensity of shorter wavelengths increases more rapidly. This is why very hot objects (such as stars) shift from glowing red to orange, yellow, white, and eventually blue-white as they get hotter.

An object is in thermal equilibrium when the rate at which it absorbs radiation equals the rate at which it emits radiation — its temperature stays constant. If an object absorbs radiation faster than it emits it, the temperature rises. If it emits faster than it absorbs, the temperature falls.

The temperature of the Earth depends on the balance between energy absorbed from the Sun, energy reflected back into space, and energy emitted by the Earth into space. Changes to the atmosphere (such as increased greenhouse gases) can alter this balance and affect the Earth’s temperature.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on lenses often ask you to draw or interpret ray diagrams — practise these until you can do them quickly and accurately. For magnification calculations, always show your working and state that magnification has no units. Black body radiation questions may ask you to explain why a dark surface cools faster than a shiny one, or to describe how the Earth’s temperature is maintained — link your answer to the balance between absorption and emission of radiation.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Convex lenses converge light and can produce real (inverted) or virtual (upright, magnified) images depending on object position. Concave lenses diverge light and always produce virtual, upright, smaller images.
  • The colour of an opaque object depends on which wavelengths it reflects — colour filters absorb certain wavelengths and transmit others.
  • All objects emit and absorb infrared radiation. A perfect black body absorbs all incident radiation and is the best emitter. The Earth’s temperature depends on the balance between absorbed and emitted radiation.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by a ‘perfect black body’ and describe how the temperature of the Earth is maintained by the balance between absorption and emission of radiation.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed and coherent explanation covering the definition of a perfect black body and a clear description of how absorption and emission balance determines the Earth’s temperature. E.g. A perfect black body absorbs all radiation incident upon it — it does not reflect or transmit any radiation. It is also the best possible emitter of radiation. All objects emit infrared radiation, and hotter objects emit more. The Earth absorbs radiation from the Sun (mainly visible light and UV). The Earth also emits infrared radiation into space. When the rate of absorption equals the rate of emission, the Earth is in thermal equilibrium and its temperature is constant. If absorption exceeds emission (e.g. due to increased greenhouse gases trapping infrared), the temperature rises.
Mid band (3-4): Reasonable explanation of black body and some reference to absorption/emission balance, but may lack detail on thermal equilibrium or the Earth’s energy balance.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements such as ‘a black body absorbs radiation’ or ‘the Earth gets heat from the Sun’, with limited development.

The point where parallel rays of light converge (convex) or appear to diverge from (concave) after passing through a lens.
The distance between the centre of a lens and its principal focus.
A lens that is thickest at the centre and refracts parallel rays of light inwards so they meet at the principal focus — also called a converging lens.
An image formed where light rays actually converge — it can be projected onto a screen.

A lens that is thinnest at the centre and refracts parallel rays of light outwards so they appear to diverge from the principal focus — also called a diverging lens.
The ratio of image height to object height — it has no units.
The continuous range of electromagnetic waves ordered by wavelength and frequency — from radio waves (longest) to gamma rays (shortest).
A transparent material that absorbs certain wavelengths of light and transmits others, so only selected colours pass through.
Reflection of light from a smooth surface where all rays reflect in a single direction — producing a clear image (e.g. a mirror).
Reflection of light from a rough surface where rays scatter in many directions — no clear image is formed.
Electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths longer than visible light but shorter than microwaves — associated with thermal energy transfer.
An idealised object that absorbs all electromagnetic radiation that falls on it, reflecting and transmitting none — it is also the best possible emitter of radiation.
The state reached when an object absorbs radiation at the same rate as it emits radiation, so its temperature remains constant.

lessons.title: Electromagnetic Induction and Transformers
lessons.content_html:
The Generator Effect

The generator effect is the reverse of the motor effect. Instead of using a current to produce motion, motion is used to produce a current. When a wire or coil moves through a magnetic field — or when a magnetic field moves past a stationary conductor — a potential difference is induced across the ends of the conductor. If the conductor is part of a complete circuit, this induced potential difference drives a current.

This process is called electromagnetic induction. It is the principle behind all generators, whether they power a bicycle light or a national power station.

Key Fact

An induced potential difference is produced when there is relative movement between a conductor and a magnetic field. It does not matter which one moves — what matters is that the magnetic field lines being “cut” by the conductor are changing.

Factors Affecting the Induced Potential Difference

The size of the induced potential difference can be increased in three ways:

1. Increasing the speed of movement — moving the conductor or magnet faster means more field lines are cut per second, producing a larger voltage. 2. Increasing the strength of the magnetic field — a stronger field means more flux is available to be cut. 3. Increasing the number of turns on the coil — each turn of wire contributes its own induced voltage, so more turns means a higher total output.

The direction of the induced current can be reversed by either reversing the direction of movement or reversing the polarity of the magnetic field. If both are reversed at the same time, the current direction stays the same.

A simple demonstration uses a bar magnet pushed into and out of a solenoid connected to a sensitive ammeter (galvanometer). As the magnet enters, the ammeter needle deflects one way. As it is removed, the needle deflects the opposite way. When the magnet is stationary inside the coil, there is no deflection because the field is not changing. Moving the magnet faster produces a larger deflection.

Alternators and Dynamos

An alternator is a generator that produces alternating current (a.c.). Inside an alternator, a coil of wire rotates between the poles of a magnet. As the coil spins, each side of the coil alternately moves up and then down through the field, so the direction of the induced current reverses every half-turn. The coil is connected to the external circuit by slip rings and carbon brushes, which maintain a continuous but reversing connection.

A dynamo produces direct current (d.c.). Its construction is almost identical to an alternator, but instead of slip rings it uses a split-ring commutator. The commutator swaps the connections to the external circuit every half-turn, so although the current in the coil reverses, the current in the external circuit always flows in the same direction.

Key Fact

Alternator = slip rings = a.c. output. Dynamo = split-ring commutator = d.c. output. This is the key difference the exam tests. Alternators are used in power stations and cars; dynamos are used in some bicycle lights.

Microphones and Loudspeakers

Microphones and loudspeakers are practical applications of electromagnetic induction and the motor effect working in reverse.

In a moving-coil microphone, sound waves hit a diaphragm, causing it to vibrate. Attached to the diaphragm is a coil of wire that sits inside a permanent magnet’s field. As the diaphragm vibrates, the coil moves back and forth within the magnetic field, and an alternating potential difference is induced across the coil. The frequency of this a.c. signal matches the frequency of the incoming sound wave, which is how sound is converted into an electrical signal.

A loudspeaker works in the opposite way. An alternating current is fed into a coil of wire (the voice coil) that sits in a permanent magnetic field. The changing current causes the coil to experience a force that alternates in direction (the motor effect), making the coil vibrate back and forth. The coil is attached to a cone, which pushes and pulls the surrounding air to produce sound waves. The frequency of the a.c. signal determines the pitch of the sound produced.

Microphone: Sound → diaphragm vibrates → coil moves in magnetic field → a.c. induced (generator effect). Converts sound energy into electrical energy.

Loudspeaker: a.c. signal → coil in magnetic field experiences alternating force → cone vibrates → sound produced (motor effect). Converts electrical energy into sound energy.

Both contain the same core components — a coil, a permanent magnet, and a diaphragm or cone — but the energy transfer is reversed.

Transformers

A transformer is a device that changes the potential difference (voltage) of an a.c. supply. Transformers only work with alternating current because they rely on a continuously changing magnetic field.

A transformer consists of two coils of insulated wire — the primary coil and the secondary coil — wound around a shared iron core. The a.c. in the primary coil creates a changing magnetic field in the iron core. This changing field passes through the secondary coil and induces an alternating potential difference across it. The iron core is made of soft iron because it magnetises and demagnetises easily, efficiently transferring the changing field.

Key Fact

Transformers only work with a.c. (not d.c.) because a direct current produces a steady magnetic field, which does not change and therefore cannot induce a potential difference in the secondary coil.

Step-Up and Step-Down Transformers

A step-up transformer increases the potential difference. It has more turns on the secondary coil than on the primary coil. A step-down transformer decreases the potential difference. It has fewer turns on the secondary coil than on the primary coil.

The relationship between the voltages and the number of turns is given by the turns ratio equation:

\(V_{p} / V_{s} = n_{p} / n_{s}\)

Where Vp is the potential difference across the primary coil, Vs is the potential difference across the secondary coil, np is the number of turns on the primary coil, and ns is the number of turns on the secondary coil.

A step-down transformer has 2000 turns on the primary coil and 100 turns on the secondary coil. The input voltage is 400 V. Calculate the output voltage.

Step 1: Write the equation: Vp / Vs = np / ns

Step 2: Substitute: 400 / Vs = 2000 / 100

Step 3: Rearrange: Vs = 400 × 100 / 2000 = 20 V

Transformers in the National Grid

The National Grid uses step-up and step-down transformers to transmit electricity efficiently across the country. Power stations generate electricity at around 25,000 V. Step-up transformers at the power station increase this to 400,000 V for transmission through overhead cables. Near homes and businesses, step-down transformers reduce the voltage back to 230 V for safe domestic use.

Transmitting at high voltage means the current is kept low (since power = voltage × current, and power stays the same). A lower current means less energy is wasted as heat in the cables, making the system more efficient. Without transformers, huge amounts of energy would be lost during transmission.

Power transferred = voltage × current (P = V × I). For a fixed power, increasing voltage decreases current. The power wasted as heat in the cables = current² × resistance (P = I² × R). Since wasted power depends on current squared, even a small reduction in current dramatically reduces energy loss. This is why the National Grid transmits at 400,000 V — the current is very small, so very little energy is lost as heat.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Transformer calculation questions are very common in the exam. Always start by writing out the equation Vp / Vs = np / ns, then substitute and rearrange. For “explain” questions about the National Grid, link three ideas in a chain: step-up transformer increases voltage → this decreases current → less energy wasted as heat (P = I²R). For questions comparing alternators and dynamos, always name the specific component that differs: slip rings vs split-ring commutator.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Electromagnetic induction occurs when a conductor moves through a magnetic field (or vice versa), inducing a potential difference — increased by faster movement, stronger fields, or more coil turns.
  • Alternators use slip rings to produce a.c.; dynamos use a split-ring commutator to produce d.c. Microphones use the generator effect; loudspeakers use the motor effect.
  • Transformers change a.c. voltage using the turns ratio Vp/Vs = np/ns. The National Grid uses step-up transformers (high V, low I) to reduce energy loss in transmission cables.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the National Grid transmits electricity at a very high voltage. In your answer, refer to the role of transformers and the effect on energy losses.

E.g. Power stations generate electricity at about 25,000 V. Step-up transformers increase this to 400,000 V for transmission through the National Grid. Since power = voltage × current, increasing voltage means current decreases for the same power. Energy wasted as heat in the cables depends on current squared (P = I²R), so a lower current dramatically reduces heat loss. Near homes, step-down transformers reduce the voltage to 230 V for safe use.

Lower band (1-2): Basic statements such as ‘high voltage reduces energy loss’ without explaining why, or mentions transformers without explaining their role.

glossary_terms.definition: The induction of a potential difference (and current in a complete circuit) when a conductor moves through a magnetic field or when a magnetic field changes around a conductor.
The energy transferred per coulomb of charge between two points, measured in volts (V).
The process of generating a potential difference across a conductor by changing the magnetic field around it or moving the conductor through a field.
Lines representing the strength and direction of a magnetic field — the closer together the lines, the stronger the field.
A type of generator that produces alternating current (a.c.) by rotating a coil inside a magnetic field, using slip rings and brushes to connect the coil to an external circuit.
Electric current that repeatedly reverses direction, typically at a frequency of 50 Hz in the UK mains supply.
Two continuous metal rings attached to the ends of a rotating coil in an alternator, allowing smooth electrical connection via brushes.
A type of generator that produces direct current (d.c.) by using a split-ring commutator to reverse the connections every half-turn, so current always flows in one direction in the external circuit.
Electric current that flows in one direction only.
A split ring of metal attached to a rotating coil that swaps the connections every half-turn, converting the alternating output of the coil into direct current.
A device that changes the potential difference of an alternating current supply, consisting of a primary coil and a secondary coil wound on an iron core.
The input coil of a transformer, connected to the a.c. supply.
The output coil of a transformer, from which the changed voltage is obtained.
A loop of soft iron that links the primary and secondary coils in a transformer, carrying the changing magnetic field between them.
A transformer where the secondary coil has more turns than the primary coil, producing a higher output voltage than the input voltage.
A transformer where the secondary coil has fewer turns than the primary coil, producing a lower output voltage than the input voltage.
The ratio of the number of turns on the secondary coil to the number of turns on the primary coil in a transformer, which equals the ratio of secondary voltage to primary voltage.
A nationwide network of cables and transformers that links power stations to consumers, transmitting electricity at high voltage and low current to reduce energy losses.

lessons.title: Space Physics: The Solar System and Beyond
lessons.content_html:
Our Solar System

Our solar system consists of the Sun at its centre, orbited by eight planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids and comets. The Sun is a main sequence star — a medium-sized star that has been fusing hydrogen into helium for about 4.6 billion years. Everything in the solar system is held in orbit by the Sun’s gravitational pull.

The eight planets, in order from the Sun, are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. The first four are rocky planets (smaller, solid surfaces), while the outer four are gas giants (much larger, mostly gas and liquid). Beyond Neptune lies a region of dwarf planets including Pluto.

Key Fact

The solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud of dust and gas called a nebula. Gravity pulled material together to form the Sun, while leftover material clumped together to form the planets and other objects.

Orbits in the Solar System

All planets orbit the Sun in slightly elliptical (oval-shaped) paths. Moons orbit planets in a similar way. gravity provides the centripetal force needed to keep an object moving in a curved path — without it, a planet would fly off in a straight line. The closer a planet is to the Sun, the stronger the gravitational pull and the faster it orbits.

A satellite is any object that orbits a planet or star. Satellites can be natural (like the Moon) or artificial (like the International Space Station). Artificial satellites orbit Earth at different heights depending on their purpose.

Natural satellites are objects that orbit planets due to gravity alone. The Moon is Earth’s only natural satellite, but Jupiter has at least 95 known moons.

Artificial satellites are human-made objects placed into orbit for specific purposes. Communications satellites sit in geostationary orbit (high altitude, 24-hour period, stays above the same point). Weather satellites use low polar orbits to scan the entire Earth.

The Life Cycle of Stars

Stars do not last forever. They are born, they live, and they die — and the way a star dies depends on its mass.

Birth of a Star

All stars begin as a nebula — a vast cloud of hydrogen gas and dust. Gravity pulls the gas together, and as the cloud contracts it heats up. The contracting ball of gas is called a protostar. When the core reaches around 15 million °C, nuclear fusion begins — hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium, releasing enormous energy. Once fusion is stable, the star becomes a main sequence star.

Key Fact

A main sequence star is in a stable phase where the outward pressure from nuclear fusion is balanced by the inward pull of gravity. This balance is called hydrostatic equilibrium and can last for billions of years. Our Sun is currently a main sequence star.

Death of a Star — Sun-Sized Stars

When a Sun-sized star runs out of hydrogen fuel, the core contracts while the outer layers expand and cool, turning it into a red giant. The red giant sheds its outer layers into space, forming a planetary nebula. The remaining core collapses to form a white dwarf — an incredibly dense remnant about the size of Earth that slowly cools and fades.

Death of a Star — Massive Stars

Stars much larger than the Sun follow a more dramatic path. After the main sequence phase, a massive star swells into a red supergiant. When the core runs out of fuel, it collapses violently, triggering an explosion called a supernova. A supernova briefly outshines an entire galaxy and blasts heavy elements (iron, gold, uranium) into space.

What remains after the supernova depends on the original mass of the star:

  • Neutron star — if the remaining core is between about 1.4 and 3 solar masses, it collapses into a neutron star. Neutron stars are incredibly dense — a teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh about a billion tonnes on Earth.
  • Black hole — if the remaining core is above about 3 solar masses, gravity is so strong that nothing can stop the collapse. The core forms a black hole, a region of space where gravity is so intense that not even light can escape.

Sun-sized stars: Nebula → Protostar → Main sequence star → Red giant → Planetary nebula → White dwarf. The process is relatively gentle — no explosion occurs. The white dwarf slowly cools and fades over billions of years.

Massive stars: Nebula → Protostar → Main sequence star → Red supergiant → Supernova → Neutron star or Black hole. The supernova is one of the most energetic events in the universe. The heavy elements scattered by supernovae eventually form new stars, planets and even living things — we are literally made of stardust.

Key Fact

Elements heavier than iron can only be created during a supernova. Every atom of gold, silver and uranium on Earth was forged in the explosion of a massive star billions of years ago.

Red-Shift and the Expanding Universe

When astronomers analysed the absorption spectra of distant galaxies, they found the dark lines were shifted towards the red end of the spectrum. This effect is called red-shift.

Red-shift happens because the galaxy is moving away from us. As the galaxy recedes, the light waves are stretched out, increasing their wavelength and shifting them towards the red end of the spectrum. This is similar to how the pitch of an ambulance siren drops as it drives away from you (the Doppler effect).

The American astronomer Edwin Hubble made a crucial discovery: the further away a galaxy is, the greater its red-shift. This means more distant galaxies are moving away from us faster. This relationship is known as Hubble’s Law and it provided the first observational evidence that the universe is expanding.

If all galaxies are moving away from us, and the most distant ones are moving fastest, the universe must be expanding in every direction. It is not that galaxies are flying through space — space itself is stretching, carrying galaxies with it. Imagine dots drawn on a balloon: as the balloon inflates, every dot moves away from every other dot, and the dots furthest apart move away from each other fastest.

If the universe is expanding now, it must have been smaller in the past. Winding the clock backwards, all the matter and energy in the universe would have been concentrated in an incredibly small, hot, dense point — the starting point for the Big Bang theory.

The Big Bang Theory

The Big Bang theory states that the universe began approximately 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense point. Space itself began to expand rapidly, and as it cooled, matter formed — first subatomic particles, then atoms, then stars and galaxies.

Two key pieces of evidence support the Big Bang theory:

  • Red-shift of galaxies — as described above, the observation that all distant galaxies are moving away from us (and the further away, the faster) shows the universe is expanding. Running this expansion backwards points to a single origin.
  • Cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR) — in 1965, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson detected faint microwave radiation coming from every direction in space. This is the leftover thermal radiation from the Big Bang itself, now cooled to about −270°C (just 2.7 K above absolute zero). The CMBR is the strongest evidence for the Big Bang because no other theory explains its existence.
Key Fact

The two main pieces of evidence for the Big Bang are red-shift (showing the universe is expanding) and cosmic microwave background radiation (the afterglow of the Big Bang, detected from every direction in space).

Dark Matter and Dark Energy

Scientists have discovered that the visible matter we can see — stars, planets, gas clouds — makes up only about 5% of the total mass-energy of the universe. The rest is made of two mysterious components.

Dark matter accounts for about 27% of the universe. It cannot be seen because it does not emit, absorb or reflect light. Scientists know it exists because galaxies rotate faster than expected from their visible mass — unseen mass must be providing extra gravitational pull.

Dark energy makes up about 68% of the universe. In the late 1990s, scientists studying distant supernovae discovered the expansion of the universe is accelerating. Dark energy is the name given to whatever force is driving this acceleration, but its true nature remains unknown.

Dark matter and dark energy are two of the biggest unsolved problems in physics. Dark matter holds galaxies together but has never been directly detected. Dark energy is pushing the universe apart at an increasing rate, yet its true nature is unknown. Together, they make up about 95% of the universe — we can only directly observe about 5% of everything that exists.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Space physics questions often ask you to describe the life cycle of a star or explain the evidence for the Big Bang. For star life cycle questions, always state the starting point (nebula) and make sure you describe both pathways — Sun-sized stars and massive stars — unless the question specifies one. For Big Bang evidence, name both red-shift and CMBR, and explain what each one shows. A common mistake is describing red-shift without linking it to the expansion of the universe — always make the connection explicit.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Solar system structure — the Sun is a main sequence star orbited by eight planets, with gravity providing the centripetal force for all orbital motion.
  • Star life cycles — all stars begin as nebulae; Sun-sized stars end as white dwarfs, while massive stars explode as supernovae, leaving neutron stars or black holes.
  • Expanding universe — red-shift and cosmic microwave background radiation are the two key pieces of evidence for the Big Bang, and dark energy is causing the expansion to accelerate.

practice_questions.text: State the name of the force that keeps planets in orbit around the Sun.
practice_questions.marks: Gravity (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe the changes that occur when a Sun-sized star reaches the end of its main sequence phase.
practice_questions.marks: The star expands and cools to become a red giant (1 mark). It then sheds its outer layers / forms a planetary nebula and the core collapses to become a white dwarf (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: The speed of light is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. The Sun is 1.5 × 10¹¹ m from the Earth. Calculate the time it takes for light to travel from the Sun to the Earth.
practice_questions.marks: time = distance ÷ speed (1 mark). time = 1.5 × 10¹¹ ÷ 3.0 × 10⁸ = 500 s (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the observation of red-shift provides evidence that the universe is expanding.
practice_questions.marks: Light from distant galaxies is shifted towards the red end of the spectrum / has increased wavelength (1 mark). This indicates the galaxies are moving away from us (1 mark). The further away a galaxy is, the greater the red-shift / the faster it is moving away, showing the universe is expanding in all directions (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Compare the end stages of the life cycle of a Sun-sized star and a star much more massive than the Sun. Explain why the outcomes are different.
practice_questions.marks: A Sun-sized star becomes a red giant then a white dwarf (1 mark). A massive star becomes a red supergiant, then explodes as a supernova, leaving a neutron star or black hole (1 mark). The massive star has a more dramatic death because it has much stronger gravitational forces acting on its core (1 mark). The greater mass means the core collapse is more violent, producing enough energy for a supernova rather than gently shedding outer layers (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: The Big Bang theory is the most widely accepted model for the origin of the universe. Evaluate the evidence that supports this theory.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed and coherent evaluation of evidence. Discusses both red-shift and CMBR in detail, explains what each shows, and links them logically to the Big Bang. May discuss the significance of CMBR as the strongest evidence.
Mid band (3-4): Describes both pieces of evidence with some explanation of how they support the Big Bang, but may lack detail or clear linkage.
Lower band (1-2): Identifies one or both pieces of evidence with limited explanation.
Indicative content:
• Red-shift: light from distant galaxies is shifted to longer wavelengths; all galaxies moving away; more distant galaxies have greater red-shift (Hubble's Law); shows the universe is expanding; if expanding now, must have been smaller in the past — points to a single origin.
• CMBR: faint microwave radiation detected from all directions; discovered by Penzias and Wilson in 1965; this is the cooled remnant of radiation from the initial expansion; temperature now ~2.7 K; no other theory adequately explains its existence.
• Together, red-shift and CMBR provide strong, independent lines of evidence supporting the Big Bang theory.
