glossary_terms.definition: The Sun and all the objects that orbit it, including eight planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids and comets.
A medium-sized star in the stable phase of its life cycle, fusing hydrogen into helium in its core.
The force of attraction between any two objects with mass. It holds planets in orbit around the Sun.
An object that orbits a planet or star. Natural satellites include moons; artificial satellites are human-made objects such as the International Space Station.
An orbit where a satellite takes exactly 24 hours to complete one revolution, so it stays above the same point on Earth's surface.
A large cloud of dust and gas in space from which stars are born when gravity causes the cloud to collapse.
The process by which small atomic nuclei combine to form a larger nucleus, releasing enormous amounts of energy. This powers stars.
A young, contracting star that has not yet begun nuclear fusion in its core.
A large, cool star formed when a main sequence star exhausts its hydrogen fuel and its outer layers expand.
The hot, dense remnant core of a Sun-sized star after it has shed its outer layers. About the size of Earth but extremely dense.
An extremely large, cool star formed when a massive star exhausts its hydrogen fuel. Much bigger than a red giant.
A massive explosion that occurs when a large star collapses at the end of its life, briefly outshining an entire galaxy.
An extremely dense remnant of a massive star after a supernova, composed almost entirely of neutrons. A teaspoon would weigh about a billion tonnes.
A region of space where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape from it.
The pattern of dark lines seen when light from a star is split into a spectrum, caused by elements in the star absorbing specific wavelengths.
The shift of light from a galaxy towards longer (redder) wavelengths, indicating the galaxy is moving away from the observer.
The change in frequency or wavelength of a wave as the source moves towards or away from the observer.
The scientific theory that the universe began from an extremely hot, dense point approximately 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding ever since.
Invisible matter that does not emit or absorb light but exerts a gravitational pull. It is thought to make up about 27% of the universe.
A mysterious force that is causing the expansion of the universe to accelerate. It is thought to make up about 68% of the universe.

lessons.title: Energy: KE, GPE and Power
lessons.description: Calculate kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy, work done and power — all recall equations you must memorise.

steps.say: Two steps. First the GPE at the top, then set it equal to KE to find the speed.

steps.done: Matches the GPE, so 14 m/s is right.

gold.display: A 3 kg rock falls from a height of 10 m. Calculate its speed just before it lands, assuming all GPE becomes KE. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

steps.say: Kinetic energy needs the speed squared: \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\).

steps.done: That is the kinetic energy, 9 J.
Back to 3 m/s, so 9 J is right.

bronze.display: A 2 kg ball moves at 3 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

steps.say: The mass is in grams, but the equation needs kilograms. Convert first.

steps.done: 4 J. The only new move was the gram-to-kilogram conversion.

silver.display: A 500 g trolley moves at 4 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

steps.say: Two identical cars crash into a wall. Car A is going 15 mph. Car B is going 30 mph, exactly twice as fast.

steps.pre: Car B is travelling how many times as fast as Car A?

steps.say: You might guess the crash is twice as bad. It is worse than that. Energy depends on the speed squared, so doubling the speed multiplies the energy by 2 × 2.

Four times the energy, four times the damage. That squared speed is the heart of the kinetic energy equation, \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\). This lesson uses it alongside four partner equations for energy and power.

steps: Decide what you are finding, then choose the matching equation.
Convert every value to base units first: kg, metres, seconds.
Substitute and calculate.
State the answer with its unit (J for energy, W for power).
method_card.title: Energy: KE, GPE and Power
method_card.content:
Five recall equations: kinetic energy \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\), gravitational PE \(E_p = mgh\), work \(W = Fs\), and power \(P = \frac{E}{t}\). Check whether your board gives you these; knowing them from memory always saves time.

Watch the traps: speed is squared, so doubling it quadruples the KE; convert grams to kilograms and minutes to seconds before substituting; use \(g = 9.8\) N/kg unless told otherwise.

steps: These need two equations or two stages. Finish the first fully before starting the second.
Energy is conserved: GPE lost becomes KE gained, so \(mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\) lets you find a speed.
For efficiency, divide the useful energy by the total energy, then multiply by 100 for a percentage.
gold.title: Gold: two steps chained

example.question: A 2 kg ball falls from 10 m. Find its speed at the bottom. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

steps: Pick the equation the quantity needs: kinetic energy \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\), gravitational PE \(E_p = mgh\), work \(W = Fs\), or power \(P = \frac{E}{t}\).
Substitute the numbers exactly as given, then calculate.
Write the answer with its unit: joules (J) for energy, watts (W) for power.
bronze.title: Bronze: one equation, straight in

example.question: A 4 kg box is lifted 3 m. Calculate the GPE gained. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

steps: If a value is not in the base unit, convert before you substitute: grams to kilograms (÷1000), minutes to seconds (×60), kilojoules to joules (×1000).
If the unknown is not the subject, rearrange the equation first, then substitute.
Give the answer in the unit the question asks for.
silver.title: Silver: convert first, or rearrange first

example.question: A 250 g ball moves at 6 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

exam_context.frequency: Very common. Energy calculations appear on almost every Paper 1.

gold.hint: Find the GPE lost over the 1000 m drop, then solve half m v squared for v.
gold.display: A skydiver of mass 75 kg falls from 4000 m to 3000 m. Calculate the speed they would reach if all the lost GPE converted to KE. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: All the gravitational PE lost turns into kinetic energy. Work out the GPE lost during the fall, set it equal to \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2\), then rearrange to find the speed v.

guided_steps.hint: Double it, then divide by the mass.

guided_steps.done: Matches the GPE lost, so 140 m/s is right.

misconceptions.message: GPE lost = mgh = 75 × 9.8 × 1000 = 735,000 J. Set ½mv² = 735,000, so v² = 2 × 735,000 ÷ 75 = 19,600 and v = 140 m/s. Forgetting the 2 gives about 99 m/s.
Use the height dropped (4000 − 3000 = 1000 m), not the total 4000 m. Using 4000 m gives 280 m/s.

gold.hint: Work done is the kinetic energy lost: KE at 20 minus KE at 8.
gold.display: A car of mass 1100 kg travels at 20 m/s. The driver brakes, and the car decelerates to 8 m/s. Calculate the work done by the brakes.

guided_steps.say: The brakes take away kinetic energy, so the work done equals the KE lost. Work out the KE before braking and the KE after braking, then subtract: KE before − KE after.

guided_steps.hint: Subtract the smaller from the larger.

guided_steps.done: Recovers 220,000 J, so 184,800 J is right.
guided_steps.hint: Add back to the starting KE.

misconceptions.message: Find the KE at both speeds and subtract: ½ × 1100 × 20² = 220,000 J and ½ × 1100 × 8² = 35,200 J, so work = 184,800 J. Squaring the difference (12²) gives 79,200 J, which is wrong.

gold.hint: Useful output is the GPE gained; total input is power times time.
gold.display: An electric motor has a power rating of 2.5 kW. It lifts an 80 kg object 6 m in 4 seconds. Calculate the efficiency of the motor. Give your answer as a percentage. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Efficiency = useful energy out ÷ total energy in × 100. The useful output is the gravitational PE given to the object; the total input is the electrical energy the motor uses.

guided_steps.done: Recovers 4704 J, so 47.04% is right.
guided_steps.hint: Total input × the efficiency fraction recovers the useful output.

misconceptions.message: Convert kW to W: 2.5 kW = 2500 W, so total input = 2500 × 4 = 10,000 J. Leaving it as 2.5 gives a total input of 10 J and an impossible 47,040%.
Efficiency = useful ÷ total × 100 = 4704 ÷ 10,000 × 100 = 47.04%. Dividing total by useful instead gives about 212%.

gold.hint: Work out each student's power with mgh divided by time, then subtract.
gold.display: Two students climb the same flight of stairs (height 4 m). Student A has mass 50 kg and takes 5 seconds. Student B has mass 70 kg and takes 8 seconds. Calculate the difference in their power output. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Find each student's power with \(P = \frac{mgh}{t}\), then subtract.

guided_steps.done: Recovers 392 W, so 49 W is right.
guided_steps.hint: Add back to Student B's power.

misconceptions.message: Power, not energy: divide each student's work by their time. P_A = 1960 ÷ 5 = 392 W, P_B = 2744 ÷ 8 = 343 W, difference = 49 W. Comparing energies (2744 − 1960) gives 784.

gold.hint: Find the GPE before and after, then subtract.
gold.display: A ball of mass 0.3 kg is dropped from a height of 10 m. It bounces back to a height of 6 m. Calculate the energy dissipated during the bounce. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: The energy dissipated (lost as heat and sound) is the drop in gravitational PE. Work out mgh at the starting height, then mgh at the bounce height, and subtract the two.

guided_steps.done: Recovers 29.4 J, so 11.76 J is right.
guided_steps.hint: Add back to the bounce GPE.

misconceptions.message: Energy dissipated is the GPE lost: mgh before minus mgh after = 29.4 − 17.64 = 11.76 J. Quoting only the starting GPE gives 29.4 J.

gold.hint: Convert MW to watts and one day to seconds, then multiply.
gold.display: A wind turbine generates 1.5 MW of power. How much energy does it transfer in one day? Give your answer in standard form.

guided_steps.say: Energy transferred is \(E = Pt\). First change the power into watts and one day into seconds, then multiply. At the end, write the answer in standard form.

guided_steps.pre: In standard form, the power of 10 is
guided_steps.hint: Move the point 11 places left from 129,600,000,000.

bronze.hint: Square the speed, then multiply by half the mass.
bronze.display: A car has a mass of 1200 kg and travels at 15 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

guided_steps.say: Kinetic energy needs the speed squared: \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 15 m/s, so 135,000 J is right.

misconceptions.message: Square the speed first: 15² = 225. Then KE = ½ × 1200 × 225 = 135,000 J.
Do not forget the ½. KE = ½ × 1200 × 225 = 135,000 J, not 270,000 J.

bronze.hint: Multiply mass by g, then by height.
bronze.display: A 0.5 kg ball is held 4 m above the ground. Calculate its gravitational potential energy. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Lifting something gives it gravitational PE: \(E_p = mgh\).

guided_steps.done: Gives 9.8 N/kg, so 19.6 J is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide back by height then mass.

misconceptions.message: Use GPE = mgh = 0.5 × 9.8 × 4 = 19.6 J. This is a mass held above the ground, so it stores gravitational PE, not KE.

bronze.hint: Work done is force times distance.
bronze.display: A force of 50 N pushes a box 8 m along the floor. Calculate the work done.

guided_steps.say: Work done is force times distance: \(W = Fs\).

guided_steps.done: Recovers 50 N, so 400 J is right.

misconceptions.message: Work done = force × distance = 50 × 8 = 400 J.

bronze.hint: Convert minutes to seconds, then divide energy by time.
bronze.display: A kettle transfers 180,000 J of energy in 3 minutes. Calculate its power in watts.

guided_steps.say: Power is how much energy is transferred each second: \(P = \frac{E}{t}\). The time must be in seconds, so change the 3 minutes into seconds first.

guided_steps.done: Recovers 180,000 J, so 1000 W is right.

misconceptions.message: Convert minutes to seconds first: 3 min = 180 s. P = 180,000 ÷ 180 = 1000 W. Dividing by 3 gives 60,000 W, which is far too big.

bronze.hint: Square the speed, then multiply by half the mass.
bronze.display: A runner of mass 60 kg sprints at 8 m/s. Calculate their kinetic energy.

guided_steps.say: Kinetic energy: \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 8 m/s, so 1920 J is right.

misconceptions.message: Square the speed: 8² = 64. KE = ½ × 60 × 64 = 1920 J. Forgetting to square gives 240 J.

bronze.hint: Multiply mass by g, then by height.
bronze.display: A bag of mass 3 kg is lifted onto a shelf 2.5 m high. Calculate the GPE gained. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Lifting gives gravitational PE: \(E_p = mgh\).

guided_steps.done: Gives 9.8 N/kg, so 73.5 J is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide back by height then mass.

bronze.hint: Divide the energy by the time.

guided_steps.say: Power is energy per second: \(P = \frac{E}{t}\).

guided_steps.done: Recovers 5000 J, so 250 W is right.

misconceptions.message: Power = energy ÷ time = 5000 ÷ 20 = 250 W. Multiplying instead gives 100,000, which is not a power.

bronze.hint: Above the ground means gravitational potential energy.
bronze.display: Which equation would you use to calculate the energy stored by an object lifted above the ground?

misconceptions.message: An object above the ground has gravitational PE. Use \(E_p = mgh\). KE is for moving objects.

silver.hint: Work out the KE in joules, then convert to kilojoules.
silver.display: A cyclist and bike have a combined mass of 80 kg and travel at 12 m/s. Calculate the kinetic energy in kJ.

guided_steps.say: Kinetic energy in joules first, then convert to kilojoules.

guided_steps.done: Recovers 5760 J, so 5.76 kJ is right.

misconceptions.message: KE = ½ × 80 × 12² = 5760 J. The question asks for kJ: 5760 ÷ 1000 = 5.76 kJ.
Square the speed first: 12² = 144. Then ½ × 80 × 144 = 5760 J = 5.76 kJ. Forgetting to square gives 0.48 kJ.

silver.hint: Convert hours to seconds, then convert the answer to kJ.
silver.display: A 60 W light bulb is left on for 2 hours. Calculate the energy transferred in kJ.

guided_steps.say: Energy transferred is power × time: \(E = Pt\). Put the time in seconds, work out the energy in joules, then divide by 1000 to convert it to kilojoules.

guided_steps.done: Gives 60 W, so 432 kJ is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide the joules by the time.

misconceptions.message: Convert hours to seconds: 2 h = 7200 s. E = 60 × 7200 = 432,000 J = 432 kJ. Leaving the answer in joules gives 432,000.

silver.hint: Find the weight first, then multiply by the height.
silver.display: A crane lifts a 400 kg load to a height of 15 m. Calculate the work done by the crane. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: You are lifting the load against gravity. First find its weight (weight = mass × g) — that is the force. Then find the work done with work = force × distance.

guided_steps.done: Recovers 3920 N, so 58,800 J is right.

misconceptions.message: First find the weight to lift: W = mg = 400 × 9.8 = 3920 N. Then work = Fs = 3920 × 15 = 58,800 J. Using the mass as the force gives 6000 J.

silver.hint: Work done equals the kinetic energy gained from rest.
silver.display: A car of mass 900 kg accelerates from rest to 30 m/s. Calculate the work done on the car.

guided_steps.say: The work done on the car becomes its kinetic energy, so the work equals the KE gained: \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2\). It starts from rest, so there is no starting KE to take away.

guided_steps.done: Back to 30 m/s, so 405,000 J is right.

misconceptions.message: Work done = the KE gained = ½ × 900 × 30² = 405,000 J. It starts from rest, so there is no KE to subtract.
Square the speed: 30² = 900. KE = ½ × 900 × 900 = 405,000 J. Forgetting to square gives 13,500 J.

silver.hint: Find the energy from Pt, then rearrange mgh to h = E divided by mg.
silver.display: A 1500 W motor lifts a 50 kg mass. How high can it lift the mass in 10 seconds? Give your answer to 1 d.p. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: This takes two equations. First find the energy the motor gives out with \(E = Pt\). That energy lifts the mass, so put it into \(E_p = mgh\) and rearrange to find the height h.

guided_steps.done: About 15,000 J, so 30.6 m is right.
guided_steps.hint: Weight × height recovers the energy, close to 15,000.

misconceptions.message: Energy = Pt = 15,000 J. Height = E ÷ (mg) = 15,000 ÷ 490 = 30.6 m. Dividing by the mass alone (forgetting g) gives 300 m.

silver.hint: Convert the mass to kilograms first, then square the speed.
silver.display: A 200 g tennis ball is served at 50 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

guided_steps.say: Kinetic energy: convert the mass to kilograms first.

guided_steps.done: Back to 50 m/s, so 250 J is right.

misconceptions.message: Convert grams to kilograms: 200 g = 0.2 kg. KE = ½ × 0.2 × 50² = 250 J. Leaving the mass in grams gives 250,000 J.

lessons.title: Efficiency and Energy Resources
lessons.description: Calculate efficiency from energy and power values, find useful and wasted energy, and interpret Sankey diagrams.

steps.say: Gold chains two equations. First the useful output, the GPE: \(E_p = mgh\).

steps.say: Now rearrange efficiency: total input = useful ÷ efficiency.

steps.say: That number, 0.1, is the bulb's efficiency: useful out ÷ total in. Every question in this lesson is that one idea, \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}}\), sometimes turned around to find a missing piece.

opener.title: How much actually gets through?
opener.display: An old light bulb is like a leaky bucket. You pour in 100 joules of electrical energy, but only 10 joules come out as light. The other 90 joules leak away as heat you can feel on the glass.

steps: Identify the useful output and the total input (both energy, or both power, never mixed).
Divide: efficiency = useful output ÷ total input.
Multiply by 100 if the question wants a percentage.
Sense check: efficiency is always below 1 (100%).
method_card.title: Efficiency and Energy Resources
method_card.content:
Efficiency tells you how much of the energy put into a device comes out in the useful form you want.

efficiency = useful output ÷ total input. Use energy values or power values, but never mix them. The answer is a decimal; multiply by 100 for a percentage.

It can never be more than 1 (100%): if yours is, you divided the wrong way round. Wasted energy = total input − useful output, and it ends up warming the surroundings.

steps: First find the useful energy: KE (\(\frac{1}{2}mv^2\)), GPE (\(mgh\)), or power × time.
Then use efficiency to reach the missing quantity, rearranging to total = useful ÷ efficiency where needed.
Convert units first (minutes to seconds), and keep energy with energy, power with power.
gold.title: Gold: chain two equations

example.question: A hoist is 0.50 efficient and lifts 20 kg to 5 m. Find the energy input. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

steps: Write efficiency = useful output ÷ total input.
Put the useful energy (or power) on top, the total underneath, and divide.
For a percentage, multiply the decimal by 100. Efficiency is always below 1 (100%).
bronze.title: Bronze: one efficiency equation

example.question: A lamp takes in 50 J and gives out 20 J of light. Find its efficiency.

steps: Sometimes find the useful energy first: useful = total − wasted.
Sometimes rearrange: total input = useful ÷ efficiency, or useful = efficiency × total.
Then finish the division (or subtraction) and give a unit or percentage.
silver.title: Silver: one move before you divide

example.question: A motor takes in 800 J and wastes 200 J. Find its efficiency.

exam_context.frequency: Very common: efficiency appears in almost every Paper 1

gold.hint: Find the GPE first (mgh), then divide it by the efficiency.
gold.display: A crane motor with an efficiency of 0.75 lifts a 120 kg steel beam to a height of 20 m. Calculate the total electrical energy input to the motor. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Two equations chained. First the useful output, the GPE gained: \(E_p = mgh\).

guided_steps.pre: Now multiply by the height h: 1176 × 20 =
guided_steps.hint: Multiply by the height to get the GPE.

guided_steps.say: That GPE is the useful output. Rearrange efficiency: total input = useful ÷ efficiency.

guided_steps.done: Back to 23,520 J, so the input is right.

guided_steps.say: So the total electrical energy input is 31,360 J.

misconceptions.message: Useful output = GPE = mgh = 120 × 9.8 × 20 = 23,520 J. Total input = useful ÷ efficiency = 23,520 ÷ 0.75 = 31,360 J.
Don't multiply useful by efficiency. Total input = useful output ÷ efficiency.

gold.hint: Square the speed for KE, then divide the KE by the efficiency.
gold.display: A car of mass 1200 kg accelerates from rest to 25 m/s. The engine has an efficiency of 0.30. Calculate the total chemical energy released from the fuel.

guided_steps.say: First the useful output, the kinetic energy gained: \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\). Square the speed first.

guided_steps.pre: Now do ½ × mass × speed²: ½ × 1200 × 625 =
guided_steps.hint: Half of mass times speed squared.

guided_steps.say: That KE is the useful output. Rearrange efficiency: total input = useful ÷ efficiency.

guided_steps.done: Back to 375,000 J, so the input is right.

guided_steps.say: So the total chemical energy released is 1,250,000 J (1.25 MJ).

misconceptions.message: First find KE gained: ½ × 1200 × 25² = ½ × 1200 × 625 = 375,000 J. This is the useful output. Total input = 375,000 ÷ 0.30 = 1,250,000 J.
Remember to square the speed: 25² = 625, not 25 × 2 = 50.

gold.hint: Find the total power (useful ÷ efficiency), then divide by 800 for the area.
gold.display: A solar panel converts sunlight into 240 W of useful electrical power. The panel is 20% efficient. The Sun delivers 800 W/m² to the panel. Calculate the area of the panel.

guided_steps.say: Two steps. First the total power the panel must receive: total input = useful ÷ efficiency.
The Sun delivers 800 W for every m². Area = total power ÷ power per m².

guided_steps.done: 1.5 m² collects 1200 W, so the area is right.
guided_steps.hint: Should return the total power needed.

guided_steps.say: So the panel area is 1.5 m².

misconceptions.message: Total input power = useful ÷ efficiency = 240 ÷ 0.20 = 1200 W. Area = total power ÷ power per m² = 1200 ÷ 800 = 1.5 m².
First find total power input, then divide by the solar intensity to find the area.

gold.hint: Convert minutes to seconds, find useful energy, then use mgh rearranged.
gold.display: A pump with a power rating of 600 W and an efficiency of 0.70 lifts water to a height of 8 m for 5 minutes. Calculate the mass of water lifted. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Several steps. First convert the time, because power is joules per second.
Total energy supplied = power × time.
Now the finish. Only 70% of that energy lifts the water. Useful energy = efficiency × total.
This useful energy is the GPE, \(E_p = mgh\), so \(m = \frac{E_p}{gh}\). First find \(gh\).

guided_steps.pre: First work out g × h, the bottom of the fraction: 9.8 × 8 =

guided_steps.done: So the mass is about 1607.1 kg.
guided_steps.hint: Useful energy over gh; round to 1 decimal place.

guided_steps.say: Check: 1607 kg of water lifted 8 m gains close to 126,000 J of GPE, matching the useful energy, so the answer is right (given to 1 d.p.).

misconceptions.message: Remember to account for the efficiency, only 70% of the input energy lifts the water.

gold.hint: Useful energy = efficiency × power × time. Work both out and compare.
gold.display: Kettle A is 88% efficient and takes 3 minutes to boil using 2000 W. Kettle B is 95% efficient and takes 3 minutes to boil using 1800 W. Which kettle transfers more useful energy to the water?
options: They transfer exactly the same amount
You cannot tell without the water's mass

misconceptions.message: Kettle A: useful = 0.88 × 2000 × 180 = 316,800 J. Kettle B: useful = 0.95 × 1800 × 180 = 307,800 J. Even though B is more efficient, A transfers more useful energy because its power rating is higher.

gold.hint: Think about conservation of energy and where wasted energy goes.
gold.display: Which statement about efficiency is correct?
options: A more powerful device is always more efficient
Efficiency can be greater than 100% if the device is very good
Wasted energy is eventually transferred to the surroundings, increasing the temperature
Renewable energy sources always have higher efficiency than fossil fuels

misconceptions.message: Efficiency can never exceed 100% (conservation of energy). Power and efficiency are different things. Wasted energy always ends up heating the surroundings, this is correct.

bronze.hint: Divide the useful heat by the total electrical energy.
bronze.display: A heater receives 2000 J of electrical energy and converts 1600 J to heat for the room. Calculate the efficiency of the heater.

guided_steps.say: Efficiency compares the useful energy out with the total energy in: \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}}\).

guided_steps.pre: Useful output (the heat for the room), in J =
guided_steps.hint: The energy that does the job you want is the 1600 J of heat.
Everything that goes in: the 2000 J of electrical energy.

guided_steps.done: Matches the 1600 J we started with, so 0.8 is right.
guided_steps.hint: This should give back the useful output.

guided_steps.say: So the efficiency is 0.8 (or 80%). Efficiency has no unit.

misconceptions.message: Divide useful by total, not total by useful. Efficiency = 1600 ÷ 2000 = 0.8.
Useful output (1600 J) is the heat for the room. Efficiency = 1600/2000 = 0.8.

bronze.hint: Divide useful by total, then multiply by 100 for a percentage.
bronze.display: A motor has an input energy of 500 J and a useful output of 350 J. Calculate the efficiency as a percentage.

guided_steps.say: Efficiency is useful ÷ total, then turned into a percentage: \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}}\).

guided_steps.hint: The energy you actually get out: 350 J.

guided_steps.pre: Turn the decimal into a percentage: 0.7 × 100 =
guided_steps.done: That is the step people forget.

guided_steps.say: So the efficiency is 70%.

misconceptions.message: Efficiency = 350/500 = 0.7. Multiply by 100 to get a percentage: 0.7 × 100 = 70%.

bronze.hint: You can divide powers directly: useful power over total power.
bronze.display: An LED bulb has an input power of 10 W and a useful light output of 7 W. Calculate the efficiency.

guided_steps.say: You can put power straight into the efficiency equation: \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}}\) works with watts too.

guided_steps.hint: The light you actually get: 7 W.

guided_steps.done: Back to 7 W, so 0.7 is right.

guided_steps.say: So the efficiency is 0.7 (or 70%).

misconceptions.message: You can use power values directly. Efficiency = useful power ÷ total power = 7 ÷ 10 = 0.7.

bronze.hint: Divide the 12,000 J of KE by the 40,000 J input, then times 100.
bronze.display: A car engine receives 40,000 J of chemical energy from fuel and converts 12,000 J to kinetic energy. Calculate the efficiency as a percentage.

guided_steps.say: Efficiency is useful ÷ total, then as a percentage: \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}}\).

guided_steps.pre: Useful output (the kinetic energy), in J =
guided_steps.hint: The energy you want: 12,000 J of KE.
The chemical energy from fuel: 40,000 J.

guided_steps.done: 30% of the fuel energy becomes movement.

guided_steps.say: So the efficiency is 30%.

misconceptions.message: Efficiency = useful ÷ total = 12,000 ÷ 40,000 = 0.3 = 30%. Don't divide 40,000 by 12,000.

bronze.hint: Turn 90% into 0.9, then multiply by the total input.
bronze.display: A kettle is 90% efficient. It receives 200,000 J of electrical energy. Calculate the useful heat energy transferred to the water.

guided_steps.say: Here we know the efficiency and the total input, and want the useful output. Rearrange: useful output = efficiency × total input.

guided_steps.done: Back to 90%, so the useful energy is right.
guided_steps.hint: Should return the 0.9 we were given.

guided_steps.say: So the useful heat transferred is 180,000 J.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange: useful output = efficiency × total input = 0.9 × 200,000 = 180,000 J. Convert 90% to 0.9 first.

bronze.hint: Multiply the total input power by the efficiency.
bronze.display: A power station has an efficiency of 0.35. The total input power is 800 MW. Calculate the useful electrical power output in MW.

guided_steps.say: We want the useful power out, knowing the efficiency and total power in. Rearrange: useful output = efficiency × total input.

guided_steps.done: Both values were in MW, so the answer stays in MW.

guided_steps.say: So the useful electrical power output is 280 MW.

misconceptions.message: Useful output = efficiency × total input = 0.35 × 800 = 280 MW.
Both values are already in MW, so the answer stays in MW. No conversion needed.

bronze.hint: Wasted = total in − useful out.
bronze.display: A Sankey diagram shows a light bulb receiving 80 J of electrical energy. The useful light output arrow has a width of 8 J. Calculate the wasted energy.

guided_steps.say: Energy is conserved: total in = useful out + wasted. So wasted = total input − useful output.

guided_steps.done: Adds back to the 80 J input, so 72 J is right.
guided_steps.hint: Useful plus wasted should give the total.

guided_steps.say: So the wasted energy is 72 J.

misconceptions.message: Wasted energy = total input − useful output = 80 − 8 = 72 J. Energy is conserved.

bronze.hint: Work out useful ÷ total for each device, then compare.
bronze.display: Which of these devices is the most efficient?
options: Device A: 500 J in, 200 J useful out
Device B: 400 J in, 300 J useful out
Device C: 1000 J in, 600 J useful out
Device D: 200 J in, 50 J useful out

misconceptions.message: Calculate each: A = 200/500 = 0.40, B = 300/400 = 0.75, C = 600/1000 = 0.60, D = 50/200 = 0.25. Device B is the most efficient at 75%.

silver.hint: Take BOTH wasted amounts off the input first, then divide.
silver.display: A motor receives 5000 J of electrical energy. It wastes 1500 J as heat and 500 J as sound. Calculate the efficiency as a percentage.

guided_steps.say: First find the useful energy. Useful = total input − all the wasted energy.

guided_steps.pre: Add up ALL the wasted energy: 1500 + 500 =

guided_steps.hint: Take the wasted energy off the input.

guided_steps.say: Now apply \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}}\).

guided_steps.done: Both wasted amounts were removed first, so 60% is right.

guided_steps.say: So the efficiency is 60%.

misconceptions.message: Useful = total − all wasted = 5000 − 1500 − 500 = 3000 J. Efficiency = 3000/5000 = 0.6 = 60%.
Remember to subtract ALL the wasted energies (heat and sound) from the input.

silver.hint: Divide the useful output by the efficiency to get the bigger total.
silver.display: A wind turbine has an efficiency of 0.40. In one hour it generates 720 kJ of useful electrical energy. Calculate the total energy input from the wind in kJ.

guided_steps.say: We know the useful output and efficiency, and want the total input. Rearrange: total input = useful output ÷ efficiency.

guided_steps.hint: Useful divided by efficiency gives the bigger total.

guided_steps.done: The total (1800 kJ) is larger than the useful output, as it must be.

guided_steps.say: So the total energy input from the wind is 1800 kJ.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange: total input = useful output ÷ efficiency = 720 ÷ 0.40 = 1800 kJ.
Don't multiply: total input = 720 ÷ 0.40 = 1800 kJ. The total must be MORE than the useful output.

silver.hint: Find the total input first (useful ÷ efficiency), then subtract the useful.
silver.display: A gas boiler is 92% efficient and provides 46,000 J of useful heat energy. Calculate the total energy wasted by the boiler.

guided_steps.say: Two steps: find the total input, then the wasted energy. First rearrange: total input = useful output ÷ efficiency.
Now the finish. Wasted = total − useful.

guided_steps.done: Adds back to the 50,000 J input, so 4000 J wasted is right.
guided_steps.hint: Useful plus wasted should give the total.

guided_steps.say: So the energy wasted is 4000 J.

misconceptions.message: First find total input: 46,000 ÷ 0.92 = 50,000 J. Then wasted = total − useful = 50,000 − 46,000 = 4000 J.

silver.hint: mgh each second is the input power; multiply it by the efficiency.
silver.display: A hydroelectric power station converts the GPE of falling water into electricity. 8000 kg of water falls through 50 m every second. The station has an efficiency of 0.85. Calculate the useful power output. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: The falling water's GPE becomes electricity. Find the GPE gained each second, \(E_p = mgh\); because it is per second, that is the input power in watts.

guided_steps.pre: Now multiply by the height h: 78400 × 50 =
guided_steps.hint: Multiply by the height to get GPE per second.

guided_steps.say: That is the total input power. Useful output = efficiency × input power.

guided_steps.done: Back to 0.85, so the useful power is right.

guided_steps.say: So the useful power output is 3,332,000 W (about 3.3 MW).

misconceptions.message: GPE per second = mgh = 8000 × 9.8 × 50 = 3,920,000 W. Useful output = efficiency × input power = 0.85 × 3,920,000 = 3,332,000 W.
Since the water falls every second, mgh gives energy per second, which is power in watts.

silver.hint: Find useful power (efficiency × total), then subtract from the total.
silver.display: An electric drill has a power rating of 750 W and an efficiency of 0.60. Calculate the power wasted as heat and sound.

guided_steps.say: Two steps: find the useful power, then the wasted power. Useful = efficiency × total input.
Now the finish. Wasted = total − useful.

guided_steps.done: Adds back to 750 W, so 300 W wasted is right.
guided_steps.hint: Useful plus wasted should give the total.

guided_steps.say: So the power wasted as heat and sound is 300 W.

misconceptions.message: Useful = efficiency × total = 0.60 × 750 = 450 W. Wasted = 750 − 450 = 300 W.
Find useful power first (efficiency × input), then subtract from total to get wasted power.

silver.hint: All the outputs must add up to the input; subtract the ones you know.
silver.display: A Sankey diagram for a coal power station shows 1000 MJ input. The useful electricity arrow is 350 MJ and the cooling tower waste arrow is 500 MJ. Calculate the energy lost through other waste pathways.

guided_steps.say: Energy is conserved: everything in must come out somewhere. Other waste = total − useful − known waste.

guided_steps.hint: What is left must be the other waste.

guided_steps.done: Adds back to 1000 MJ, so 150 MJ is right.
guided_steps.hint: All the outputs should add to the input.

guided_steps.say: So the energy lost through other pathways is 150 MJ.

misconceptions.message: Total in = all out. Other waste = 1000 − 350 − 500 = 150 MJ. Energy is always conserved.

problem_bank.gold_description: Chain two equations: find the useful energy (KE, GPE, or power × time) first, then bring in efficiency.

method_card.title: Circuit Calculations
method_card.content:
Circuit questions rest on Ohm's law \(V = IR\) and charge flow \(Q = It\), plus the rules for combining resistors.

In series the current is the same everywhere and resistances add. In parallel each branch sees the full voltage, branch currents add, and the total resistance is smaller than the smallest resistor. For power use \(P = VI\) or \(P = I^2R\). Put time in seconds before \(Q = It\).

steps: Break a mixed network down: reduce the parallel part first, then add the series resistor to get the total.
Or chain equations: find the current with \(I = V/R\), then feed it into \(P = I^2R\) or \(Q = It\).
Always check: put your answer back into the original equation and confirm it returns a given value.

Or combine resistors first. Series: add them. Parallel: \(\frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2}\), then flip. A parallel total is always smaller than the smallest resistor.
Then it is a bronze question: substitute and compute.

method_card.title: Electrical Power and Energy Bills
method_card.content:
Four recall equations give electrical power and energy: \(P = VI\), \(P = I^2R\), \(E = Pt\) and \(E = QV\). Pick the one that matches the quantities you are given.

Bills measure energy in kilowatt hours. One kWh is the energy a 1 kW appliance uses in 1 hour, which is 3,600,000 J. Convert power to kW and time to hours, multiply for the energy in kWh, then multiply by the price per unit for the cost.

Check whether your exam gives you these equations or expects them from memory.

method_card.title: Density, SHC and Latent Heat
method_card.content:
Three equations: density \(\rho = m/V\), specific heat capacity \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\), and latent heat \(E = mL\). Check which of these your board gives you and which you need to recall.

Use SHC when the temperature changes, latent heat when the state changes (melting or boiling), and both added together when a substance heats up and then changes state. During a state change the temperature stays constant.

Convert grams to kilograms before substituting, and watch volume units: cm³ and m³ give different density units. Temperature change means final minus initial.

steps: Some questions need two calculations: heat a substance (\(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\)) and change its state (\(E = mL\)), then add the energies.
Others give power and time: find the energy with \(E = Pt\), then rearrange to get c or L.
Work each part in full, keep the units, and add or divide only at the end.

guided_steps.say: So the specific heat capacity is \(600\) J/(kg°C).

misconceptions.message: Convert time: 2 min = 120 s. Energy supplied = Pt = 40 × 120 = 4800 J. Δθ = 30 − 20 = 10°C. Rearrange ΔE = mcΔθ → c = ΔE/(mΔθ) = 4800 ÷ (0.8 × 10) = 4800 ÷ 8 = 600 J/(kg°C).
Rearrange ΔE = mcΔθ to c = ΔE ÷ (m × Δθ). Don't multiply all three together.

gold.hint: Energy lost by the water = melting energy + warming energy of the melted ice.
gold.display: An ice cube of mass 0.05 kg at 0°C is dropped into 0.3 kg of water at 25°C. The ice melts and the final temperature of the water is 21°C. Use this data to estimate the specific latent heat of fusion of ice. SHC of water = 4200 J/(kg°C).

guided_steps.say: Energy lost by the warm water equals energy gained by the ice as it melts and then warms. Set them equal and solve for L.

guided_steps.hint: The warm water drops from 25 to 21.

guided_steps.pre: Energy to warm the melted ice from 0 to 21: 0.05 × 4200 × 21 =

guided_steps.hint: Total gained minus the warming part.

guided_steps.done: L = 12,600 J/kg, the estimate for the ice.

guided_steps.say: So the specific latent heat of fusion is about \(12{,}600\) J/kg.

misconceptions.message: Energy lost by warm water = mcΔθ = 0.3 × 4200 × 4 = 5040 J. Energy gained by ice = melting + warming = 0.05L + 0.05 × 4200 × 21 = 0.05L + 4410. Set equal: 5040 = 0.05L + 4410. 0.05L = 630. L = 12,600 J/kg.
Energy lost by warm water = energy gained by ice (melting + warming). Set up: 0.3 × 4200 × 4 = 0.05 × L + 0.05 × 4200 × 21. Solve for L = 12,600 J/kg.

bronze.hint: Density is mass divided by volume, both already in base units.
bronze.display: An iron block has a mass of 3.9 kg and a volume of 0.0005 m³. Calculate its density.

guided_steps.say: Density is mass shared over volume: \(\rho = \frac{m}{V}\). Both values are already in kg and m³, so go straight in.

guided_steps.hint: It is given in kg already: 3.9.
Dividing by 0.0005 is the same as × 2000.

guided_steps.done: Back to the mass we started with, so the density is 7800 kg/m³.

guided_steps.say: So \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³.

misconceptions.message: Density = mass ÷ volume, not volume ÷ mass. ρ = 3.9 ÷ 0.0005 = 7800 kg/m³.

bronze.hint: Rearrange to mass = density × volume.
bronze.display: A liquid has a density of 800 kg/m³ and occupies a volume of 0.002 m³. Calculate its mass.

guided_steps.say: Density and volume are given, and we want the mass. Rearrange \(\rho = \frac{m}{V}\) to \(m = \rho V\).

guided_steps.done: That returns the density, so the mass is 1.6 kg.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange ρ = m/V to get m = ρ × V = 800 × 0.002 = 1.6 kg.

bronze.hint: Find the temperature change first, then multiply m × c × Δθ.
bronze.display: A 2 kg block of aluminium is heated from 25°C to 75°C. The SHC of aluminium is 900 J/(kg°C). Calculate the energy transferred.

guided_steps.say: Heating with no state change means specific heat capacity: \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\). First find the temperature change.

guided_steps.done: Back to the 50°C change, so the energy is 90,000 J.
guided_steps.hint: Energy ÷ (m × c) returns the temperature change.

bronze.equation_hint: Given on equation sheet: \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\)

misconceptions.message: Use the temperature change, not the final temperature. Δθ = 75 − 25 = 50°C. ΔE = 2 × 900 × 50 = 90,000 J.

bronze.hint: Temperature change is 100 − 20, then m × c × Δθ.
bronze.display: A 3 kg block of water is heated. The SHC of water is 4200 J/(kg°C). The temperature rises from 20°C to 100°C. Calculate the energy supplied.

guided_steps.say: Temperature is changing, so use SHC: \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\). Find the change first.

guided_steps.done: Back to the 80°C change, so the energy is 1,008,000 J.
guided_steps.hint: Energy ÷ (m × c) returns the temperature change.

bronze.equation_hint: Given on equation sheet: \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\)

bronze.hint: State change, so energy = mass × latent heat.
bronze.display: Calculate the energy needed to melt 0.5 kg of ice. The specific latent heat of fusion of water is 334,000 J/kg.

guided_steps.say: Melting is a state change, so use latent heat: \(E = mL\). No temperature change here.

guided_steps.done: Back to L, so the energy is 167,000 J.
guided_steps.hint: Energy ÷ mass returns the latent heat.

misconceptions.message: E = m × L = 0.5 × 334,000 = 167,000 J. Don't divide, multiply mass by the specific latent heat.

bronze.hint: Boiling is a state change: energy = mass × latent heat of vaporisation.
bronze.display: Calculate the energy needed to boil 0.1 kg of water at 100°C. The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2,260,000 J/kg.

guided_steps.say: Boiling is a state change, so use latent heat: \(E = mL\). Use the vaporisation value.

guided_steps.done: Back to L, so the energy is 226,000 J.
guided_steps.hint: Energy ÷ mass returns the latent heat.

misconceptions.message: This is a state change (boiling), so use E = mL. E = 0.1 × 2,260,000 = 226,000 J. Don't use SHC, the temperature isn't changing during boiling.

bronze.hint: A state change at constant temperature uses latent heat.
bronze.display: Which equation would you use to calculate the energy needed to change the state of a substance without changing its temperature?

misconceptions.message: State changes (melting, boiling) use latent heat: E = mL. SHC (mcΔθ) is for temperature changes, not state changes.

bronze.hint: Density is mass divided by volume.
bronze.display: A stone has a mass of 0.15 kg and a volume of 0.00005 m³. Calculate its density.

guided_steps.say: Density is mass over volume: \(\rho = \frac{m}{V}\). Both units are already base units.

guided_steps.done: Back to the mass, so the density is 3000 kg/m³.

guided_steps.say: So \(\rho = 3000\) kg/m³.

misconceptions.message: ρ = m ÷ V = 0.15 ÷ 0.00005 = 3000 kg/m³. Divide mass by volume, not the other way round.

silver.hint: Convert 400 g to kg, find Δθ, then convert the answer to kJ.
silver.display: A 400 g piece of copper is heated from 18°C to 118°C. The SHC of copper is 385 J/(kg°C). Calculate the energy transferred in kJ.

guided_steps.say: Temperature is changing, so SHC: \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\). The mass is in grams and the answer is wanted in kJ, so convert carefully.

guided_steps.done: 15.4 kJ, matching the answer wanted in kilojoules.

guided_steps.say: So \(\Delta E = 15.4\) kJ.

silver.equation_hint: Given on equation sheet: \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\)

misconceptions.message: Find the temperature change first: Δθ = 118 − 18 = 100°C, not 118°C.

silver.hint: Rearrange to Δθ = energy ÷ (m × c).
silver.display: A heater supplies 50,400 J to 2 kg of water. The SHC of water is 4200 J/(kg°C). Calculate the temperature rise.

guided_steps.say: Energy and mass are given, and we want the temperature rise. Rearrange \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\) to \(\Delta\theta = \frac{\Delta E}{mc}\).

guided_steps.pre: First multiply the mass by the specific heat capacity (m × c): 2 × 4200 =
guided_steps.hint: Multiply mass by specific heat capacity.

guided_steps.done: Back to the 50,400 J supplied, so the rise is 6°C.
guided_steps.hint: m × c × Δθ should return the energy.

guided_steps.say: So \(\Delta\theta = 6\)°C.

silver.equation_hint: Given on equation sheet: \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\)

silver.hint: Convert the density to g/cm³, then volume = mass ÷ density.
silver.display: A gold ring has a density of 19,300 kg/m³ and a mass of 9.65 g. Calculate its volume in cm³. (1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³)

guided_steps.say: We want the volume, so rearrange \(\rho = \frac{m}{V}\) to \(V = \frac{m}{\rho}\). The mass is in grams, so convert the density to grams per cm³ to match.

guided_steps.done: Back to the 9.65 g mass, so the volume is 0.5 cm³.

guided_steps.say: So \(V = 0.5\) cm³.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange ρ = m/V to V = m/ρ. Don't multiply mass by density.

silver.hint: Find the rise with Δθ = energy ÷ (m × c), then add the start temperature.
silver.display: An immersion heater provides 836,000 J to heat 2.5 kg of water. The SHC of water is 4200 J/(kg°C). The starting temperature is 15°C. Calculate the final temperature.

guided_steps.say: Find the temperature rise first, then add the starting temperature. Rearrange to \(\Delta\theta = \frac{\Delta E}{mc}\).

guided_steps.pre: Multiply the mass by the specific heat capacity (m × c): 2.5 × 4200 =

guided_steps.done: 94.6°C, the final temperature, not just the rise.

guided_steps.say: So the final temperature is \(94.6\)°C.

silver.equation_hint: Given on equation sheet: \(\Delta E = mc\Delta\theta\)

misconceptions.message: You found the temperature rise (79.6°C), but the question asks for the final temperature. Add the starting temperature: 15 + 79.6 = 94.6°C.

silver.hint: Convert 250 g to kg, then energy = mass × latent heat.
silver.display: Calculate the energy needed to melt 250 g of ice at 0°C. The specific latent heat of fusion of water is 334,000 J/kg.

guided_steps.say: Melting is a state change: \(E = mL\). The mass is in grams, so convert first.

guided_steps.done: Back to L, so the energy is 83,500 J.
guided_steps.hint: Energy ÷ mass returns the latent heat.

misconceptions.message: Convert g to kg first: 250 g = 0.25 kg. E = mL = 0.25 × 334,000 = 83,500 J.

silver.hint: Keep grams and cm³: density = mass ÷ volume.
silver.display: A metal block of volume 60 cm³ has a mass of 162 g. Calculate its density in g/cm³.

guided_steps.say: The question asks for g/cm³, so keep grams and cm³ as they are: \(\rho = \frac{m}{V}\).

guided_steps.done: Back to the 162 g mass, so the density is 2.7 g/cm³.

guided_steps.say: So \(\rho = 2.7\) g/cm³.

misconceptions.message: The question asks for g/cm³, so keep the units as given: ρ = 162 ÷ 60 = 2.7 g/cm³. Don't convert to kg and m³.
Density = mass ÷ volume = 162 ÷ 60 = 2.7 g/cm³.

steps.say: Two energy stores. Find the elastic PE, then set it equal to the kinetic energy.

steps.done: Back to 1 J, so v = 2 m/s.

steps.pre: Pushing a crate takes effort. Push with a steady 10 N force for 3 m: that is 10 × 3 = 30 'pushes' of effort. Now push the same 10 N for 6 m. Effort = 10 × 6 =
steps.say: A pushing puzzle. No equations, just think about effort.

steps.pre: And if you push harder, 20 N, over that same 6 m? Effort = 20 × 6 =
steps.say: Harder push, more effort again.

steps: Choose the equation: weight, work done, spring force, or elastic energy.
Convert units first: extension cm to m (divide by 100), and find weight before work done when lifting.
Substitute and calculate.
State the answer with its unit (N, J, N/m).
method_card.title: Forces, Work Done and Elasticity
method_card.content:
Four equations live here. Three are recall: weight \(W = mg\), work done \(W = Fs\), and spring force \(F = ke\). One is usually given: elastic energy \(E_e = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\) (check whether your board supplies it).

Weight is a force in newtons, so it often becomes the force in a work-done sum. Work done needs the distance moved in the direction of the force, so against gravity use the height. Extension is the change in length (stretched minus natural), converted to metres.

steps: Multi-step problems link equations: weight, then work done, then power \(P = W_d ÷ t\).
Elastic energy \(E_e = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\) squares the extension, so doubling the stretch stores four times the energy.
Watch for distractors: work against gravity uses only the vertical height, and a resultant force subtracts friction first.
gold.title: Gold: chain equations or square the extension

example.question: A hoist lifts a 50 kg load 6 m in 20 s. Calculate the power. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

steps: Pick the right equation: weight \(W = mg\), work done \(W = Fs\), or spring force \(F = ke\).
Write it, substitute the numbers, and multiply. In bronze the values are already in kg, N and m.
State the answer with its unit: N for force and weight, J for work, N/m for a spring constant.
bronze.title: Bronze: one equation, values ready to use

example.question: A bag has a mass of 5 kg. Calculate its weight. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

steps: Same equations, but tidy the numbers first. Extensions in cm must become metres: divide by 100.
Lifting? Find the weight with \(W = mg\), then use that weight as the force in \(W = Fs\).
Rearranging \(F = ke\) for k gives \(k = F ÷ e\). Substitute only after the units are right.
silver.title: Silver: convert a unit or rearrange first

example.question: A spring, spring constant 40 N/m, is stretched from 10 cm to 30 cm. Calculate the force.

exam_context.frequency: Very high: weight and work done appear almost every year, and springs link to required practicals.

gold.hint: Weight, then work done, then divide by the time.
gold.display: A person of mass 65 kg walks up 12 m of stairs in 15 seconds. Calculate the power they develop. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Three steps: weight, then work done climbing, then power.
Power is work done per second: \(P = W_d ÷ t\).

guided_steps.hint: Divide the work done by the time.

guided_steps.done: Back to 7644 J, so P = 509.6 W is right.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply power by time to get work done.

misconceptions.message: Find the weight first: 65 × 9.8 = 637 N. Work done = 7644 J, power = 509.6 W. Using the mass as the force (65 × 12 ÷ 15 = 52) skips the weight.

gold.hint: Find the extension, convert to metres, square it, then half k e squared.
gold.display: A spring has a spring constant of 200 N/m. It is stretched from its natural length of 8 cm to 20 cm. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored in the spring.

guided_steps.say: Elastic potential energy \(E_e = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\). Find the extension, convert to metres, then square.
Now substitute into \(E_e = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\).

guided_steps.pre: Check by finding the squared extension again. Half the spring constant is ½ × 200 = 100, so 1.44 ÷ 100 =
guided_steps.done: Back to e² = 0.0144, so Eₑ = 1.44 J is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide by 100 (which is ½ × 200) to recover e².

misconceptions.message: Extension is the change: 20 − 8 = 12 cm = 0.12 m, not the full 20 cm. Using 0.20 m gives ½ × 200 × 0.04 = 4 J.
Square the extension: 0.12² = 0.0144. Forgetting to square (½ × 200 × 0.12) gives 12 J.

gold.hint: Rearrange to k = 2E divided by e squared.
gold.display: A spring stores 0.72 J of elastic PE when extended by 0.06 m. Calculate the spring constant.

guided_steps.say: Rearrange \(E_e = \frac{1}{2}ke^2\) for k: \(k = 2E_e ÷ e^2\).
Now divide.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the doubled energy by e².

guided_steps.done: Back to 0.72 J, so k = 400 N/m is right.

misconceptions.message: Rearranging ½ke² for k gives k = 2E ÷ e². Forgetting the 2 (0.72 ÷ 0.0036) gives 200, half the real value.
e is squared: 0.06² = 0.0036. Using 0.06 instead (1.44 ÷ 0.06) gives 24.

gold.hint: Subtract friction to get the resultant force, then multiply by distance.
gold.display: A box of mass 40 kg is pushed 5 m across a rough floor by a force of 300 N. The friction force is 120 N. Calculate the resultant work done on the box.

guided_steps.say: The box feels two forces. Find the resultant first, then \(W = Fs\). The mass is not needed.

guided_steps.hint: Take friction from the pushing force.

guided_steps.say: Now \(W = Fs\) with the resultant force.

guided_steps.done: Back to the 180 N resultant, so W = 900 J is right.

misconceptions.message: Use the resultant force, not just the applied force. Resultant = 300 − 120 = 180 N, so W = 180 × 5 = 900 J. Using 300 gives 1500 J.
The mass (40 kg) is a distractor here. Work done needs a force and a distance, not the mass.

gold.hint: Elastic energy equals kinetic energy; solve for v.
gold.display: A spring with spring constant 50 N/m is compressed by 0.1 m. The stored energy is transferred to a 0.02 kg ball. Assuming all elastic PE converts to kinetic energy, calculate the speed of the ball.

guided_steps.say: Two energy stores. First the elastic PE, then set it equal to the kinetic energy.
All of this becomes kinetic energy: \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 0.25\). Rearrange: \(v^2 = 2E ÷ m\).

guided_steps.hint: Double the energy, divide by the mass.

guided_steps.done: Back to 0.25 J, so v = 5 m/s is right.

misconceptions.message: Elastic PE = ½ × 50 × 0.1² = 0.25 J. Set equal to KE: ½ × 0.02 × v² = 0.25, so v² = 25 and v = 5 m/s.
Square the compression: 0.1² = 0.01, giving Eₑ = 0.25 J.

gold.hint: Work against gravity uses only the vertical height.
gold.display: A crane lifts a 350 kg beam 8 m and also moves it 15 m horizontally. Calculate the total work done by the crane against gravity. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Work against gravity uses only the vertical height. First the weight, then \(W = Fs\) with the height.
Lift the weight through the vertical height of 8 m. The 15 m sideways does no work against gravity.

guided_steps.hint: Weight times the vertical height only.

guided_steps.done: Back to the 3430 N weight, so 27,440 J is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide by the height to recover the weight.

misconceptions.message: Work against gravity uses only the vertical height. Weight = 3430 N, so W = 3430 × 8 = 27,440 J. Adding the 15 m sideways (using 23 m) gives 78,890 J.
Gravity is a vertical force, so only the vertical height matters. The horizontal 15 m is a distractor.

bronze.hint: Weight is a force: multiply the mass by g.
bronze.display: A book has a mass of 1.5 kg. Calculate its weight. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Weight is a force: \(W = mg\), mass times gravitational field strength.

guided_steps.hint: The mass is already given in kilograms.

guided_steps.say: Substitute into \(W = mg\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 1.5 kg, so W = 14.7 N is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide the weight by g to get the mass.

misconceptions.note: gave the mass instead of the weight
misconceptions.message: Weight is a force in newtons, not the mass. Multiply: W = 1.5 × 9.8 = 14.7 N.

bronze.hint: Work done is force times distance.
bronze.display: A force of 200 N is used to push a box 6 m along the floor. Calculate the work done.

guided_steps.say: Work done is \(W = Fs\): force times distance moved.

guided_steps.hint: The force is given in newtons.

guided_steps.say: Substitute into \(W = Fs\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 200 N, so W = 1200 J is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide the work by the distance.

misconceptions.message: Work done = force × distance = 200 × 6 = 1200 J.

bronze.hint: Multiply the spring constant by the extension.
bronze.display: A spring has a spring constant of 25 N/m and is extended by 0.2 m. Calculate the force on the spring.

guided_steps.say: Hooke's law: \(F = ke\), spring constant times extension.
Substitute into \(F = ke\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 0.2 m, so F = 5 N is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide force by k to get the extension.

misconceptions.message: F = k × e, so multiply: 25 × 0.2 = 5 N. Dividing k by e (giving 125) is the slip.

bronze.hint: Use the Moon's g value, not Earth's.
bronze.display: An astronaut has a mass of 80 kg. Calculate their weight on the Moon, where g = 1.6 N/kg.

guided_steps.say: Weight \(W = mg\). Use the Moon's gravitational field strength, not Earth's.
Substitute into \(W = mg\).

guided_steps.done: Back to g = 1.6, so W = 128 N is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide weight by mass to get g.

misconceptions.message: Use the Moon's g = 1.6, not Earth's 9.8. W = 80 × 1.6 = 128 N. Using 9.8 gives 784 N.

bronze.hint: Work done is force times distance.
bronze.display: A dog pulls a sled with a force of 150 N over a distance of 20 m. Calculate the work done.

guided_steps.say: Work done is \(W = Fs\): force times distance moved.

guided_steps.hint: The force is given in newtons.

guided_steps.say: Substitute into \(W = Fs\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 150 N, so W = 3000 J is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide the work by the distance.

misconceptions.message: Work done = F × s = 150 × 20 = 3000 J.

bronze.hint: Find the extension, convert it to metres, then divide the force by it.
bronze.display: A spring has a natural length of 10 cm. When a 4 N force is applied, it stretches to 18 cm. Calculate the spring constant in N/m.

guided_steps.say: Hooke's law is \(F = ke\). You know F and the lengths, so find the extension, then rearrange for k.

guided_steps.hint: Take the natural length from the stretched length.

guided_steps.say: Rearrange \(F = ke\) to \(k = F ÷ e\).

guided_steps.hint: Divide the force by the extension in metres.

guided_steps.done: Back to 4 N, so k = 50 N/m is right.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply k by extension to get the force.

misconceptions.message: Convert cm to m first: 8 cm = 0.08 m. k = 4 ÷ 0.08 = 50 N/m. Dividing by 8 gives 0.5, which is wrong.
Extension is the change in length, not the total length: 18 − 10 = 8 cm.

bronze.hint: Weight uses mass and gravity.
bronze.display: Which equation gives the weight of an object?

misconceptions.message: Weight = mass × gravitational field strength (W = mg). W = Fs is work done, not weight. They share the letter W but mean different things.

bronze.hint: Weight is mass times g, in newtons.
bronze.display: A weightlifter raises a 60 kg barbell. Calculate the weight of the barbell. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Weight is a force: \(W = mg\), mass times gravitational field strength.

guided_steps.hint: The mass is already given in kilograms.

guided_steps.say: Substitute into \(W = mg\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 60 kg, so W = 588.0 N is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide the weight by g to get the mass.

misconceptions.note: gave the mass instead of the weight
misconceptions.message: Weight is a force in newtons, not the mass. W = 60 × 9.8 = 588 N.

silver.hint: Find the weight first, then use it as the force in work done.
silver.display: A crate of mass 25 kg is lifted 3 m onto a shelf. Calculate the work done against gravity. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Lifting: first find the weight, then use it as the force in \(W = Fs\).
That weight is the force you lift against. Now \(W_d = Fs\).

guided_steps.hint: Multiply the weight by the height.

guided_steps.done: Back to the 245 N weight, so 735 J is right.

misconceptions.message: Find the weight first: W = mg = 245 N. Then work done = 245 × 3 = 735 J. Using the mass directly (25 × 3 = 75) skips the weight step.

silver.hint: Extension is the change in length; convert cm to metres before substituting.
silver.display: A spring has a spring constant of 80 N/m. It is stretched from its natural length of 12 cm to 27 cm. Calculate the force applied.

guided_steps.say: Hooke's law \(F = ke\). Find the extension, convert to metres, then substitute.
Substitute into \(F = ke\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 0.15 m, so F = 12 N is right.

misconceptions.message: Convert cm to m first: 15 cm = 0.15 m. F = 80 × 0.15 = 12 N. Using 15 gives 1200 N.
Use the extension (27 − 12 = 15 cm), not the total stretched length.

silver.hint: Weight, then work done, then divide by the time for power.
silver.display: A forklift lifts a 200 kg pallet 4 m in 10 seconds. Calculate the power of the forklift. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Three steps: weight, then work done, then power.
Power is work done per second: \(P = W_d ÷ t\).

lessons.description: Calculate speed, acceleration and use distance-time and velocity-time graphs — including the higher-only SUVAT equation v² = u² + 2as.

gold.label: Together: the gold move

steps.say: The SUVAT equation \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\). Check whether your board gives it to you. From rest, u = 0.

steps.done: 30 m/s. Remember to square root at the end.

gold.display: A motorbike accelerates from rest at 5 m/s² over 90 m. Calculate its final velocity. Use \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\).

steps.say: Speed = distance ÷ time: \(v = \frac{s}{t}\). Metres and seconds already, so no conversion.

steps.done: 90 m, matching. Speed = 6 m/s.

opener.label: Before any equations

steps.say: No equations yet, just common sense. You walk a 60 m corridor, end to end, and it takes 30 seconds. Spread the 60 m evenly across the 30 seconds.
That number, metres per second, is speed. You just did speed = distance ÷ time without being told. Now you speed up: over 4 seconds your speed climbs steadily from 2 m/s to 6 m/s.
steps.hint: Speed rose by 6 − 2 = 4 m/s, spread over 4 seconds.

steps.say: That steady gain, 1 metre per second every second, is acceleration. Two ideas, both just sharing a change over time: speed shares distance over time (\(v = \frac{s}{t}\)), acceleration shares change in speed over time (\(a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\)). The rest of this lesson is those two, plus reading them off graphs.

opener.display:
A 60 m corridor.
You walk it, end to end, in 30 seconds.

steps: Choose the equation: speed \(v = s/t\), acceleration \(a = \Delta v/\Delta t\), or distance \(s = vt\).
Convert to base units first: metres, seconds and m/s (km/h ÷ 3.6 = m/s).
For graphs: gradient of a distance-time graph = speed; area under a velocity-time graph = distance.
Substitute, calculate, and state the answer with its unit.
method_card.title: Speed, Acceleration and Graphs
method_card.content:
Speed is distance ÷ time (\(v = s/t\)); acceleration is change in speed ÷ time (\(a = \Delta v/\Delta t\)). Both need base units: metres and seconds.

On a distance-time graph the gradient gives the speed. On a velocity-time graph the gradient gives the acceleration and the area underneath gives the distance, found by splitting into triangles and rectangles.

The higher-tier equation \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\) links speed, acceleration and distance; it gives \(v^2\), so square root at the end. Slowing down counts as negative acceleration.

steps: Two equations may chain: find acceleration from \(F = ma\), then a speed from \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\). Check whether your board gives you the SUVAT equation.
That equation gives \(v^2\), so square root at the end. Slowing down means a is negative.
For a velocity-time graph, distance = area under the line: split into triangles and rectangles and add them.
gold.title: Gold: multi-step and graphs

steps: Pick the right equation: speed \(v = \frac{s}{t}\), acceleration \(a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\), or distance \(s = vt\).
The values are already in metres, seconds and m/s, so substitute straight in and calculate.
Acceleration uses the change in speed (final minus start), not just the final speed. Slowing down is negative.

steps: The values arrive in the wrong units: km, minutes, or km/h. Convert to metres and seconds before substituting.
Handy conversions: 1 km = 1000 m, 1 minute = 60 s, and km/h ÷ 3.6 = m/s.
For uniform acceleration, distance = average speed × time, where average speed = (start + end) ÷ 2.

gold.hint: Use v² = u² + 2as with u = 0, then square root.
gold.display: A car accelerates from rest at 3 m/s². Calculate its velocity after travelling 150 m.

guided_steps.say: This uses the SUVAT equation \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\). Check whether your board gives you this equation or expects you to recall it. From rest, u = 0.

guided_steps.done: 30 m/s. The equation gives v², so square root at the end.

misconceptions.message: The equation gives v² = 0 + 2 × 3 × 150 = 900, so you must square root: v = √900 = 30 m/s, not 900 m/s.

gold.hint: Use v² = u² + 2as with final speed 0 and a negative acceleration.
gold.display: A car travelling at 20 m/s brakes with a deceleration of 4 m/s². Calculate the braking distance.

guided_steps.say: Use \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\) with u = 20 m/s, final v = 0 (it stops), and a = −4 m/s² (slowing). Check whether your board gives you this equation.

guided_steps.done: Braking distance = 50 m.

misconceptions.message: Deceleration means a = −4 m/s². With v = 0: 0 = 20² + 2 × (−4) × s = 400 − 8s, so s = 50 m. Using a = +4 gives −50 m, which is impossible for a distance.
v² = u² + 2as with v = 0: 0 = 400 − 8s, so 8s = 400 and s = 50 m.

gold.hint: Distance is the area under the graph: two triangles and a rectangle.
gold.display: The velocity-time graph shows a complete journey. Calculate the total distance travelled.

guided_steps.say: Distance = area under the velocity-time graph. Split into three parts: a triangle (0 to 6 s), a rectangle (6 to 8 s), and a triangle (8 to 14 s).

misconceptions.message: Three sections: triangle (0 to 6 s) = ½ × 6 × 15 = 45 m, rectangle (6 to 8 s) = 2 × 15 = 30 m, triangle (8 to 14 s) = ½ × 6 × 15 = 45 m; total 120 m. Forgetting the middle rectangle gives only 90 m.
Find the area under the graph, not the gradient. Split into triangles and rectangles.

gold.hint: Use v² = u² + 2as with u = 0 and a = 9.8, then rearrange for s.
gold.display: A stone is dropped from rest and hits the ground at 24.5 m/s. Calculate the height it fell from. Use \(g = 9.8\) m/s².

guided_steps.say: Falling from rest, so u = 0, and v = 24.5 m/s at the ground. Use \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\) with a = g = 9.8 m/s². Check whether your board gives you this equation.

guided_steps.done: Matches 24.5². Height ≈ 30.6 m.

gold.hint: Find acceleration from F = ma, then use v² = u² + 2as.
gold.display: A car of mass 1200 kg is travelling at 15 m/s. It accelerates over 100 m to reach a new speed. The resultant force on the car is 3600 N. Calculate the final speed of the car. Give your answer to 1 d.p.

guided_steps.say: Two equations. First get acceleration from \(F = ma\), then the final speed from \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\). Check whether your board gives you the second equation.

guided_steps.pre: Square root and round to 1 d.p.: v = √825 =
guided_steps.done: √825 = 28.72, which rounds to 28.7 m/s.
guided_steps.hint: Work out √825, then give 1 decimal place.

misconceptions.message: First a = F ÷ m = 3600 ÷ 1200 = 3 m/s², then v² = u² + 2as = 225 + 600 = 825, so v = √825 = 28.7 m/s. Forgetting to add u² gives √600 = 24.5 m/s.
Two equations here: F = ma gives a = 3 m/s², then v² = u² + 2as gives the final speed.

gold.hint: Split into two phases; use the average speed for the accelerating part.
gold.display: A cyclist accelerates from 4 m/s to 10 m/s in 3 seconds, then travels at a constant 10 m/s for another 7 seconds. Calculate the total distance covered in 10 seconds.

guided_steps.say: Split the journey into two phases. Phase 1: accelerating from 4 to 10 m/s over 3 s, use the average speed. Phase 2: constant 10 m/s for 7 s.

guided_steps.hint: Add the two speeds, then halve.

guided_steps.done: Distance = 91 m.

misconceptions.message: Two phases. Accelerating (0 to 3 s): average speed = (4 + 10) ÷ 2 = 7 m/s, distance = 21 m. Constant (3 to 10 s): 10 × 7 = 70 m. Total = 91 m. Counting only the constant phase gives 70 m.
During the acceleration use the average speed (7 m/s), not 10 m/s. Using 10 m/s for the whole 10 s gives 100 m instead of 91 m.

bronze.hint: Speed is distance divided by time.
bronze.display: A cyclist travels 600 m in 40 seconds. Calculate their speed.

guided_steps.say: Speed = distance ÷ time: \(v = \frac{s}{t}\). The values are already in metres and seconds, so no conversion is needed.

guided_steps.done: 600 m, matching the distance. Speed = 15 m/s.
guided_steps.hint: Speed × time should return the distance.

misconceptions.message: Speed = distance ÷ time = 600 ÷ 40 = 15 m/s. Dividing time by distance (40 ÷ 600) is upside down.

bronze.hint: Acceleration is the change in speed divided by the time.
bronze.display: A car accelerates from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 10 seconds. Calculate its acceleration.

guided_steps.say: Acceleration = change in speed ÷ time: \(a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\). Change in speed means final minus starting.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the change in speed by the time.

guided_steps.done: 20 m/s gained, matching 25 − 5. Acceleration = 2 m/s².
guided_steps.hint: Acceleration × time should return the change in speed.

misconceptions.message: Use the change in speed, not the final speed: Δv = 25 − 5 = 20 m/s, so a = 20 ÷ 10 = 2 m/s². Using 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5 forgets to subtract the starting speed.

bronze.hint: Distance is speed multiplied by time.
bronze.display: A runner moves at a constant speed of 4 m/s for 30 seconds. Calculate the distance covered.

guided_steps.say: Distance = speed × time: rearranged from \(v = \frac{s}{t}\) to \(s = vt\). Units are already m/s and s.

guided_steps.done: Back to 4 m/s, the given speed. Distance = 120 m.
guided_steps.hint: Distance ÷ time should return the speed.

misconceptions.message: Distance = speed × time = 4 × 30 = 120 m. Do not divide.

bronze.hint: Find the change in speed, then divide by the time; the deceleration is its size.
bronze.display: A train decelerates from 30 m/s to 10 m/s in 4 seconds. Calculate the deceleration.

guided_steps.say: Acceleration = change in speed ÷ time: \(a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\). Slowing down gives a negative value, and the deceleration is its size.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the change by the time; keep the minus.

guided_steps.done: The minus sign just means slowing down. Deceleration = 5 m/s².

misconceptions.message: Δv = 10 − 30 = −20 m/s, so a = −20 ÷ 4 = −5 m/s². The minus just means slowing down; the deceleration is its size, 5 m/s².

bronze.hint: On a distance-time graph, speed is the gradient: rise over run.
bronze.display: The distance-time graph shows a journey. Calculate the speed during the first 15 seconds.

guided_steps.say: On a distance-time graph, speed = gradient = rise ÷ run. Read the rise and run over the first 15 seconds.

guided_steps.hint: Read the graph at t = 15 s.

guided_steps.done: 60 m in 15 s, matching the graph. Speed = 4 m/s.
guided_steps.hint: Speed × time should return the distance.

bronze.equation_hint: Gradient of a distance-time graph = speed

misconceptions.message: Speed = gradient = rise ÷ run = 60 ÷ 15 = 4 m/s. Doing run ÷ rise (15 ÷ 60 = 0.25) inverts the gradient.

bronze.hint: Distance is speed multiplied by time.

guided_steps.say: Distance = speed × time: \(s = vt\). Units are m/s and s already.

guided_steps.done: Back to 340 m/s. Distance = 170 m.

misconceptions.message: Distance = speed × time = 340 × 0.5 = 170 m. Dividing (340 ÷ 0.5 = 680) uses the wrong operation.

bronze.hint: From rest the starting speed is 0; acceleration is the change in speed over time.
bronze.display: A bus accelerates from rest to 18 m/s in 6 seconds. Calculate its acceleration.

guided_steps.say: Acceleration = change in speed ÷ time: \(a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}\). From rest means the starting speed is 0.

guided_steps.hint: Final minus starting; from rest the start is 0.
Divide the change by the time.

guided_steps.done: 18 m/s gained, matching from rest to 18. Acceleration = 3 m/s².
guided_steps.hint: Acceleration × time returns the change in speed.

misconceptions.message: From rest means u = 0, so Δv = 18 − 0 = 18 m/s and a = 18 ÷ 6 = 3 m/s².

bronze.hint: Rearrange distance = speed × time to time = distance ÷ speed.
bronze.display: How long does it take a car travelling at 20 m/s to cover 500 m?

guided_steps.say: Start from \(s = vt\) and rearrange for time: \(t = \frac{s}{v}\). Units are m and m/s already.

guided_steps.done: 500 m covered, matching. Time = 25 s.
guided_steps.hint: Speed × time should return the distance.

misconceptions.message: Rearrange s = vt to t = s ÷ v = 500 ÷ 20 = 25 s.

silver.hint: Convert km to metres and minutes to seconds before dividing.

guided_steps.say: Speed = distance ÷ time, but first convert to base units: metres and seconds.

guided_steps.done: 54,000 m = 54 km. Speed = 30 m/s.

misconceptions.message: Convert first: 54 km = 54,000 m and 30 min = 1800 s, so v = 54,000 ÷ 1800 = 30 m/s. Leaving time in minutes (54,000 ÷ 30 = 1800) is a unit slip.

guided_steps.say: First convert 108 km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6. The car stops, so the final speed is 0.

guided_steps.hint: Stops, so the final speed is 0: 0 − 30.
Divide the change by the time; keep the minus.

guided_steps.done: The minus means slowing. Deceleration = 6 m/s².

misconceptions.message: Convert first: 108 km/h ÷ 3.6 = 30 m/s. Δv = 0 − 30 = −30 m/s, so a = −30 ÷ 5 = −6 m/s²; deceleration = 6 m/s². Using 108 ÷ 5 = 21.6 skips the conversion.
To convert km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6: 108 ÷ 3.6 = 30 m/s.

silver.hint: Distance is the area under the graph: split into a triangle and a rectangle.
silver.display: The velocity-time graph shows a car's journey. Calculate the total distance travelled in 20 seconds.

guided_steps.say: On a velocity-time graph, distance = area under the line. Split it into a triangle (0 to 10 s) and a rectangle (10 to 20 s).

guided_steps.pre: Cross-check with average speed: mean speed = 15 m/s over 20 s gives 15 × 20 =
guided_steps.done: Both routes give 300 m. Distance = 300 m.
guided_steps.hint: The mean of a 0 to 20 climb then a hold at 20 is 15 m/s.

misconceptions.message: Split the area: triangle (0 to 10 s) = ½ × 10 × 20 = 100 m, rectangle (10 to 20 s) = 10 × 20 = 200 m, total 300 m. Treating the whole graph as one triangle (½ × 20 × 20 = 200) misses the flat top.
Distance is the area under a velocity-time graph, not the gradient. Split it into a triangle and a rectangle.

silver.hint: Distance = average speed × time; average speed = (start + end) ÷ 2.
silver.display: A car accelerates uniformly from 8 m/s to 20 m/s in 4 seconds. Calculate the distance it travels. (Hint: average speed × time)

guided_steps.say: For uniform acceleration, distance = average speed × time. Average speed = (start + end) ÷ 2.

guided_steps.hint: Add the two speeds, then halve.

guided_steps.done: Back to the 14 m/s average. Distance = 56 m.
guided_steps.hint: Distance ÷ time returns the average speed.

misconceptions.message: For uniform acceleration use the average speed: (8 + 20) ÷ 2 = 14 m/s, so distance = 14 × 4 = 56 m. Using the final speed (20 × 4 = 80) overcounts.

silver.hint: Find the final speed first, then use the average speed to get the distance.
silver.display: A sprinter accelerates at 4 m/s² from rest. Calculate their speed after 3 seconds, and the distance covered.

guided_steps.say: Two steps. First find the final speed with \(v = u + at\), then use the average speed to get distance. Starting from rest, u = 0.

guided_steps.pre: The question asks for distance, not speed. Distance (m) =
guided_steps.done: 18 m. Do not stop at the 12 m/s speed.

silver.equation_hint: \(v = u + at\) and average speed \(= \frac{u + v}{2}\)

misconceptions.message: v = u + at = 0 + 4 × 3 = 12 m/s is the speed, but the question asks for the distance: average speed = (0 + 12) ÷ 2 = 6 m/s, distance = 6 × 3 = 18 m.

silver.hint: To turn km/h into m/s, divide by 3.6.
silver.display: A car travels at 90 km/h. Convert this speed to m/s.

guided_steps.say: Convert km/h to m/s. One route: turn km into metres and hours into seconds. 90 km/h means 90 km every hour.

guided_steps.done: Same answer. The ÷3.6 shortcut is just ×1000 then ÷3600. Speed = 25 m/s.

steps.pre: Turn it around. For the 2 kg ball, that 10 N push gives an acceleration of 10 ÷ 2 =
steps.say: You just felt Newton's second law: force = mass × acceleration, \(F = ma\). Double the mass, double the force for the same acceleration.
So \(a = F/m\). That one equation, plus \(p = mv\) for momentum and \(v = f\lambda\) for waves, is this whole lesson.

steps: Pick the equation the question points to: \(F = ma\), \(p = mv\), \(v = f\lambda\) or \(T = 1/f\).

method_card.title: Newton's Laws, Momentum and Waves
method_card.content:
Newton's second law \(F = ma\) always uses the resultant force. If friction or weight acts, subtract it from the driving force first. Constant velocity means the resultant force is zero.

Momentum \(p = mv\) is conserved in collisions: total before equals total after. It is higher tier only.

Waves: \(v = f\lambda\), and period \(T = 1/f\). Convert frequency to hertz and lengths to metres before substituting. Check whether your board gives you the period equation.

steps: Some problems need two equations. Momentum: total \(mv\) before a collision equals total \(mv\) after.
Find the intermediate value first (a resultant force, a combined mass, or a frequency), then feed it into the second equation.
For very large or very small numbers, give the answer in standard form.
