guided_steps.done: Matches the 12 kg m/s before, so v = 3 m/s.

misconceptions.message: After they stick, combined mass = 3 + 1 = 4 kg. v = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 m/s. Using only 3 kg gives 4.

gold.hint: Momentum before = bullet only; divide by the total mass after.
gold.display: A 0.05 kg bullet is fired at 400 m/s into a 2.95 kg block of wood on a frictionless surface. The bullet embeds in the block. Calculate the velocity of the block and bullet after the collision.

guided_steps.say: Momentum is conserved. The bullet carries all the momentum before.

guided_steps.hint: Bullet plus block, now stuck together.

guided_steps.say: That 20 kg m/s is shared by 3 kg. \(v = p \div m\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 3 kg, so v = 6.67 m/s.
guided_steps.hint: Momentum divided by your velocity. Round to the nearest whole.

misconceptions.message: Total mass after = 0.05 + 2.95 = 3 kg. v = 20 ÷ 3 = 6.67 m/s. Using only 2.95 kg gives 6.78.

gold.hint: Resultant force = thrust − weight, then a = F ÷ m.
gold.display: A rocket of mass 500 kg fires its engines, producing a thrust of 8000 N. Its weight is 4900 N. Calculate the resultant force and the acceleration.

guided_steps.say: Find the resultant force: thrust up minus weight down.
guided_steps.hint: Weight pulls down, so subtract it.

guided_steps.say: Now \(a = F \div m\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 3100 N, so a = 6.2 m/s².

misconceptions.message: Resultant = thrust − weight = 8000 − 4900 = 3100 N. a = 3100 ÷ 500 = 6.2 m/s². Using 8000 N gives 16.

gold.hint: Convert MHz to Hz (× 10⁶), then λ = v ÷ f; give the answer in standard form.
gold.display: A radio station broadcasts at 98.5 MHz. The speed of radio waves is \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s. Calculate the wavelength in standard form.

guided_steps.pre: 98.5 MHz = 98.5 × 10⁶ Hz ('M' means × 10⁶). To rewrite it as A × 10⁷, move the decimal point one place left, so 98.5 becomes A =
guided_steps.say: The equation is \(v = f\lambda\), rearranged to \(\lambda = v \div f\). Give the answer in standard form. First fix the frequency.

guided_steps.pre: When you divide powers of ten, subtract the powers: 10⁸ ÷ 10⁷, so n = 8 − 7 =
guided_steps.say: Now the powers of ten.

guided_steps.hint: Move the decimal one place right. To 2 d.p.

guided_steps.pre: In standard form the number in front sits between 1 and 10. 3.05 already does, so λ = 3.05 × 10ⁿ, where n =
guided_steps.done: The wavelength is 3.05 m, written 3.05 × 10⁰ m.
guided_steps.hint: 3.05 needs no further shift, so the power is zero.

misconceptions.message: 98.5 MHz = 9.85 × 10⁷ Hz. λ = (3 × 10⁸) ÷ (9.85 × 10⁷) = 3.05 × 10⁰ m. Forgetting to convert MHz gives 3.05 × 10⁶.

gold.hint: Resultant = m × a, then friction = driving − resultant.
gold.display: A car of mass 1000 kg accelerates at 2 m/s² for 8 seconds. The driving force is 3200 N. Calculate the friction force acting on the car.

guided_steps.say: First the resultant force from \(F = ma\).
guided_steps.hint: Mass times acceleration. The 8 seconds is not needed.

guided_steps.say: Friction is what is left: driving force minus resultant.
guided_steps.hint: Take the resultant off the driving force.

guided_steps.done: Gives back the resultant 2000 N, so friction = 1200 N.
guided_steps.hint: It should equal the resultant force.

misconceptions.message: Resultant = ma = 2000 N. Friction = driving − resultant = 3200 − 2000 = 1200 N. Adding gives 5200.

gold.hint: Rearrange v = fλ to f = v ÷ λ; subtract the powers of ten.
gold.display: An X-ray has a wavelength of \(1 \times 10^{-10}\) m. The speed of EM waves is \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s. Calculate the frequency of the X-ray. Give your answer in standard form.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(v = f\lambda\), rearranged to \(f = v \div \lambda\). Give the answer in standard form.
guided_steps.hint: Just the fronts of each number.

guided_steps.pre: Now the powers. Dividing 10⁸ by 10⁻¹⁰ means subtracting the powers: 8 − (−10). Subtracting a negative is the same as adding: 8 + 10 =
guided_steps.say: Now the powers of ten. Dividing subtracts them, and subtracting a negative adds.

guided_steps.pre: Check by reversing: v = f × λ, so the powers add: 18 + (−10). Adding a negative is the same as subtracting: 18 − 10 =
guided_steps.done: Gives 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the original speed, so f = 3 × 10¹⁸ Hz.

misconceptions.message: f = v ÷ λ. Dividing subtracts the powers: 8 − (−10) = 18, so f = 3 × 10¹⁸ Hz. Adding them by mistake gives 10⁻².

bronze.hint: Rearrange F = ma to a = F ÷ m, then divide.
bronze.display: A resultant force of 240 N acts on an 80 kg trolley. Calculate its acceleration.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(F = ma\). We want the acceleration, so rearrange to \(a = F \div m\).
guided_steps.hint: Read it straight from the question.
It is already in kg, no conversion needed.

guided_steps.say: Now divide.

guided_steps.done: It gives back 240 N, so a = 3 m/s².

misconceptions.message: a = F ÷ m = 240 ÷ 80 = 3 m/s². Multiplying (240 × 80) is the slip.

bronze.hint: F = ma. Multiply mass by acceleration.
bronze.display: Calculate the force needed to accelerate a 1500 kg car at 2 m/s².

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(F = ma\). Force is the subject already, so no rearranging.
Multiply.

guided_steps.done: Back to 2 m/s², so F = 3000 N.
guided_steps.hint: Divide your force by the mass.

misconceptions.message: F = ma = 1500 × 2 = 3000 N. Dividing (1500 ÷ 2 = 750) is the slip; here you multiply.

bronze.hint: v = f × λ. Multiply frequency by wavelength.
bronze.display: A wave has a frequency of 500 Hz and a wavelength of 0.68 m. Calculate its speed.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(v = f\lambda\): speed equals frequency times wavelength.
Multiply.

guided_steps.done: Back to 500 Hz, so v = 340 m/s.
guided_steps.hint: Divide your speed by the wavelength.

misconceptions.message: v = f × λ = 500 × 0.68 = 340 m/s. Dividing (500 ÷ 0.68) gives about 735, but here you multiply.

bronze.hint: Rearrange v = fλ to f = v ÷ λ.
bronze.display: A water wave has a speed of 2 m/s and a wavelength of 0.5 m. Calculate its frequency.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(v = f\lambda\). We want frequency, so rearrange to \(f = v \div \lambda\).
Divide.

guided_steps.done: Back to 2 m/s, so f = 4 Hz.
guided_steps.hint: Multiply your frequency by the wavelength.

misconceptions.message: f = v ÷ λ = 2 ÷ 0.5 = 4 Hz. Multiplying (2 × 0.5 = 1) is the slip.

bronze.hint: a = F ÷ m. Divide force by mass.
bronze.display: A 10 N force accelerates a 2 kg object. Calculate the acceleration.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(F = ma\). We want acceleration, so \(a = F \div m\).
Divide.

guided_steps.done: Back to 10 N, so a = 5 m/s².

misconceptions.message: a = F ÷ m = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 m/s². Multiplying (10 × 2 = 20) is the slip.

bronze.hint: Period T = 1 ÷ frequency.
bronze.display: A wave has a frequency of 200 Hz. Calculate its period.

guided_steps.say: Period and frequency are reciprocals: \(T = 1 \div f\).
Divide 1 by the frequency.
guided_steps.hint: 1 shared into 200 equal parts is a small decimal.

guided_steps.done: Back to 200 Hz, so T = 0.005 s.

misconceptions.message: T = 1 ÷ f = 1 ÷ 200 = 0.005 s. Period and frequency are reciprocals; the answer is not 200.

bronze.hint: Newton's second law relates force, mass and acceleration.
bronze.display: Which equation links force, mass and acceleration?

misconceptions.message: Newton's second law: F = ma. p = mv is momentum, v = fλ is wave speed, W = mg is weight.

bronze.hint: Rearrange v = fλ to λ = v ÷ f.
bronze.display: A wave has a speed of 330 m/s and a frequency of 660 Hz. Calculate the wavelength.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(v = f\lambda\). We want wavelength, so \(\lambda = v \div f\).
Divide.

guided_steps.done: Back to 330 m/s, so λ = 0.5 m.

misconceptions.message: λ = v ÷ f = 330 ÷ 660 = 0.5 m. Dividing the wrong way (660 ÷ 330 = 2) is the slip.

silver.hint: Find the resultant force (driving minus friction) first, then a = F ÷ m.
silver.display: A car has a driving force of 3500 N and a friction force of 500 N. Its mass is 1200 kg. Calculate its acceleration.

guided_steps.say: First find the resultant force: driving force minus friction.
guided_steps.hint: Take the friction off the driving force.

guided_steps.say: Now \(a = F \div m\) with the resultant force.

guided_steps.done: Back to 3000 N, so a = 2.5 m/s².

misconceptions.message: Use the resultant force, not the driving force. Resultant = 3500 − 500 = 3000 N, so a = 3000 ÷ 1200 = 2.5 m/s². Using 3500 N gives about 2.92.
Divide the resultant by the mass: a = 3000 ÷ 1200 = 2.5 m/s², not 1200 ÷ 3000.

silver.hint: Convert to Hz and metres first, then v = f × λ.
silver.display: A sound wave has a frequency of 2 kHz and a wavelength of 17 cm. Calculate the speed of sound.

guided_steps.say: Convert to base units first. \(v = f\lambda\) needs hertz and metres.
Now multiply.

guided_steps.done: Back to 2000 Hz, so v = 340 m/s.
guided_steps.hint: Divide your speed by the wavelength.

misconceptions.message: Convert 17 cm to 0.17 m first. v = 2000 × 0.17 = 340 m/s. Leaving it as 17 gives 34000.

silver.hint: Convert grams to kg, subtract friction for the resultant, then a = F ÷ m.
silver.display: A 500 g toy car is pushed with a force of 4 N. Friction is 2 N. Calculate its acceleration.

guided_steps.say: Convert the mass, then find the resultant force.

guided_steps.hint: Take the friction off the push.

guided_steps.say: Now \(a = F \div m\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 2 N, so a = 4 m/s².

misconceptions.message: Convert 500 g to 0.5 kg. Resultant = 4 − 2 = 2 N, so a = 2 ÷ 0.5 = 4 m/s². Using 500 kg gives 0.004.
Subtract friction first: resultant = 4 − 2 = 2 N, then a = 2 ÷ 0.5 = 4 m/s². Using 4 N gives 8.

silver.hint: Rearrange p = mv to v = p ÷ m.
silver.display: A moving object of mass 4 kg has a momentum of 20 kg m/s. Calculate its velocity.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(p = mv\). We want velocity, so \(v = p \div m\).
Divide.

guided_steps.done: Back to 20 kg m/s, so v = 5 m/s.

misconceptions.message: v = p ÷ m = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 m/s. Multiplying (20 × 4 = 80) is the slip.

silver.hint: Convert GHz to Hz (× 10⁹), then λ = v ÷ f.
silver.display: A microwave has a frequency of 2.45 GHz. The speed of EM waves is \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s. Calculate the wavelength. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

guided_steps.pre: GHz means giga-hertz, and 'giga' means × 10⁹ (a billion). So 2.45 GHz = 2.45 × 10ⁿ Hz. The power n =
guided_steps.say: The equation is \(v = f\lambda\). We want wavelength, so \(\lambda = v \div f\). First convert GHz.
guided_steps.hint: Giga means times a thousand million, 10⁹.

guided_steps.pre: When you divide powers of ten, subtract the powers: 10⁸ ÷ 10⁹, so n = 8 − 9 =
guided_steps.say: Now the powers of ten.

guided_steps.hint: Move the decimal one place left. To 2 d.p.

guided_steps.say: The wavelength is 0.12 m, about 12 cm.

misconceptions.message: 2.45 GHz = 2.45 × 10⁹ Hz. λ = v ÷ f = (3 × 10⁸) ÷ (2.45 × 10⁹) = 0.12 m. Dividing the other way gives about 8.2.

silver.hint: Find frequency (f = 1 ÷ T) first, then λ = v ÷ f.
silver.display: A wave has a period of 0.02 s. Calculate its frequency, then find the wavelength if the wave speed is 5 m/s.

guided_steps.say: Two steps. First frequency from the period: \(f = 1 \div T\).
Now the wavelength: \(\lambda = v \div f\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 5 m/s, so λ = 0.1 m.

silver.equation_hint: Given on equation sheet: \(T = \frac{1}{f}\), then \(v = f\lambda\)

misconceptions.message: f = 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50 Hz, then λ = 5 ÷ 50 = 0.1 m. Stopping at 50 gives the frequency, not the wavelength.

steps: Write the formula and count every atom, watching subscripts and brackets.
Add the Ar values to get Mr (Mr has no unit).
For amount, use moles = mass ÷ Mr, and rearrange it for mass or Mr.
State the answer with its unit: mol, g, or %.
method_card.title: Relative Formula Mass and Moles
method_card.content:
\(M_r\) is the sum of the \(A_r\) of every atom in the formula. A subscript multiplies the atom before it, and a bracket multiplies everything inside it.

Amount links to mass through \(\text{moles} = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{M_r}\), which rearranges to \(\text{mass} = \text{moles} \times M_r\) or \(M_r = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{moles}}\).

Percentage by mass of an element is \(\dfrac{\text{its mass in the formula}}{M_r} \times 100\).

steps: Percentage by mass: \(\dfrac{\text{mass of that element}}{M_r} \times 100\). Find \(M_r\) first, then the element's share, then × 100.
Finding Mr from a measurement: rearrange \(\text{moles} = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{M_r}\) to \(M_r = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{moles}}\).
Round only at the end, to the decimal places the question asks for.

steps: Mr: add one \(A_r\) for every atom in the formula. A small subscript multiplies the atom before it, so CO₂ has two oxygens.
Amount: \(\text{moles} = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{M_r}\), and rearranged \(\text{mass} = \text{moles} \times M_r\).
Mr has no unit. Moles are in mol and mass in g, so state the unit in your final answer.

Keep the unit with the final answer: mol or g.

method_card.title: Balancing Equations and Reacting Masses
method_card.content:
Reacting-mass questions use one fixed method. Start from a balanced equation: the numbers in front of each formula give the mole ratio, the bridge between substances. Do not confuse these coefficients with the small subscript numbers.

Given a mass, turn it into moles first (moles = mass ÷ \(M_r\)). Use the ratio to find moles of the target substance, then convert back to a mass with its own \(M_r\). Check whether the question wants conservation of mass (mass in = mass out) or a gas volume (moles × 24 dm³ at room conditions).

steps: With two given masses, find moles of each and use the ratio to see which runs out first. That is the limiting reactant.
Base the product amount on the limiting reactant only.
For a gas, volume = moles × 24 dm³. For a missing mass, use conservation: reactant mass in = product mass out.

steps: Count every bond: multiply each bond energy by how many of that bond there are.

ΔH = bonds broken − bonds made.

method_card.title: Bond Energy Calculations
method_card.content:
ΔH = bonds broken − bonds made. Breaking bonds takes energy in (endothermic); making bonds gives energy out (exothermic).

Count carefully: multiply each bond energy by the number of those bonds (4 C–H in CH₄, not 1). Add the reactant bonds for broken, the product bonds for made, then subtract.

A negative answer means energy is released overall (exothermic); a positive answer means energy is absorbed (endothermic).

steps: Big molecules mean many bonds: draw them out and count every C–H, C=C, C=O and O–H before you multiply.
If the equation shows more than one mole of fuel, find ΔH for the whole equation, then divide by the number of moles for a per-mole answer.
To compare fuels per gram, divide each energy change by the mass of that many moles (mass = moles × Mr).

steps: Every bond has an energy. Breaking a bond needs energy in; making a bond gives energy out.
Add all the bond energies in the reactants (bonds broken) and all in the products (bonds made). Multiply each by how many of that bond there are.
ΔH = bonds broken − bonds made. A negative answer means the reaction gives out energy (exothermic).

steps: Molecules can hold several of the same bond: CH₄ has 4 C–H bonds, 2H₂O has 4 O–H bonds. Multiply each bond energy by its count before adding.
If the question gives ΔH and one total, rearrange: made = broken − ΔH, or broken = ΔH + made.
Read the sign: negative ΔH is exothermic (energy out), positive ΔH is endothermic (energy in).

method_card.title: Rates from Graphs and Concentrations
method_card.content:
Rate of reaction measures how fast a quantity changes: rate = change in quantity ÷ time. The quantity may be gas volume (cm³), mass lost (g), or product made.

On a graph, a steeper curve means a faster reaction; a flat line means it has finished. Mean rate between two points is the change in height divided by the change in time.

Concentration = mass ÷ volume, with volume in dm³. 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³, so divide a cm³ volume by 1000 first.

steps: Rearrange for what is asked: volume = mass ÷ concentration, or mass = concentration × volume.
Convert between cm³ and dm³ as the final step (× 1000 or ÷ 1000).
For two-curve graphs, read the right line, then divide by the time interval.

steps.say: A bigger image does not mean a bigger cell. Work out each actual size (image ÷ magnification, images already in μm: 40 mm = 40,000 μm, 45 mm = 45,000 μm), then compare.

steps.pre: How many times longer is the printed bee than the real bee?

steps.say: That number, 6, is the magnification: how many times bigger the image is than the real thing. So \(\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{actual size}}\).
Cells are the tricky part: they are far smaller than a ruler's markings, so a real cell might be 0.05 mm while its image is 50 mm. Before you can divide, both sizes must be in the same unit.

steps.pre: There are how many μm (micrometres) in 1 mm?

steps.say: Convert first, then divide. That single habit is the whole lesson.

steps: Decide what you are finding: magnification, image size, or actual size.
Convert both sizes to the same unit before dividing.

method_card.title: Magnification and Unit Conversions
method_card.content:
Magnification links three quantities: \(\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{actual size}}\). You are given two and find the third.

The rule that saves most marks: both sizes must be in the same unit before you divide, so convert first. Going to a smaller unit (mm → μm → nm) multiply by 1000; going larger, divide by 1000.

Rearrange when needed: actual size = image ÷ magnification, image size = magnification × actual. Magnification has no unit.

steps: Multi-step questions chain a conversion with a calculation, or compare two cells.
To compare sizes fairly, work out each actual size first, then subtract or divide. Never compare image sizes directly.
For very small lengths, finish in standard form: one digit before the point, then the power of 10.
gold.title: Gold: two steps or a comparison

steps: Read off the image size and the actual size. Put both in the same unit first: mm to μm means multiply by 1000.
Divide: \(\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{actual size}}\).
Magnification has no unit; a length answer keeps its unit.

Convert units before or after so the answer is in the unit asked for.
Standard form: 1 μm = 10⁻⁶ m and 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m.

method_card.title: Punnett Squares and Genetic Probability
method_card.content:
A Punnett square shows the four equally likely allele combinations a child can inherit. A capital letter is a dominant allele (shown if present); a lowercase letter is recessive (shown only as two copies, like bb).

Homozygous means two identical alleles (BB or bb); heterozygous means two different (Bb), also called a carrier when the recessive allele causes a disorder. Bb and bB are the same genotype, so count them together. Read carefully whether the question wants a ratio, a fraction, or a percentage.

steps: Some crosses are not simple dominant and recessive. In codominance and incomplete dominance the heterozygote has its own phenotype (roan, pink), so count it separately.
Sex-linked alleles sit on the X chromosome; a son has only one X, so one recessive X allele already shows.
To work backwards, use a recessive child (double-recessive genotype) to pin down what alleles each parent must carry.

gold.hint: The no-dimples child must be dd, so each parent had a d to give while still showing dimples.
gold.display: A couple both have dimples (dominant trait, D). They have a child without dimples. What are the genotypes of both parents?

guided_steps.say: The child has NO dimples. Dimples (D) is dominant, so the no-dimples child must be the double-recessive genotype dd.

guided_steps.pre: How many capital D alleles does a dd child carry?
guided_steps.hint: A recessive trait shows only with two lowercase alleles.

guided_steps.say: So the child inherited one d from EACH parent. But both parents SHOW dimples, so each also carries a D. A parent with one D and one d is written Dd.

guided_steps.pre: How many d alleles must each dimpled parent carry to give a dd child?
guided_steps.hint: The child needs one d from each side.

guided_steps.pre: From Dd × Dd, how many of the four boxes are dd?
guided_steps.hint: Only the box taking d from both parents is dd.

guided_steps.pre: From DD × Dd, how many boxes could be dd?
guided_steps.done: Only Dd × Dd can give a dd child, so both parents are Dd (the third option).
guided_steps.hint: DD has no d to pass, so no box can be dd.

misconceptions.message: The child without dimples is dd, so inherited a d from each parent. Both parents show dimples, so each also has a D. Both must be Dd.
DD × DD can only give DD. DD × Dd cannot give dd. Only Dd × Dd can produce a dd child.

gold.hint: With incomplete dominance the RW heterozygote is pink; count the RW boxes.
gold.display: Red flower colour (R) is incompletely dominant with white (W). Heterozygous (RW) flowers are pink. If two pink flowers are crossed, what percentage of offspring will be pink?

guided_steps.say: RW × RW gives RR (red), RW (pink), RW (pink), WW (white). With incomplete dominance, RW shows as pink.

guided_steps.hint: Two boxes mix one R with one W.
Only the top-left box is RR.

guided_steps.done: 2 of 4 are pink, so 50% is right.

misconceptions.message: If you answered 25, you counted only one box. RW × RW gives RR, RW, RW, WW, so 2 of 4 are pink = 50%.
With incomplete dominance the heterozygote has a blend phenotype. RW × RW gives 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white.

gold.hint: Only the affected son (Xb Y) is colour-blind; the other three boxes have normal vision.
gold.display: Colour blindness is sex-linked and recessive, carried on the X chromosome. A carrier mother (Xb on one X) and a father with normal vision have children. What percentage of ALL their children would you expect to have normal colour vision?

guided_steps.say: The four children are: a normal-vision daughter, a carrier daughter, a normal-vision son, and a colour-blind son (Xb Y). Only that last son is affected.

guided_steps.pre: How many of the four children are colour-blind?
guided_steps.hint: Only the son who inherits Xb from his mother.

guided_steps.pre: How many have normal colour vision?
guided_steps.hint: Four children minus the one affected son.

guided_steps.done: 3 of 4 children have normal vision, so 75% is right.

misconceptions.message: If you answered 25, that is the colour-blind fraction. Three of the four children have normal vision, so 75%.
The father's Y chromosome carries no allele for this trait. Only the son who gets Xb from his mother is colour-blind.

gold.hint: A 3 to 1 ratio predicts 90 to 30; check how close 91 to 29 is.
gold.display: In a genetics experiment, 120 pea plants are produced from a monohybrid cross. 91 have round seeds and 29 have wrinkled seeds. What is the expected ratio, and does the actual data closely fit it?
options: Expected 3:1, and yes: 91:29 is about 3.1:1, which is close
Expected 1:1, and no: the data does not fit
Expected 3:1, but no: 91:29 is too far from 90:30
Expected 1:3, and yes: the data fits well

misconceptions.message: A 3:1 ratio predicts 90 round : 30 wrinkled. Actual is 91:29. 91 ÷ 29 is about 3.1:1, very close to 3:1.
Real data rarely matches predicted ratios exactly. 91:29 is close enough to 3:1 (predicted 90:30) to support the model.

gold.hint: Only the OO box gives type O; that is one box out of four.
gold.display: A man with blood type A (genotype AO) and a woman with blood type B (genotype BO) have children. What percentage of their children could have blood type O?

guided_steps.say: The father AO passes A or O. The mother BO passes B or O. The grid is AB, AO, BO, OO.

guided_steps.pre: How many boxes are OO (type O)?
guided_steps.hint: Only the box taking O from both parents.

guided_steps.pre: How many boxes are NOT type O?
guided_steps.hint: AB, AO and BO all carry an A or a B.

guided_steps.done: 1 of 4 is type O, so 25% is right.

misconceptions.message: If you answered 0, remember each parent carries a hidden O. AO × BO gives AB, AO, BO, OO, so the OO box is type O: 25%.
A and B are codominant with each other but both are dominant over O. Only OO gives type O blood.

gold.hint: Each pregnancy is independent, so the earlier children do not change the odds.
gold.display: Two parents who are both heterozygous (Ff) for cystic fibrosis already have 3 children, none affected. Out of every 4 children from this cross, how many would you expect to have cystic fibrosis?

guided_steps.say: Each pregnancy is independent, so the 3 healthy children already born do not change anything. Ff × Ff gives FF, Ff, Ff, ff.

guided_steps.pre: How many of the four boxes are ff (cystic fibrosis)?
guided_steps.hint: Only the ff box has the condition.

guided_steps.pre: How many are unaffected (FF or Ff)?
guided_steps.hint: Four boxes minus the one ff box.

guided_steps.done: 1 in 4, no matter how many healthy children came before.

misconceptions.message: If you answered 0, that is the gambler's fallacy. The 3 healthy children do not change the odds: Ff × Ff still expects 1 in 4 affected.
Previous children being unaffected does NOT raise or lower the chance for the next. It stays at 1 in 4.

bronze.hint: Build the 2 by 2 grid for Bb by Bb, then count how many BB, Bb and bb you get.

guided_steps.hint: Two boxes mix one B with one b.

guided_steps.say: So far 1 BB and 2 Bb. One box is left.

guided_steps.hint: The bottom-right box takes b from both parents.

guided_steps.done: That gives 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb, which is the first option.

misconceptions.message: Bb × Bb gives BB, Bb, Bb, bb, which is 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb.

bronze.hint: Only tt gives the short plant. Count how many of the four boxes are tt.
bronze.display: Tall pea plants (T) are dominant to short (t). If two heterozygous plants (Tt × Tt) are crossed, what fraction of offspring would you expect to be short?

misconceptions.message: Tt × Tt gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt. Only tt is short = 1 out of 4 = 1/4.

bronze.hint: Homozygous means two identical alleles; dominant means capital letters.
bronze.display: What is the genotype of an organism that is homozygous dominant for a trait represented by the letter A?

misconceptions.message: Homozygous = two identical alleles. Dominant = capital letter. So homozygous dominant = AA.

bronze.hint: One parent gives only B, the other gives only b, so every box is Bb.
bronze.display: A homozygous dominant parent (BB) is crossed with a homozygous recessive parent (bb). What percentage of offspring will be heterozygous (Bb)?

guided_steps.say: BB can only pass B. bb can only pass b. So every box mixes one B with one b.

guided_steps.pre: How many of the four boxes are Bb?
guided_steps.hint: Every box gets B from one parent and b from the other.

guided_steps.pre: How many boxes are BB or bb (homozygous)?
guided_steps.hint: Neither parent can give a matching pair.

guided_steps.pre: Check they total four: Bb (4) + others (0) =
guided_steps.done: All four offspring are Bb, so 100% heterozygous is right.

bronze.hint: Any box with at least one capital B shows the dominant phenotype.
bronze.display: In a Bb × Bb cross, how many out of 4 offspring would you expect to show the dominant phenotype?

guided_steps.say: Bb × Bb gives BB, Bb, Bb, bb. Any box with at least one B shows the dominant phenotype.

guided_steps.pre: How many boxes contain at least one B?
guided_steps.hint: BB, Bb and Bb all have a capital B.
Only the bb box shows the recessive phenotype.
Take the one recessive box away from four.

guided_steps.done: All four boxes accounted for, so 3 show the dominant phenotype.

misconceptions.message: If you answered 1, that is the recessive count. BB, Bb and Bb all show the dominant phenotype, so it is 3.

bronze.hint: A gamete carries just one allele from the pair, not both.
bronze.display: A parent with genotype Bb produces gametes. Which alleles can be in the gametes?

misconceptions.message: Each gamete gets one allele from each pair. A Bb parent makes gametes with either B or b, never both.

bronze.hint: Both parents can only pass b, so work out how many boxes are bb.
bronze.display: Two homozygous recessive parents (bb × bb) are crossed. How many out of 4 offspring will show the recessive phenotype?

guided_steps.say: Each parent is bb, so each parent can only pass a b allele.

guided_steps.pre: How many different alleles can a bb parent pass?
guided_steps.hint: Both of its alleles are b.

guided_steps.pre: So how many of the four boxes contain a capital B?
guided_steps.hint: Neither parent has a B to give.

guided_steps.done: Every offspring is bb, so all 4 show the recessive phenotype.

misconceptions.message: If you answered 1, you assumed a 3:1 cross. Here BOTH parents are bb, so every box is bb: all 4 show the recessive phenotype.

bronze.hint: Homozygous means BB or bb. Count both, not just one.
bronze.display: A Bb × Bb cross produces four offspring. What percentage of the offspring would you expect to be homozygous (either BB or bb)?

guided_steps.say: Bb × Bb gives BB, Bb, Bb, bb. Homozygous means two identical letters, so BB and bb both count.

guided_steps.hint: Only the top-left box is BB.
Only the bottom-right box is bb.
Add the BB and bb counts.

guided_steps.done: 2 of the 4 boxes are homozygous, so 50% is right.

misconceptions.message: If you answered 25, you counted only BB. Homozygous also includes bb, so BB + bb = 2 out of 4 = 50%.
Homozygous means two identical alleles, so both BB and bb count. 1 BB + 1 bb = 2 out of 4 = 50%.

silver.display: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (f). Two parents who are both carriers (Ff) have a child. What is the percentage chance that the child is a carrier but does NOT have cystic fibrosis?

guided_steps.say: Ff × Ff gives FF, Ff, Ff, ff. A carrier is Ff: two different alleles, but no disease.

guided_steps.hint: Two boxes mix one F with one f.
Only the ff box has the condition.

guided_steps.done: 2 of 4 are carriers, so 50% is right.

misconceptions.message: If you answered 75, you counted ff as well. A carrier is Ff only: 2 out of 4 = 50%.

silver.hint: Cross Bb with bb, then count how many boxes are bb.

guided_steps.say: Bb passes B or b. bb passes only b. So the grid is Bb, Bb, bb, bb.

guided_steps.hint: Two boxes take the B from the Bb parent.
Two boxes take the b from the Bb parent.
The bb boxes show the recessive phenotype.

guided_steps.done: 2 of 4 are recessive, so the answer is 2.

misconceptions.message: If you answered 1, you used a Bb × Bb ratio. Bb × bb gives Bb, Bb, bb, bb, so 2 boxes are recessive.

silver.hint: Cross Dd with dd and count how many boxes carry a D.
silver.display: Polydactyly is caused by a dominant allele (D). A father with polydactyly (Dd) and an unaffected mother (dd) have children. What is the probability of a child having polydactyly?

misconceptions.message: Dd × dd gives Dd, Dd, dd, dd. Two have polydactyly (Dd) = 2 out of 4 = 50% = 1 in 2.

silver.hint: Three out of four boxes show the dominant phenotype; scale that up to 200.
silver.display: If 200 offspring are produced from a Bb × Bb cross, how many would you expect to show the DOMINANT phenotype?

guided_steps.say: Bb × Bb gives BB, Bb, Bb, bb. Three of the four boxes show the dominant phenotype.

guided_steps.pre: How many of the four boxes show the dominant phenotype?
guided_steps.hint: Any box with at least one B.

guided_steps.pre: The 200 plants are shared equally between the 4 boxes, so each box stands for 200 ÷ 4 =

guided_steps.done: 150 of 200 show the dominant phenotype.
guided_steps.hint: Add the dominant and recessive totals.

misconceptions.message: If you answered 50, that is the recessive quarter. The dominant phenotype is 3 out of 4, so 3/4 of 200 = 150.

silver.hint: Half the boxes are non-rollers (rr); find half of 80.

guided_steps.hint: Two boxes take the r from the Rr parent.

guided_steps.hint: Split 80 equally between the four boxes.

guided_steps.done: 40 of 80 are non-rollers.

silver.hint: Half the children are carriers; find half of 20.
silver.display: Sickle cell trait is caused by allele S. A carrier (AS) and an unaffected person (AA) have 20 children. How many would you expect to be carriers (AS)?

guided_steps.say: The carrier AS passes A or S. The unaffected AA passes only A. The grid is AA, AA, AS, AS.

guided_steps.pre: How many of the four boxes are carriers (AS)?
guided_steps.hint: Two boxes take the S from the AS parent.

guided_steps.pre: The 20 children are shared equally between the 4 boxes, so each box stands for 20 ÷ 4 =
guided_steps.hint: Split 20 equally between the four boxes.

guided_steps.done: 10 of 20 are carriers.

steps.say: Two quick puzzles, no formulas, just common sense.

steps.pre: Five friends pool their pocket money: £4, £8, £6, £7, £5. Shared out equally, how much each? £

steps.pre: You earned £8 an hour. Your boss adds £2, so now £10. Out of your original £8, the £2 rise is what percentage?
steps.hint: £2 is a quarter of £8, and a quarter is 25%.

steps.say: That is percentage change: the rise divided by what you STARTED with, times 100. The original (£8) always goes on the bottom. Mean and percentage change are two of the three skills here; the third, estimating a population from quadrats, is just a mean scaled up.

steps: Decide which you need: a mean, a percentage change, or a population estimate.
Mean: add the values, then divide by how many there are (drop any anomaly if told to).
Percentage change: (new − original) ÷ original × 100. The original goes on the bottom.
Population: mean per quadrat × (total area ÷ quadrat area).
method_card.title: Sampling, Mean and Percentage Change
method_card.content:
Three calculations that recur across both Biology papers.

Mean: add every value, then divide by how many there are. Watch for an anomalous result (an outlier): the question may tell you to leave it out.

Percentage change: (new − original) ÷ original × 100. Always divide by the original. A negative answer is a decrease; an answer above 100% just means the value more than doubled.

Population estimate: find the mean count per quadrat, then scale up by (total area ÷ quadrat area). Keep the two divisions apart: count over quadrats for the mean, area over area for the scale.

steps: Two ideas in one question: often a mean (or two) followed by a percentage change, or a population built from a raw total.
Do each part in order and label your intermediate values so you feed the right number into the next step.
Read the data carefully: use the exact years or days named, and ignore distractor values.

gold.hint: Compare only the first and last years; ignore the middle.

guided_steps.say: The middle years are a distraction. Percentage change compares only 2020 (450) and 2025 (468).

guided_steps.pre: Divide the change by the original: 18 ÷ 450 =
Multiply by 100 to turn it into a percentage: 0.04 × 100 =

guided_steps.done: It matches the rise of 18, so 4% is right.

misconceptions.message: The question asks for the overall change from 2020 to 2025. Original = 450, final = 468. (468 − 450) ÷ 450 × 100 = 18 ÷ 450 × 100 = 4%.
Don't add the two separate percentage changes: just compare 2020 to 2025 directly: (468 − 450) ÷ 450 × 100 = 4%.

gold.hint: Find both means, then the percentage change between them.
gold.display: A student uses 0.5 m² quadrats to sample a 300 m² field. In 10 quadrats they find: 2, 4, 3, 1, 5, 3, 4, 2, 3, 3 dandelions. The same field is surveyed a month later with results: 5, 7, 6, 4, 8, 6, 5, 7, 6, 6. Calculate the percentage change in estimated population.

guided_steps.say: Population scales with the mean, so the percentage change in population equals the change in the mean. Find both means.

guided_steps.pre: Percentage change = (change in mean ÷ original mean) × 100 = (3 ÷ 3) × 100 =
guided_steps.hint: Divide by the original mean of 3, then ×100.

guided_steps.say: So the population rose by 100%: it doubled.

guided_steps.pre: Check: a doubling means the new mean is twice the old. 2 × 3 =
guided_steps.done: 6 is double 3, confirming a 100% increase.

gold.hint: Total over quadrats for the mean; area over area to scale up.

guided_steps.say: Two divisions, keep them apart: total count ÷ number of quadrats gives the mean; total area ÷ quadrat area gives the scale-up.

guided_steps.hint: Total plants over number of quadrats.

guided_steps.pre: Each quadrat covers 0.25 m². Divide the field area by the quadrat area to find how many fit: 750 ÷ 0.25 =
guided_steps.hint: Field area over quadrat area, not 750 ÷ 15.

guided_steps.pre: Check via density: plants per m² = 6 ÷ 0.25 =
guided_steps.hint: How many in a full square metre.

guided_steps.done: Same 18000 by a second route, so it is right.

misconceptions.message: Mean per quadrat = 90 ÷ 15 = 6. Quadrats in field = 750 ÷ 0.25 = 3000. Population = 6 × 3000 = 18,000.
Total area ÷ quadrat area = 750 ÷ 0.25 = 3000 (not 750 ÷ 15). Mean = 6. Population = 6 × 3000 = 18,000.

options: Student 1: more quadrats gives a more representative sample of the whole area
Student 2: larger quadrats cover more ground so the data is better

Random placement reduces bias, but increasing the number of quadrats improves reliability by making the mean more representative.

After excluding the anomaly, you have 4 values, not 5. Sum = 0.50, mean = 0.50 ÷ 4 = 0.125 mm.
